subjects.name: Mathematics
objectives: CO1: Provide a basic understanding of fundamental mathematical concepts such as sets, functions, matrix algebra, and discrete mathematics.
CO2: Enable students to use mathematical models and techniques to analyze and understand problems in computer science.
CO3: Demonstrate how mathematical principles give succinct abstraction of computer science problems and help analyze them efficiently.

syllabus.topics: Set Introduction, Objectives, Representation of Sets (Roster Method, Set Builder Method), Types of Sets (Null Set, Singleton Set, Finite Set, Infinite Set, Equal Set, Equivalent Set, Disjoint Set, Subset, Proper Subset, Power Set, Universal Set), Operation with Sets (Union, Intersection, Difference, Symmetric Difference), Universal Sets, Complement of a Set.
Logic Statement, Connectives, Basic Logic Operations (Conjunction, Disjunction, Negation), Logical Equivalence/Equivalent Statements, Tautologies, Contradictions.

Matrices Introduction, Types of Matrix (Row, Column, Rectangular, Square, Diagonal, Scalar, Unit, Null, Comparable, Equal), Scalar Multiplication, Negative of Matrix, Addition, Difference, Multiplication of Matrices, Transpose of a Matrix.
Progressions Introduction, Arithmetic Progression (A.P.), Sum of Finite number of quantities in A.P., Arithmetic Means, Geometric Progression (G.P.), Geometric Mean.

notes.title: Set Theory & Operations
notes.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Sets can be defined via Roster Method (listing elements) or Set-Builder Method (describing rules).
definitions: The set of all subsets of a given set A, denoted by P(A). If |A| = n, then |P(A)| = 2^n.
A Δ B = (A - B) ∪ (B - A), representing elements in either set A or set B, but not both.
exam_points: Number of subsets of a set with n elements is 2^n.
De Morgan's Laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

notes.title: Mathematical Logic & Truth Tables
notes.explanation: Mathematical logic analyzes formal statements using logical connectives: Conjunction (AND - ∧), Disjunction (OR - ∨), Negation (NOT - ¬).
definitions: A compound statement that is always true for all truth values of its component variables.
A compound statement that is always false for all truth values of its component variables.
notes.example: p ∨ ¬p is a Tautology, whereas p ∧ ¬p is a Contradiction.
exam_points: Two statements are logically equivalent if they have identical truth values in all rows of a truth table.

notes.title: Matrix Algebra
notes.explanation: Matrices structure rectangular arrays of numbers across rows and columns. Matrix multiplication A × B is valid only when columns in A equal rows in B.
definitions: Formed by interchanging rows and columns of matrix A, denoted as A^T or A'.
notes.example: If A is of order 2×3 and B is of order 3×2, then matrix product AB is valid and yields order 2×2.
exam_points: Matrix multiplication is non-commutative: AB ≠ BA in general.
(AB)^T = B^T A^T.

notes.title: Progressions (A.P. & G.P.)
notes.explanation: An Arithmetic Progression (A.P.) increases or decreases by a constant common difference d. A Geometric Progression (G.P.) multiplies terms by a constant common ratio r.
definitions: For two numbers a and b, A.M. = (a + b) / 2.
For two positive numbers a and b, G.M. = √(a * b).
notes.example: A.P. nth term T_n = a + (n - 1)d; Sum S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]. G.P. nth term T_n = a * r^(n-1).
exam_points: For any two unequal positive real numbers, A.M. > G.M.

questions: State and prove De Morgan's Laws using set theory operations.
If set A has 5 elements, calculate the total number of elements in its Power Set P(A).
Construct a truth table to prove that (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p ≡ ¬p ∧ q.
Define Tautology and Contradiction. Verify whether (p ∧ (p → q)) → q is a tautology.
Given matrices A and B, find AB and BA and demonstrate that matrix multiplication is non-commutative.
Explain various types of matrices with examples (Diagonal, Unit, Scalar, Null).
Find the sum of first n terms of an Arithmetic Progression whose first term is 'a' and common difference is 'd'.
Insert three Geometric Means between 2 and 32.

quiz.question: If a set A has 4 elements, how many elements does its Power Set P(A) contain?
quiz.explanation: Power Set cardinality is given by 2^n. For n = 4, 2^4 = 16.

quiz.question: A logical statement that is always true regardless of input truth values is called a:
quiz.explanation: A Tautology evaluates to true under all possible input interpretations.

quiz.question: For matrix product AB to be defined, if matrix A has dimension m × n, matrix B must have dimension:
quiz.explanation: The number of columns in the first matrix (n) must equal the number of rows in the second matrix.

quiz.question: What is the Geometric Mean (G.M.) between 4 and 16?

subjects.name: Problem Solving Techniques
objectives: CO1: Express the logical flow used in Programming.
CO2: Design algorithms for solving various real life problems.
CO3: Implement programs using C.
CO4: Choose the right data type and statements for programs.
CO5: Explain various concepts of C programming language.

syllabus.topics: Logic Development: Data Representation, Flowcharts, Problem Analysis, Decision Trees/Tables, Pseudocode, Algorithms. Fundamentals: Character set, Identifiers, Key Words, Data types, Constants, Variables, Expressions, Statements, Symbolic Constants. Operations and Expressions: Arithmetic, Unary, Relational, Logical, Assignment, Conditional Operators, Library functions.
Data Input and Output: Formatted & Unformatted I/O. Control Statements: While, Do–while, For statements, Nested loops, If–else, Switch, Break and Continue statements.

Functions: Brief overview, defining, accessing functions, passing arguments to functions, specifying argument data types, function prototypes, recursion. Arrays: Defining, processing arrays, passing arrays to a function, multi-dimensional arrays. Strings: String declaration, string functions, string manipulation. Storage Class: Automatic, external, static variables.

Structures & Unions: Defining and processing a structure, user-defined data types, structures and pointers, passing structures to functions, unions. Pointers: Understanding Pointers, Accessing Address of Variable, Declaration/Initialization, Accessing Variable through Pointer, Pointers and Arrays. File Handling: File Operations, Processing Data Files.

notes.title: Algorithms, Flowcharts & Identifiers
notes.explanation: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure to solve a computational problem. Flowcharts visually represent this flow using standard geometric symbols.
definitions: User-defined names assigned to variables, functions, and arrays in C programming.
A constant defined using preprocessor directives (e.g., #define PI 3.14159).
notes.example: Conditional Operator: max = (a > b) ? a : b;
exam_points: Keywords are reserved words (e.g., int, float, switch) and cannot be used as variable identifiers.
Unary operators operate on a single operand (e.g., ++, --, sizeof).

notes.title: Control Structures & I/O Functions
notes.explanation: Control structures govern program execution flow. Entry-controlled loops (for, while) test conditions before loop execution; exit-controlled loops (do-while) evaluate after at least one iteration.
definitions: Functions like printf() and scanf() that format data according to specified type conversion specifiers (%d, %f, %c).
notes.example: Switch statement handles multiway branching based on discrete integer or character constants.
exam_points: The break statement exits the innermost enclosing loop or switch block.
The continue statement skips remaining statements in the current loop iteration.

notes.title: Functions, Recursion & Storage Classes
notes.explanation: Functions modularize code. Recursion occurs when a function calls itself directly or indirectly, requiring a base termination condition.
definitions: Variables declared with 'static' preserve their assigned values across multiple function calls.
notes.example: Recursion Factorial: int fact(int n) { return (n <= 1) ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); }
exam_points: Automatic variables (auto) are local to their function block and lost upon exit.
Array index positions strictly start at zero in C.

notes.title: Pointers, Structures, Unions & Files
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory address locations of variables. Structures allow grouping heterogeneous data types into a single named entity, while Unions share common memory allocations.
definitions: A composite data type where all members share the same memory location, equal to the size of its largest member.
notes.example: Pointers: int x = 10; int *ptr = &x; printf("%d", *ptr); prints 10.
exam_points: Structure members are accessed using '.' (dot operator) or '->' (arrow operator for pointers).
File operations rely on FILE pointers using fopen(), fclose(), fread(), fwrite(), fprintf(), and fscanf().

questions: Draw a flowchart and write pseudocode to find the largest of three numbers.
Explain various types of C operators with precedence and associativity.
Differentiate between while loop and do-while loop with syntax and examples.
Explain formatted and unformatted I/O functions in C with examples.
Explain recursion with a C program to generate Fibonacci series.
Differentiate between call-by-value and call-by-reference argument passing.
Compare Structures and Unions in C based on memory layout and usage.
Write a C program to copy the content of one file into another file using file handling functions.

quiz.question: Which of the following loops guarantees execution of its body at least once?
quiz.explanation: do-while is an exit-controlled loop that tests its condition after executing the body once.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to obtain the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator '&' returns the memory address location of an operand.

quiz.question: How much memory is allocated to a Union containing an int (4 bytes), char (1 byte), and double (8 bytes)?
quiz.explanation: A Union allocates memory equal to the size of its largest member (double = 8 bytes).

quiz.question: Which variable storage class retains its value across function calls throughout program execution?
quiz.explanation: Static variables retain their assigned values between function calls.

notes.title: C Practical Implementation Tips
notes.explanation: C practicals emphasize compiling code, debugging syntax errors, validating edge test cases, and managing memory efficiently.
definitions: Functions like getchar(), putchar(), gets(), and puts() that process raw character data without format specifications.
notes.example: Reading string safely: fgets(str, sizeof(str), stdin);
exam_points: Always open files with proper mode checks (e.g., if (fp == NULL) handle error).

questions: Explain the difference between gets() and fgets() functions in C.
Demonstrate how memory is shared inside a Union compared to a Structure.

quiz.question: Which C library function is used to calculate string length without counting the null terminator?
quiz.explanation: strlen() returns string character count up to, but not including, '\0'.

subjects.name: Computer Architecture
objectives: CO1: Identify the various internal and peripheral components of computer system.
CO2: Categorize different number systems.
CO3: Outline the role of various components of computer system.
CO4: Identify micro-operations.
CO5: Comment on the design of Combinational & Sequential circuits.

syllabus.topics: Logic Gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR, NAND & NOR as Universal Gates, Logic Gates Applications. Boolean Algebra: Introduction, Theorems, Simplification of Boolean Expressions, SOP & POS Forms, Realization using Gates, K-Maps, Simplification using K-Maps.

Combinational Logic Circuits: Half Adder & Half Subtractor, Full Adder & Full Subtractor, Parallel Binary Adder, Binary Adder/Subtractor. Multiplexers & Demultiplexers, Implementation of Boolean equations using MUX and DEMUX, Encoders & Decoders.
Sequential Logic Circuits: Latch, Flip Flops (R-S, J-K, Master-Slave J-K, D, T Flip-Flops), Race Around Condition and Elimination, Applications of Flip-Flops.

Introduction to Computer Organization: Computer and CPU, Stored Program Concept (Von Neumann vs Harvard Architecture), RISC and CISC Architecture. Register Transfer & Micro-operations: Registers, Instruction Formats, Types of Instructions (Memory Reference, Register Reference, I/O Instructions). Common Bus System: Address, Data, Control Buses (16-bit).

notes.title: Universal Gates & K-Maps
notes.explanation: NAND and NOR gates are universal because any Boolean logic function can be synthesized using exclusively NAND or exclusively NOR gates.
definitions: A graphical method for simplifying Boolean expressions into minimal Sum of Products (SOP) or Product of Sums (POS) forms.
notes.example: De Morgan's Theorem: (A + B)' = A' · B' and (A · B)' = A' + B'.
exam_points: NAND gate produces 0 output only when all inputs are 1.
Gray code ordering is mandatory in adjacent cells of K-Maps to ensure single-bit changes.

notes.title: Combinational Logic Circuits
notes.explanation: Combinational logic circuit outputs depend solely on present inputs. Key examples include Adders, Subtractors, Multiplexers, and Decoders.
definitions: A digital data selector that routes one of 2^n input lines to a single output line using n select lines.
notes.example: Full Adder equations: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in; Carry = AB + BC_in + AC_in.
exam_points: A Decoder with n input lines can generate up to 2^n minterms.

notes.title: Sequential Circuits & Flip-Flops
notes.explanation: Sequential logic outputs depend on present inputs and past output states stored in memory elements (Flip-Flops).
definitions: Occurs in J-K Flip-Flops when J=1, K=1, and clock pulse width exceeds logic propagation delay, causing rapid toggling.
notes.example: Master-Slave J-K Flip-Flop resolves Race-Around using two flip-flops triggered on opposite clock edges.
exam_points: D Flip-Flop acts as a delay or data storage element (Output Q = Input D).
T Flip-Flop acts as a toggle switch when T = 1.

notes.title: Computer Organization & Architectures
notes.explanation: Computer organization governs hardware interconnections. Von Neumann architecture uses unified memory for instructions and data; Harvard architecture uses separated memory channels.
definitions: RISC uses reduced simple instructions executed in single clock cycles; CISC uses complex multi-cycle instructions.
notes.example: Common bus systems route Address, Data, and Control signals across CPU components.
exam_points: Instruction Cycle consists of Fetch, Decode, and Execute phases.
Register-reference instructions require no memory access.

questions: Prove that NAND is a Universal Gate by implementing AND, OR, and NOT functions using NAND gates.
Minimize the Boolean expression F(A,B,C,D) = ∑m(0,1,2,5,8,9,10,11,14,15) using K-Map.
Design a Full Adder logic circuit using Half Adders and basic gates.
Explain the working of an 8:1 Multiplexer with truth table and logic diagram.
Explain Race-Around condition in J-K Flip-Flop and how Master-Slave J-K Flip-Flop eliminates it.
Differentiate between Combinational and Sequential logic circuits.
Compare Von Neumann and Harvard Computer Architectures.
Explain RISC vs CISC computer architectures with characteristics.

quiz.question: Which digital logic gate acts as a Universal Gate?
quiz.explanation: NAND (and NOR) gates can synthesize all standard Boolean operations.

quiz.question: How many select lines are required for a 16-to-1 Multiplexer (16:1 MUX)?
quiz.explanation: A MUX with 2^n inputs requires n select lines. For 16 inputs, 2^4 = 16, so 4 select lines are required.

quiz.question: Which Flip-Flop condition occurs when J=1 and K=1 with clock high?
quiz.explanation: Setting J=1 and K=1 causes the output state to Toggle.

quiz.question: Which architecture uses unified physical memory for storing both data and program instructions?
quiz.explanation: Von Neumann architecture features a shared memory system for data and instructions.

subjects.name: Office Automation

Web Browser Configuration, Search Engine Operators, Email setup & management, Online Banking basics, Digital payments, Blogs.

notes.title: Mail Merge & VLOOKUP
notes.explanation: Mail Merge automates mass customized letter or email creation. VLOOKUP searches for specific column values in spreadsheet tables.
definitions: Cell reference anchored using dollar signs ($A$1) that remains fixed during formula copying.
notes.example: VLOOKUP syntax: =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])
exam_points: Pivot Tables aggregate, summarize, and explore complex tabular datasets.

questions: Explain Mail Merge process in Word step-by-step.
Differentiate between Relative, Absolute, and Mixed cell referencing in Excel.

quiz.question: Which Excel formula function searches vertically for a matching key in the first column of a table array?
quiz.explanation: VLOOKUP searches for a specified key down the left-most column of a table array.

objectives: 1. Provide learning environment to practice listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills.
2. Assist students to carry on tasks through guided instructions and materials.
3. Effectively integrate English language learning with employability skills.
4. Provide hands-on experience through case studies, mini-projects, group/individual presentations.

syllabus.topics: Word Formation, Foreign Root words in English, Prefixes and Suffixes, Synonyms, Antonyms, Standard Abbreviations.
Sentence Structures, Phrases and Clauses, Proper Punctuation, Coherence, Paragraph Organization, Precise Writing Techniques.
Subject-Verb Agreement, Noun-Pronoun Agreement, Misplaced Modifiers, Articles, Prepositions, Redundancies.

syllabus.unit: Unit-IV: Nature and Style of Sensible Writing
syllabus.topics: Describing, Defining, Classifying, Providing Evidence, Writing Introductions/Conclusions, Comprehension, Précis Writing, Essay Writing.
Listening Comprehension, Pronunciation, Intonation, Stress and Rhythm, Workplace Communication, Conversations, Interviews, Formal Presentations (Language Lab).

notes.title: Subject-Verb Agreement & Précis
notes.explanation: Subjects and verbs must agree in number (singular/plural). Précis writing involves summarizing a passage clearly in approximately one-third of its original length.
definitions: A concise, clear summary of a longer text preserving its essential meaning and key logic.
notes.example: Incorrect: Either the students or the teacher are present. Correct: Either the students or the teacher is present.
exam_points: A précis should strictly be written in third person and in continuous narrative form.

questions: Explain Subject-Verb agreement rules with five distinct example sentences.
What are misplaced modifiers? Explain with corrective examples.

quiz.question: What is the recommended length of a written Précis relative to its original passage length?
quiz.explanation: A précis should summarize original text to roughly one-third of its total word count.

subjects.name: Indian Knowledge System
objectives: Provide foundational exposure to traditional Indian knowledge systems, science, philosophy, health, and literature.

syllabus.topics: Indian Culture and Civilization, Indian Vision for Human Society, Indian Science, Indian Town Planning and Architecture, Indian Mathematics and Astronomy, Indian Aesthetics, Indian Health, Wellness and Ayurveda.

notes.title: Traditions & Scientific Heritage
notes.explanation: Explores ancient Indian contributions to mathematics, astronomy, architecture, and holistic health systems like Ayurveda.
definitions: Traditional Indian system of medicine focusing on holistic bodily and mental well-being.
notes.example: Vedic mathematics algorithms and ancient town planning structures in Indus Valley Civilization.
exam_points: Covers classical Indian astronomy, geometry, and philosophy.

questions: Discuss the significance of ancient Indian mathematics and astronomy.
Explain the core principles of holistic health and wellness in Ayurveda.

quiz.question: Which ancient Indian system focuses on holistic health and herbal medicine?
quiz.explanation: Ayurveda is the traditional Indian system of medicine and natural healing.

subjects.name: Environmental Science and Sustainability
objectives: 1. Familiarize students with basic environmental concepts, business operational impacts, and sustainability challenges.
2. Equip students to make decisions considering environmental consequences.
3. Enable future business graduates to become environmentally sensitive, responsible managers.

syllabus.topics: Environment, Natural Resources, and Sustainability: Components and segments of environment, Man-environment relationship, Sustainability concept, Conservation of resources (deforestation, water conservation, energy/food security), Inter/Intra-generational equity.

Ecosystems, Biodiversity, and Sustainable Practices: Ecosystem structures & functions, Biodiversity significance & threats, Homeostasis, Carrying capacity, In-situ and Ex-situ conservation, India as a Mega-diverse nation.

Environmental Pollution, Waste Management, Sustainable Development: Air, Water, Noise, Soil, Marine pollution, Climate change, Greenhouse effect, Ozone depletion, Cleaner technologies, Solid waste management, Disaster management.

Social Issues, Legislation, Practical Applications: Environmental Ethics, Water Act 1974, Environment Protection Act 1986, Air Act 1981, Environmental refugees, Ecological economics, Population demographics.

notes.title: Environment, Natural Resources & Sustainability Concepts
notes.explanation: The environment consists of biotic and abiotic components spanning the Atmosphere, Hydrosphere, Lithosphere, and Biosphere. Human interactions have evolved from survival-based consumption to heavy industrial exploitation, necessitating sustainable resource management and equitable access across present and future generations.
definitions: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The moral and ethical obligation to preserve natural resources and environmental quality for future generations.
Fair and equitable distribution of resources and environmental benefits/burdens among different groups within the present generation.
notes.example: Implementing rainwater harvesting and renewable energy transition to ensure long-term water and energy security.
exam_points: Distinguish between Inter-generational and Intra-generational equity.
Highlight the transition of the man-environment relationship from pre-industrial to modern times.
List key strategies for conserving food, water, and energy resources.

notes.title: Ecosystem Dynamics & Biodiversity Conservation
notes.explanation: Ecosystems function through energy flow and nutrient cycling, maintaining internal equilibrium via homeostasis. Biodiversity protection involves in-situ mechanisms (protecting natural habitats) and ex-situ mechanisms (preserving species outside natural habitats).
definitions: The maximum population size of a species that an ecosystem can sustainably support without undergoing resource degradation.
The dynamic balance and self-regulating capacity of an ecosystem to resist external disturbances.
The conservation of genetic resources and species within their natural habitats (e.g., National Parks, Sanctuaries).
The preservation of components of biological diversity outside their natural habitats (e.g., Botanical Gardens, Seed Banks).
notes.example: Project Tiger operates as an in-situ conservation initiative in designated Tiger Reserves across India.
exam_points: In-situ conservation protects species directly in their natural habitats.
Ex-situ conservation acts as a backup for critically endangered species using botanical gardens and gene banks.
India is recognized as one of the 17 mega-diverse countries due to high species richness and endemic biodiversity hotspots.

notes.title: Environmental Pollution, Climate Change & Waste Management
notes.explanation: Anthropogenic activities generate air, water, soil, noise, and marine pollution. Global challenges like climate change, global warming driven by greenhouse gases, and ozone layer depletion require clean technologies, waste reduction, and disaster preparedness.
definitions: The warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere caused by atmospheric gases (CO2, CH4, N2O) trapping heat radiation.
Industrial processes and technologies designed to minimize waste output, reduce energy consumption, and lower environmental footprint.
The systematic control of generation, storage, collection, transport, processing, and disposal of solid waste.
notes.example: Municipal bio-composting and sanitary landfilling system for solid waste management.
exam_points: Identify major greenhouse gases and explain their mechanism in global climate change.
Compare municipal solid waste processing methods: composting vs. incineration vs. landfilling.
Outline the primary steps of the disaster management cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery.

notes.title: Environmental Ethics, Legislation & Socio-Economic Dimensions
notes.explanation: Legal frameworks provide mandatory standards for pollution control and environmental protection in India. Social issues such as environmental migration, population growth pressures, and ecological economics shape corporate and public policy.
definitions: The branch of philosophy that considers the moral relationship of human beings to the environment and non-human entities.
People displaced from their habitats due to severe environmental degradation, natural disasters, or climate change impact.
An interdisciplinary field linking ecological systems with economic systems to account for natural capital and ecosystem services.
notes.example: The Environment Protection Act of 1986 serves as an umbrella framework for environmental protection and regulatory coordination in India.
exam_points: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 establishes Central and State Pollution Control Boards.
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 regulates air emissions and standards.
Environment Protection Act, 1986 empowers the Central Government to take all necessary measures to protect environmental quality.

questions: Define sustainability and explain the key differences between inter-generational and intra-generational equity.
Discuss the major natural resource conservation challenges regarding water and energy security.
Analyze the evolution of the man-environment relationship and its impacts on modern eco-systems.
Differentiate between In-situ and Ex-situ biodiversity conservation with suitable examples.
Explain the concepts of ecosystem homeostasis and carrying capacity.
Discuss why India is designated as a Mega-diverse nation and outline major threats to its biodiversity.
Explain the Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming along with their impacts on global climate.
Discuss the causes, consequences, and global efforts surrounding stratospheric ozone layer depletion.
Describe the components of integrated Solid Waste Management and cleaner industrial technologies.
Elaborate on the salient features and objectives of the Environment Protection Act, 1986.
What is environmental ethics? Contrast anthropocentric and ecocentric worldviews.
Explain the concept of ecological economics and discuss the issues faced by environmental refugees.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of Ex-Situ biodiversity conservation?
quiz.explanation: Botanical gardens preserve organisms outside their natural habitats (Ex-situ).

quiz.question: Which Indian Act acts as an umbrella legislation for environmental protection?
quiz.explanation: The Environment Protection Act 1986 provides an umbrella framework for broad regulatory oversight.

quiz.question: Which gas is primarily responsible for stratospheric ozone layer depletion?
quiz.explanation: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere, which break down ozone molecules.

quiz.question: Which Indian environmental legislation serves as an umbrella framework empowering the government to coordinate pollution control agencies?
options: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
quiz.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act of 1986 serves as an umbrella act to bridge gaps in previous environmental laws and coordinate regulatory action.

quiz.question: The maximum population size of a species that an ecosystem can sustainably support without degrading is called:
quiz.explanation: Carrying Capacity is the maximum threshold of individuals an ecosystem can maintain without suffering resource depletion.

subjects.name: Human Values, De-addiction and Traffic Rules

2. Facilitate development of a Holistic perspective towards life, profession, and happiness based on human reality.
3. Highlight implications of holistic understanding in ethical human conduct and nature interactions.

syllabus.topics: Course Introduction: Need, Basic Guidelines, Content & Process for Value Education. Self-Exploration, Natural Acceptance, Experiential Validation, Continuous Happiness & Prosperity, Right Understanding, Relationship & Physical Facilities.
Harmony in Human Being: Co-existence of sentient 'I' and material 'Body', Needs of Self ('I' - Sukh) and Body ('Suvidha'), Sanyam and Swasthya.
Harmony in Family & Society: Nyaya, Trust (Vishwas), Respect (Samman), Undivided Society (Akhand Samaj), Universal Order (Sarvabhaum Vyawastha).
Harmony in Nature & Existence: Four orders of nature, Recyclability, Self-regulation, Co-existence (Sah-astitva).
Implications on Professional Ethics: Ethical Human Conduct, Humanistic Education, Competence in professional ethics, People-friendly & eco-friendly production systems.

notes.title: Need, Guidelines & Process of Value Education
notes.explanation: Value Education enables humans to live with continuous happiness and prosperity by establishing Right Understanding. The process relies on Self-Exploration through Natural Acceptance and Experiential Validation rather than external dogmas or belief systems.
definitions: The intrinsic, invariant human capability to evaluate what is naturally right, leading to unconditional internal harmony.
The process of observing internally, verifying proposals on the basis of natural acceptance, and validating them through living.
Clear and holistic understanding of harmony at all four levels: Self, Family/Society, Nature, and Existence.
notes.example: Prioritizing trust and respect in relationships (Right Relationship) over accumulating excessive physical possessions (Suvidha).
exam_points: Value Education requires universal, rational, natural, and verifiable guidelines.
Physical facilities are necessary for the Body, but Right Understanding and Right Relationships are essential for the Self ('I').
Happiness is living in state of harmony; Unhappiness is living in disharmony/contradiction.

notes.title: Harmony in Human Being ('I' & Body) and Health/De-addiction
notes.explanation: A human being is a co-existence of the sentient Self ('I') and the material Body. 'I' is conscious and seeks qualitative fulfillment like happiness (Sukh), while the Body is physico-chemical and needs quantitative facilities (Suvidha). Sanyam (Self-regulation) ensures Swasthya (Health of the Body), which is severely disrupted by substance addiction.
definitions: The feeling of responsibility in 'I' for the nurturing, protection, and right utilization of the Body.
The state where the body acts according to 'I' and body parts are in harmony with each other.
The systematic psychological and physiological process of overcoming substance dependency to restore physical health and mental clarity.
notes.example: Eating nutritious food to nurture the body represents right utilization through Sanyam, whereas substance abuse destroys physical health and mental control.
exam_points: Needs of 'I' (Happiness, Respect) are continuous and qualitative.
Needs of Body (Food, Clothing) are temporary and quantitative.
Sanyam is the foundation for lasting Swasthya (Health).

notes.title: Harmony in Family & Society (Akhand Samaj & Universal Order)
notes.explanation: Family is the foundational unit of human interaction. Harmony in family is achieved through Justice (Nyaya), which is rooted in foundational values such as Trust (Vishwas) and Respect (Samman). Extending this harmony from family to society forms an Undivided Society (Akhand Samaj) and Universal Human Order (Sarvabhaum Vyawastha).
definitions: The foundational value in relationships; the clarity that the other person naturally intends my happiness and prosperity.
Right evaluation of the other person based on 'I' (Self) rather than physical features, wealth, or beliefs.
An Undivided Society free from discrimination based on caste, gender, creed, wealth, or nation.
notes.example: Evaluating individuals based on their character and natural acceptance rather than their social status or possessions.
exam_points: Trust (Vishwas) is the foundational value in relationships; Love (Prem) is the complete value.
Differentiate between Right Evaluation (Respect), Over-evaluation, Under-evaluation, and Otherwise-evaluation.
The expansion of harmony flows: Individual -> Family -> Society -> Nature -> Existence.

notes.title: Harmony in Nature & Existence (Co-Existence / Sah-astitva)
notes.explanation: Nature consists of four interrelated orders: Material, Bio/Plant, Animal, and Human Order. While the first three orders exist in natural balance, self-regulation, and recyclability, the Human Order must develop Right Understanding to live in mutual fulfillment and Co-existence (Sah-astitva).
definitions: The state of existence where all units exist harmoniously together in space, being mutually fulfilling to each other.
Interactions among units of nature where each unit enriches and sustains the other.
notes.example: Plants enrich soil and produce oxygen for animals, demonstrating natural recyclability and mutual fulfillment.
exam_points: Recall the four orders of nature: Material (Padartha Awastha), Bio (Prana Awastha), Animal (Jana Awastha), and Human (Gyana Awastha).
Explain how the first three orders are mutually fulfilling while humans currently disrupt ecological balance due to lack of understanding.
Space is all-pervading, calm, and equilibrium; units are active, limited, and submerged in space.

notes.title: Professional Ethics, Production Systems & Traffic Rules
notes.explanation: Holistic understanding guides Ethical Human Conduct in professional life, promoting people-friendly and eco-friendly technologies. It incorporates social responsibility, adherence to traffic regulations for civic safety, and active prevention of addictions in work environments.
definitions: Behavior driven by right understanding that ensures mutual happiness with humans and mutual prosperity with nature.
Regulatory, warning, and legal frameworks governing road usage to prevent accidents and safeguard human life.
notes.example: Using zero-waste eco-friendly manufacturing processes alongside strict adherence to road safety norms like wearing helmets and avoiding DUI (Driving Under Influence).
exam_points: Characteristics of ethical professional conduct: competence, ethical decision-making, and sustainable technology design.
Core categories of traffic signs: Mandatory/Regulatory, Cautionary/Warning, and Informational.
Social and economic impacts of addiction on workplace productivity and traffic safety.

questions: Explain the process of Self-Exploration with a neat block diagram.
Differentiate between the needs of the Self ('I') and the needs of the 'Body' in terms of time, quantity, and nature.
Critically examine the current scenario where physical facilities are prioritized over relationships and right understanding.
What is Sanyam? How does it lead to Swasthya (health of the body)?
Discuss the physical, psychological, and social impacts of substance addiction and the steps required for effective de-addiction.
Explain how the activities of 'I' (Desiring, Thinking, Expecting) differ from the activities of the Body.
Define Trust (Vishwas). Distinguish between intention and competence with a suitable example.
What is Respect (Samman)? How do we differentiate between Right Evaluation and Discrimination?
Explain the concept of Akhand Samaj (Undivided Society) and how harmony expands from family to universal order.
List and explain the four orders of nature along with their key attributes and natural characteristics.
Explain the concept of Co-existence (Sah-astitva) in existence with reference to units submerged in space.
Discuss the recyclability and self-regulation present in nature.
What is Ethical Human Conduct? How can professional competence be integrated with human values?
Explain the critical necessity of traffic rules, mandatory road signs, and safe driving etiquette.
Describe eco-friendly and people-friendly production systems in modern technology practice.

quiz.question: According to Value Education, what is the fundamental nature of the needs of the Self ('I') compared to the needs of the Body?
options: Both 'I' and Body needs are continuous and quantitative.
'I' needs are continuous & qualitative (e.g., Happiness); Body needs are temporary & quantitative (e.g., Food).
'I' needs are temporary & physical; Body needs are continuous & emotional.
Both 'I' and Body needs are temporary and material.
quiz.explanation: The Self ('I') requires qualitative, continuous fulfillment such as respect, trust, and happiness (Sukh). The Body requires physical, quantitative facilities (Suvidha) like food or shelter.

quiz.question: The feeling of responsibility in the Self ('I') for the nurturing, protection, and right utilization of the Body is called:
quiz.explanation: Sanyam (Self-regulation) is the internal feeling of responsibility toward the body, which leads to Swasthya (Health).

quiz.question: What is considered the foundational value (Mool Moolya) in human-to-human relationships?
quiz.explanation: Trust (Vishwas)—the assurance that the other person naturally intends your happiness and prosperity—is the foundational value. Love (Prem) is the complete value.

quiz.question: Which order of nature possesses the characteristic of 'Gyana Awastha' (Knowledge Order)?
quiz.explanation: Human beings constitute the Knowledge/Gyana Order, possessing the potential for right understanding and self-exploration.

quiz.question: Mandatory traffic signs that indicate laws and prohibitions (e.g., Stop, No Entry) are typically rendered in which geometric shape?
quiz.explanation: Mandatory or regulatory traffic signs are generally circular (with exceptions like the octagonal STOP sign), cautionary signs are triangular, and informatory signs are rectangular.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Statistics, Collection and Presentation of Data, Measures of Central Tendency: Mean, Median, Mode, Geometric Mean, Harmonic Mean.
Measures of Dispersion: Range, Quartile Deviation, Mean Deviation, Standard Deviation, Variance, Coefficient of Variation.
Correlation Analysis: Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation, Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient.
Regression Analysis: Regression Lines, Regression Equations, Linear Regression, Probability Foundations.

notes.title: Introduction to Statistics & Data Collection
notes.explanation: Statistics involves collecting, organizing, presenting, and analyzing data. Data is collected via primary or secondary sources and summarized using tabular or graphical presentations.
definitions: Data collected directly from first-hand sources by the investigator for a specific research purpose.
Pre-existing data gathered from secondary publications, census reports, or public records.
notes.example: Conducting a door-to-door survey yields primary data, whereas analyzing government census reports uses secondary data.
exam_points: Distinguish between primary and secondary data collection techniques.
Explain direct personal observation vs. indirect oral investigation.

notes.title: Measures of Dispersion & Variability
notes.explanation: Dispersion measures the extent of scatter or variation of data points around their central value. Range, Quartile Deviation, Mean Deviation, Standard Deviation, and Variance quantify data spread.
definitions: Square root of the arithmetic mean of squared deviations from the mean value.
A relative measure of dispersion defined as (Standard Deviation / Mean) * 100, used to compare consistency between datasets.
notes.example: Variance = (Standard Deviation)^2. A lower Coefficient of Variation indicates higher data consistency.
exam_points: Standard deviation is unaffected by shift of origin but affected by change of scale.
Coefficient of Variation allows direct comparison between two series with different units.

notes.title: Correlation Analysis
notes.explanation: Correlation analyzes the strength and direction of linear relationships between two variables using Karl Pearson's coefficient (parametric) and Spearman's rank correlation (non-parametric).
definitions: A quantitative measure of degree and direction of linear relationship between two variables, bounded between -1 and +1.
A measure assessing monotonicity between ranked variables: R = 1 - (6 * Sum(d^2)) / (n * (n^2 - 1)).
notes.example: If r = +0.95, a strong positive linear correlation exists between the two variables.
exam_points: Karl Pearson correlation values range strictly between -1 and +1.
Spearman's correlation handles qualitative rank data like beauty, intelligence, or preferences.

notes.title: Regression Analysis & Probability Basics
notes.explanation: Regression analysis estimates the mathematical relationship between dependent and independent variables using least-squares lines. Probability provides the fundamental framework for statistical inference.
definitions: The line of best fit minimizing the sum of squared vertical/horizontal errors between observed points and predicted values.
Slopes of regression lines: b_yx represents change in Y per unit change in X. The geometric mean of b_yx and b_xy equals r.
notes.example: Regression equation of Y on X: (Y - Mean_Y) = b_yx * (X - Mean_X).
exam_points: The product of the two regression coefficients equals the square of the correlation coefficient: r^2 = b_yx * b_xy.
If one regression coefficient is greater than 1, the other must be less than 1.

questions: Define Measures of Central Tendency and derive the empirical relationship between Mean, Median, and Mode.
Calculate Arithmetic Mean, Geometric Mean, and Harmonic Mean for a given continuous frequency distribution.
Compare primary and secondary data collection methods, stating advantages and limitations of each.
Calculate Standard Deviation and Variance for a grouped frequency dataset.
Define Coefficient of Variation and explain how it evaluates relative consistency between two factory production lines.
Differentiate between Quartile Deviation and Mean Deviation with respective mathematical formulas.
Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation between two dataset variables.
Explain Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient and compute rank correlation when ranks are tied.
Differentiate clearly between Correlation and Regression analysis.
Explain regression lines and derive regression equations of Y on X and X on Y using the principle of least squares.
State and prove important mathematical properties of regression coefficients.
Introduce basic concepts of probability, classical definition, and addition theorem of probability.

quiz.question: What is the empirical relationship between Mean, Median, and Mode for a moderately skewed distribution?
quiz.explanation: The empirical formula established by Karl Pearson states Mode = 3 * Median - 2 * Mean.

quiz.question: Which measure of central tendency is best suited for calculating average speed and velocity?
quiz.explanation: Harmonic Mean is the reciprocal mean ideal for rates, ratios, and speeds over equal distances.

quiz.question: The square root of Variance is equal to:
quiz.explanation: Standard Deviation is defined mathematically as the positive square root of Variance.

quiz.question: What is the theoretical range of Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient?
quiz.explanation: Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient r ranges strictly bounded between -1 and +1.

quiz.question: If the two regression coefficients are b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45, what is the correlation coefficient r?

syllabus.topics: Basic Concepts: Data Structures definitions, Abstract Data Types (ADT), Algorithm Complexity (Time and Space Big-O notation), Arrays, Sparse Matrices.
Stacks: Array implementation, Operations (Push, Pop, Peek), Infix to Postfix conversion, Postfix evaluation. Queues: Linear Queue, Circular Queue, Priority Queue, Deque.
Singly Linked Lists: Operations (Insertion, Deletion, Traversal), Circular Linked Lists, Doubly Linked Lists.
Searching & Sorting: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Linear & Binary Search.

notes.title: Data Structure Basics, ADTs & Asymptotic Notation
notes.explanation: Data structures organize data for efficient access and modification. Abstract Data Types define behavior independently of implementation. Algorithm efficiency is analyzed using Big-O time and space complexity.
definitions: A mathematical model for data structures specifying operations and behavior without dictating internal implementation.
A matrix in which the majority of elements are zero, efficiently represented using 3-tuple array representation.
notes.example: Representing a 100x100 matrix with only 10 non-zero values using 3-tuple (Row, Column, Value) format saves memory.
exam_points: Big-O measures upper bound worst-case algorithm time complexity.
Row-major vs Column-major memory address calculation formulas for 2D arrays.

notes.title: Stacks & Queues
notes.explanation: Stacks operate on Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order, while Queues follow First-In-First-Out (FIFO) access patterns. Circular queues solve memory wastage issues seen in linear array-based queues.
definitions: Last In First Out ordering where elements inserted last are popped first.
A queue implementation where the last position connects back to the first position to reuse deallocated space.
notes.example: Stack application: Function call management, undo mechanisms, and expression parsing.
exam_points: Circular queues eliminate memory wastage present in linear array queues by computing (rear + 1) % MAX.
Evaluating postfix expressions uses a stack to store operands and perform operations on top values.

notes.title: Linked Lists (Singly, Doubly, Circular)
notes.explanation: Linked lists consist of dynamic nodes holding data and pointers to subsequent nodes, facilitating efficient memory allocation and O(1) insertions/deletions at known pointers.
definitions: A linked list where each node contains data, a pointer to the next node, and a pointer to the previous node.
A linked list variation where the last node pointer points back to the head node instead of NULL.
notes.example: Node structure: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; struct Node* prev; };
exam_points: Doubly linked lists enable bidirectional traversal at the cost of additional memory overhead per node.
Inserting at the beginning of a singly linked list takes O(1) time.

notes.title: Searching & Sorting Algorithms
notes.explanation: Searching locates target elements within collections, while sorting orders data. Divide-and-conquer algorithms like Quick Sort and Merge Sort outperform simple sorting algorithms.
definitions: A search technique on sorted arrays that repeatedly divides the search interval in half, running in O(log n) time.
A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that partitions arrays around pivot elements.
notes.example: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time complexity, whereas Quick sort has O(n^2) worst-case time.
exam_points: Binary search requires input arrays to be sorted beforehand.
Quick Sort average time complexity is O(n log n), while Insertion Sort works best on nearly-sorted data.

questions: Define Abstract Data Types (ADT) and explain Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta asymptotic notations.
Explain Sparse Matrix representation with 3-tuple notation and write an algorithm for its transpose.
Derive memory address mapping formulas for 2D arrays in Row-Major and Column-Major ordering.
Write an algorithm to convert an Infix expression into a Postfix expression using a Stack.
Explain Circular Queue implementation using arrays and show how overflow and underflow conditions are handled.
Explain evaluation of Postfix expressions with a step-by-step stack execution trace for '5 3 + 8 2 / *'.
Write C functions to insert and delete nodes at arbitrary positions in a Singly Linked List.
Compare Singly Linked Lists, Doubly Linked Lists, and Circular Linked Lists in terms of memory and operations.
Write an algorithm to reverse a Singly Linked List in-place.
Compare Quick Sort and Merge Sort algorithms with algorithmic steps, trace, and time/space complexities.
Explain Binary Search algorithm and prove its O(log n) time complexity.
Differentiate between Stable and Unstable sorting algorithms with suitable examples.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity for accessing an element in an array by its index?
quiz.explanation: Arrays provide direct random access to elements by index in constant O(1) time.

quiz.question: Which data structure follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) execution order?
quiz.explanation: Stacks strictly follow LIFO order for push and pop operations.

quiz.question: In a circular queue implemented using an array of size MAX, what condition indicates that the queue is FULL?
quiz.explanation: A circular queue is full when the next position after rear modulo MAX equals front.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of a Doubly Linked List over a Singly Linked List?
options: Uses less memory space per node
Faster random element access by index
quiz.explanation: Doubly linked lists contain both next and prev pointers, enabling bidirectional traversal.

quiz.question: What is the average time complexity of the Quick Sort algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Quick Sort has an average-case time complexity of O(n log n).

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Operating System Functions, System Calls, OS Structures. Process Management: Process Concepts, Process Control Block (PCB), Process States, CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Priority, Round Robin).

Process Synchronization: Critical Section Problem, Semaphores, Classic Synchronization problems (Producer-Consumer, Dining Philosophers). Deadlocks: Characterization, Prevention, Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery.
Memory Management: Swapping, Contiguous Allocation, Paging, Segmentation, Virtual Memory, Page Replacement Algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal).
Storage & File Systems: File Concepts, Access Methods, Directory Structure, Disk Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN).

notes.title: CPU Scheduling & Process Control Block
notes.explanation: Operating systems manage hardware resource abstraction and schedule CPU execution across multiple concurrent processes. System calls act as interfaces between user applications and system kernels.
definitions: Process Control Block storing state, PID, registers, CPU scheduling info, and memory pointers for active processes.
A programmatic request made by an application to request services from the operating system kernel.
notes.example: Round Robin scheduling uses a fixed time quantum to allocate CPU turns fairly across ready queue processes.
exam_points: Shortest Job First (SJF) gives theoretical minimum average waiting time.
Round Robin performance depends heavily on the chosen time quantum size.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlock Management
notes.explanation: Concurrent processes require synchronization mechanisms like semaphores to solve critical section issues. Deadlocks occur when processes freeze while holding and waiting for resources.
definitions: A protected integer variable used for process synchronization via wait() [P] and signal() [V] atomic operations.
A deadlock avoidance algorithm that checks system state safety before granting resource requests.
notes.example: Counting semaphores manage access to resource pools with multiple available instances.
exam_points: Four deadlock conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.
Banker's algorithm uses Need = Max - Allocation matrices to verify safe execution sequences.

notes.title: Memory Management & Virtual Memory
notes.explanation: Memory management divides physical memory into fixed pages or variable segments. Virtual memory utilizes demand paging to execute processes larger than available physical RAM.
definitions: A memory management scheme allocating physical memory in fixed-size blocks (frames) matching logical page sizes.
An interrupt raised when a program accesses a logical page not currently loaded in physical RAM.
notes.example: Least Recently Used (LRU) replaces the page that has not been referenced for the longest time period.
exam_points: Belady's Anomaly occurs in FIFO page replacement where increasing frames increases page faults.
Segmentation divides memory into logical units (main, stack, symbol table) reflecting user views.

notes.title: File Systems & Disk Scheduling
notes.explanation: Disk scheduling algorithms order I/O requests to minimize disk arm head movement time across storage tracks.
definitions: The time required for the disk arm to move read/write heads to the target cylinder track.
Elevator disk scheduling algorithm moving head end-to-end across tracks servicing pending requests.
notes.example: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) selects requests closest to the current head position.
exam_points: SSTF reduces seek time compared to FCFS but may cause starvation for distant requests.
C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) provides more uniform wait times by servicing requests in one direction only.

questions: Compare FCFS, SJF, Priority, and Round Robin CPU scheduling algorithms with a Gantt chart numerical example.
Explain Process Control Block (PCB) structure and draw the process state transition diagram.
What are System Calls? Explain user mode vs kernel mode execution transitions.
Explain Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance with a numerical safety-check example.
Describe the Critical Section Problem and show how counting semaphores solve the Producer-Consumer problem.
State the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss deadlock prevention techniques.
Compare FIFO, LRU, and Optimal page replacement algorithms given a reference string.
Explain Paging and Segmentation memory management architectures with page table translation diagrams.
What is Belady's Anomaly? Demonstrate it using the FIFO page replacement algorithm.
Explain Disk Scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN) and calculate total head movements for a request queue.
Discuss file allocation methods: Contiguous, Linked, and Indexed allocation with pros and cons.
Explain directory structures (Single-level, Two-level, Tree-structured, Acyclic-Graph).

quiz.question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm gives minimal average waiting time for a given set of processes?
quiz.explanation: Shortest Job First (SJF) minimizes average waiting time across all processes.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for a deadlock to occur?
quiz.explanation: NO Preemption is required for deadlock. If preemption is allowed, deadlocks can be broken.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used by operating systems for Deadlock Avoidance?
quiz.explanation: Banker's Algorithm tests for safety by simulating allocation before granting resources.

quiz.question: Belady's Anomaly is associated with which page replacement algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Belady's Anomaly occurs in FIFO where allocating more page frames increases page fault rates.

quiz.question: Which disk scheduling algorithm services requests by moving the disk head back and forth like an elevator?
quiz.explanation: SCAN moves the disk head from one end of the disk to the other, servicing requests along the way.

syllabus.topics: OOP Concepts, C++ Tokens, Operators, Control Structures, Functions, Function Overloading, Inline Functions, Default Arguments.
Classes and Objects: Specifying a class, Access Specifiers, Memory Allocation for Objects, Static Data Members & Member Functions, Friend Functions, Constructors and Destructors.
Inheritance: Single, Multilevel, Multiple, Hierarchical, and Hybrid Inheritance. Operator Overloading, Virtual Base Classes.
Polymorphism: Pointers to Objects, Virtual Functions, Pure Virtual Functions, Abstract Classes, File I/O Streams, Exception Handling.

notes.title: OOP Paradigm & C++ Features
notes.explanation: Object-Oriented Programming structures programs around objects containing data and code. C++ supports function overloading, inline functions, and default arguments to improve performance and code reusability.
definitions: Defining multiple functions with the same name but different parameter signatures within the same scope.
A function expanded in-line at the point of call by the compiler to eliminate call overhead.
notes.example: void print(int i); void print(double d); demonstrates compile-time function overloading.
exam_points: Inline functions reduce function call overhead for small, frequently called routines.
Default arguments must be specified from right to left in parameter lists.

notes.title: Classes, Constructors & Destructors
notes.explanation: Classes encapsulate variables and functions. Access specifiers (private, protected, public) enforce data hiding. Constructors initialize objects, while destructors clean up resources.
definitions: A non-member function granted explicit access to private and protected class members.
A constructor initializing an object using another existing object of the same class: ClassName(const ClassName &obj).
notes.example: class Sample { public: Sample() { cout << "Created"; } ~Sample() { cout << "Destroyed"; } };
exam_points: Static member variables are shared across all instances of a class.
Destructors carry no arguments, return no values, and cannot be overloaded.

notes.title: Inheritance & Operator Overloading
notes.explanation: Inheritance allows derived classes to inherit attributes from base classes. Virtual base classes resolve diamond inheritance ambiguity. Operator overloading gives custom meanings to standard C++ operators.
definitions: A base class designated with 'virtual' during inheritance to prevent duplicate base instances in hybrid structures.
Redefining standard C++ operators (+, -, <<) to operate on user-defined class objects.
notes.example: Complex operator+(const Complex& obj) overloads the '+' operator for custom complex number addition.
exam_points: Operators that CANNOT be overloaded: :: (scope), . (dot), .* (pointer-to-member), sizeof, ternary (?:).
Virtual base classes eliminate duplicate inherited parent copies in hybrid diamond structures.

notes.title: Polymorphism, Virtual Functions & Streams
notes.explanation: Polymorphism enables objects to respond differently to identical function calls. Virtual functions achieve runtime polymorphism via dynamic vtables. Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function.
definitions: A virtual function declared with '= 0' having no definition in the base class, forcing derived classes to implement it.
A class containing at least one pure virtual function, preventing direct instantiation.
notes.example: virtual void draw() = 0; defines a pure virtual function inside an abstract Base class.
exam_points: Runtime polymorphism is achieved using base class pointers pointing to derived class objects with virtual functions.
Exception handling uses try, catch, and throw blocks.

questions: Explain core Object-Oriented Programming concepts: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism.
Differentiate between Inline Functions and Macros with C++ code examples.
Explain Function Overloading with rules and write a program demonstrating overloaded calculateArea() functions.
Define Constructors and Destructors. Explain Default, Parameterized, and Copy Constructors with code.
What is a Friend Function? Write a C++ program using a friend function to swap private values of two classes.
Explain Static Data Members and Static Member Functions with code demonstrating object counting.
Explain multiple inheritance and resolve ambiguity using Virtual Base Classes with a diamond hierarchy code example.
Write a C++ program to overload the '+' binary operator for adding two Complex objects.
Differentiate between Single, Multilevel, Multiple, and Hybrid Inheritance with syntax diagrams.
Differentiate between Compile-time and Runtime Polymorphism in C++.
What are Pure Virtual Functions and Abstract Classes? Demonstrate dynamic binding with base pointers.
Explain C++ File I/O stream classes (ifstream, ofstream, fstream) and write a file read/write program.

quiz.question: Which OOP concept isolates internal implementation details and exposes only necessary public interfaces?
quiz.explanation: Data abstraction hides internal complexity and shows only essential background features to users.

quiz.question: Which function type can access private class members without being a member of that class?
quiz.explanation: A friend function is granted explicit access to private and protected members of the declaring class.

quiz.question: Which mechanism resolves ambiguous variable access in C++ hybrid inheritance?
quiz.explanation: Virtual base classes eliminate duplicate inherited parent copies in hybrid diamond structures.

quiz.question: Which operator CANNOT be overloaded in C++?
quiz.explanation: Scope resolution operator (::), member access (.), member pointer (.*), sizeof, and ternary (?:) cannot be overloaded.

quiz.question: How is a pure virtual function declared in a C++ base class?
quiz.explanation: Pure virtual functions are assigned '= 0' in base class declarations.

syllabus.topics: HTML5 Basics: Structural Tags, Text Formatting, Lists, Tables, Forms, Multimedia Elements, Semantic HTML Tags.
CSS3 Styling: Selectors, Box Model, Flexbox, Grid Layout, Transitions, Responsive Web Design, Media Queries.
JavaScript Basics: Variables, Data Types, Operators, Control Flow, Functions, DOM Manipulation, Event Handling.
Advanced JavaScript & Web Tools: Form Validation, JSON Parsing, Introduction to AJAX, Web Hosting Basics, Version Control using Git.

notes.title: HTML5 & Semantic Markup
notes.explanation: HTML5 structures web documents. Semantic elements like <header>, <nav>, <article>, and <footer> provide meaning to document content for accessibility and search engines.
definitions: HTML markup using tags that convey structural meaning about contained data rather than pure presentation.
Interactive document sections containing input controls (<input>, <select>, <textarea>) to gather user input.
notes.example: <input type="email" required> provides native HTML5 client-side email format validation.
exam_points: Semantic tags (<section>, <article>, <aside>) improve SEO and screen reader accessibility.
HTML5 native video and audio tags eliminate third-party media plugin requirements.

notes.title: CSS3 Layouts, Flexbox & Grid
notes.explanation: CSS controls web styling and layouts. The Box Model structures margin, border, padding, and content. Flexbox (1D) and CSS Grid (2D) enable responsive web design.
definitions: Layout structure consisting of Content, Padding, Border, and Margin wrapping every HTML element.
One-dimensional layout engine for aligning items in flexible rows or columns.
notes.example: @media (max-width: 768px) { body { font-size: 14px; } } adjusts mobile styling.
exam_points: Media queries (@media) enable responsive layouts tailored to screen viewports.
Flexbox aligns items along main and cross axes, whereas CSS Grid handles simultaneous row/column layouts.

notes.title: JavaScript Fundamentals & DOM Manipulation
notes.explanation: JavaScript adds dynamic behavior to websites. The Document Object Model (DOM) represents HTML elements as nodes accessible for event handling and manipulation.
definitions: Document Object Model: A tree structural interface representing HTML page nodes for programmatic scripting.
Attaching listener functions to elements to respond to user interactions like clicks, inputs, and mouse moves.
notes.example: document.getElementById('btn').addEventListener('click', handleClick); handles click events.
exam_points: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped variable declarations.
DOM manipulation methods like querySelector and addEventListener power client-side interactivity.

notes.title: Advanced JS, Validation, AJAX & Git
notes.explanation: Client-side validation validates user input prior to server submission. AJAX fetches asynchronous server data without full page refreshes. Git manages code versioning.
definitions: Asynchronous JavaScript and XML: Technique to send and fetch data from server APIs asynchronously in background.
JavaScript Object Notation: Lightweight data-interchange format parsed via JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify().
notes.example: fetch('https://api.example.com/data').then(res => res.json()) fetches asynchronous API data.
exam_points: JSON parsing via JSON.parse() converts JSON strings into native JavaScript objects.
Git version control tracks code changes across development branches.

questions: Explain HTML5 semantic elements (<header>, <nav>, <section>, <article>, <footer>) and their benefits over <div>.
Create a complex HTML5 Form featuring inputs for text, password, email, radio, checkbox, dropdown, and submit button.
Differentiate between ordered lists (<ol>), unordered lists (<ul>), and description lists (<dl>).
Explain the CSS Box Model with a neat labeled diagram showing content, padding, border, and margin.
Compare CSS Flexbox and CSS Grid layout models stating appropriate use cases for each.
Write a CSS media query code snippet to make a 3-column desktop website layout stack into 1 column on mobile screens.
Explain DOM manipulation and event handling in JavaScript with complete code examples.
Differentiate between var, let, and const variable declarations in JavaScript.
Explain JavaScript functions, arrow functions, and scope (Global vs Local vs Block scope).
Write a complete JavaScript script to validate an email format and password strength in an HTML form.
Explain AJAX working mechanism and write a Fetch API script to request and render JSON data.
Outline essential Git version control commands (git init, add, commit, push, pull, branch).

quiz.question: Which structural HTML5 tag is best suited for wrapping independent, self-contained news or blog content?
quiz.explanation: <article> represents standalone, self-contained compositions intended for independent distribution.

quiz.question: Which CSS property converts an HTML container into a flexible one-dimensional layout model?
quiz.explanation: display: flex invokes 1D flexbox layout models across row or column axes.

quiz.question: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable in modern ES6 JavaScript that CANNOT be reassigned?
quiz.explanation: const creates immutable, block-scoped reference bindings that cannot be reassigned.

quiz.question: Which built-in JavaScript method parses a JSON formatted string into a JavaScript object?
quiz.explanation: JSON.parse() converts valid JSON string data into native JavaScript objects.

quiz.question: Which technology enables fetching data from web servers asynchronously without refreshing the entire web page?
quiz.explanation: AJAX and Fetch API execute asynchronous network requests to update parts of web pages dynamically.

subjects.name: Entrepreneurship Setup and Launch
objectives: 1. Understand core concepts of entrepreneurship through relatable real-life examples.
2. Begin to see themselves as problem-solvers and creators.
3. Learn about business paths (content creation, drop-shipping, cloud kitchen, gig economy, local services) and choose one.
4. Launch a micro-hustle (online or offline) to earn their first income (Target: ₹10,000).
5. Build confidence and self-belief by active doing.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Entrepreneurship: Solving problems and value creation. Entrepreneurial Mindset: Curiosity, taking initiative, learning by doing, resilience. 5 Business Paths: Content creation, drop-shipping, cloud kitchen/food business, gig economy, local services. Value Mapping: Connecting needs, skills, and offers.
Action & Execution: Choosing a path, defining a clear offer (what, for whom, why). Reaching out to real potential customers. Reflection and iteration. Aiming for the first ₹100 earned.

Customer Insights & Scaling: Identifying target audience needs, gathering customer feedback, refining offer delivery. Core values: Resilience, honesty, effort. Consistency in earning tasks. Final reflection on total revenue, grit, and ongoing support systems.

notes.title: Entrepreneurial Mindset & Value Mapping
notes.explanation: Entrepreneurship is about spotting societal problems, taking initiative, and creating value for revenue rather than waiting for large capital investment.
definitions: A practical model connecting 3 elements: What people need + What I can do/enjoy + What offer I can create.
A small-scale, low-risk business initiative launched quickly to validate products and generate early revenue.
notes.example: People need affordable student meals + I can cook using a home kitchen = ₹40 tiffin service offer.
exam_points: Micro-hustles prioritize rapid customer outreach, low overhead, and iterative learning.
5 business paths: Content creation, drop-shipping, cloud kitchen, gig economy, local services.

notes.title: Offer Definition & Customer Outreach
notes.explanation: Execution starts by crafting a clear value offer specifying what service is provided, for whom, and why it solves their problem. Achieving initial revenue builds momentum.
definitions: A concise statement describing the specific benefit delivered to target customers solving a clear pain point.
Direct communication channels (word-of-mouth, social media, local visits) used to engage potential buyers.
notes.example: Reaching out directly to campus hostel students with custom print/design service offers.
exam_points: Early customer feedback drives offer iteration and pricing adjustments.
Earning the initial ₹100 validates customer demand and builds entrepreneurial confidence.

notes.title: Customer Feedback & Business Scaling
notes.explanation: Scaling requires gathering customer feedback, maintaining delivery consistency, and practicing resilience to reach the target revenue goal of ₹10,000.
definitions: The ability of an entrepreneur to navigate rejections, setbacks, and operational challenges while refining their offer.
Strategies to satisfy existing customers so they make repeat purchases or refer new buyers.
notes.example: Offering loyalty discounts to repeat cloud kitchen customers to increase total monthly revenue.
exam_points: The curriculum sets a semester revenue milestone target of ₹10,000.
Consistent tracking of income and expenses is essential for evaluating hustle profitability.

questions: Explain the 3 core components of a personal Value Map with a concrete micro-business example.
Outline the 5 business paths explored in the course (content creation, drop-shipping, cloud kitchen, gig economy, local services).
Discuss the key traits of an Entrepreneurial Mindset compared to a traditional job-seeker mindset.
How do you craft an effective micro-hustle offer? Define the 'What, For Whom, and Why' framework.
Describe techniques for performing direct customer outreach without spending money on paid advertising.
Explain the importance of earning the first ₹100 in validating business ideas.
Discuss how customer feedback is gathered and utilized to refine product/service offerings.
Explain key strategies required to scale micro-hustle earnings toward the ₹10,000 target.
Reflect on the role of grit, resilience, and ethics in sustaining long-term entrepreneurial initiatives.

quiz.question: Which framework connects customer needs, personal skills, and proposed offers to form a business opportunity?
quiz.explanation: A Value Map bridges 'People Need', 'I Can', and 'My Offer'.

quiz.question: What is the primary semester revenue target set in the EMC-101-25 curriculum?
quiz.explanation: The semester revenue target for the hands-on micro-hustle is set at ₹10,000.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 5 business paths emphasized in the course?
quiz.explanation: Heavy manufacturing requires substantial capital; the course focuses on accessible micro-hustles like cloud kitchens, drop-shipping, content, gig work, and local services.

quiz.question: What is the initial monetary validation milestone aimed for during Weeks 4-7?
quiz.explanation: Aiming for the first ₹100 earned serves as the initial validation milestone.

quiz.question: Which core soft skill enables an entrepreneur to persist through sales rejections and operational setbacks?
quiz.explanation: Resilience and grit empower entrepreneurs to iterate through failures and continue building.

subjects.name: Indian Constitution
objectives: CO1: Analyze the Indian Constitution's history, Preamble, Fundamental Rights, and basic structure.
CO2: Describe the roles of the President, Prime Minister, and the legislative bodies (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha).
CO3: Examine the powers of the Governor, Chief Minister, and State Secretariat.
CO4: Assess local government bodies like District Administration, Municipal Corporations, and Zila Panchayats.
CO5: Analyze the role of the Election Commission in conducting free and fair elections.

syllabus.topics: History of the Making of Indian Constitution, Preamble, Basic Structure and Interpretation, Fundamental Rights and Duties, Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
Structure of the Indian Union, President (Role and Powers), Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha).
Governor (Role and Powers), Chief Minister and Council of Ministers, State Secretariat.
District Administration, Municipal Corporation, Zila Panchayat.
Role and Functioning of Election Commission, Chief Election Commissioner, State Election Commissions.

notes.title: Fundamental Rights, DPSPs & Basic Structure
notes.explanation: The Indian Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights (Part III) to citizens and sets Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) for governance. The Kesavananda Bharati case established the Basic Structure Doctrine.
definitions: The introductory statement outlining core constitutional objectives: Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity.
Judicial principle holding that Parliament cannot alter essential constitutional features via amendments.
notes.example: Article 19(1)(g) grants rights to practice any trade or business, subject to public interest restrictions.
exam_points: Part III contains enforceable Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35).
Part IV contains non-justiciable Directive Principles (Articles 36-51).

notes.title: Union Executive & Parliament
notes.explanation: The President acts as executive head, while real executive power resides in the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. Parliament consists of Lok Sabha (House of People) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
definitions: The lower house of Parliament comprising directly elected representatives of the people.
The upper house representing Indian States and Union Territories as a permanent body.
notes.example: Money bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha under Article 109.
exam_points: The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of Parliament and State Assemblies.
The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers responsible to the Lok Sabha.

notes.title: State Executive & Administration
notes.explanation: State government mirrors Union structures. The Governor acts as constitutional head, while the Chief Minister leads political executive operations assisted by the State Secretariat.
definitions: Constitutional executive head of a state appointed by the President of India.
Elected head of the state government exercising real executive authority.
notes.example: Article 163 provides for a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor.
exam_points: The Governor holds discretionary powers regarding reservation of bills for Presidential assent.
State Secretariat coordinates administrative policy execution across state departments.

notes.title: Local Governance (73rd & 74th Amendments)
notes.explanation: Local self-governance decentralizes power to grassroots levels via Municipal Corporations (urban) and Zila Panchayats (rural).
definitions: The apex district tier of the Panchayati Raj rural local self-government system.
Urban local governing body handling civic administration for large metropolitan cities.
notes.example: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act 1992 constitutionalized rural Panchayati Raj institutions.
exam_points: District Collector/Magistrate heads the district administration hierarchy.
74th Amendment Act constitutionalized urban local bodies (Nagarpalikas).

notes.title: Election Commission of India
notes.explanation: Article 324 establishes the Election Commission of India as an autonomous constitutional authority conducting free and fair elections for Parliament and State Legislatures.
definitions: Head of the Election Commission enjoying security of tenure similar to a Supreme Court judge.
Guidelines issued by the EC to regulate political parties and candidates during election campaigns.
notes.example: ECI deploys Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and VVPAT audit trails during general elections.
exam_points: State Election Commissions handle local body elections (Panchayats and Municipalities), not ECI.
Article 324 vests superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the ECI.

questions: Explain the salient features of the Indian Constitution and discuss the significance of the Preamble.
Differentiate between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV).
What is the Basic Structure Doctrine? Discuss its origin in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
Describe executive, legislative, and emergency powers vested in the President of India.
Explain the composition, powers, and legislative relationship between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
Discuss the role and powers of the Prime Minister as the real head of the Union Executive.
Examine the role, appointment, and discretionary powers of the State Governor.
Explain the powers and functions of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers in State Governance.
Describe the administrative structure and functions of the State Secretariat.
Discuss the structure and functions of District Administration and the role of the District Collector.
Explain the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts regarding rural and urban local bodies.
Examine the role and constitutional powers of the Election Commission of India in conducting fair elections.

quiz.question: Which Part of the Indian Constitution contains the Fundamental Rights of citizens?
