quiz.explanation: Part III (Articles 12 to 35) defines Fundamental Rights.

quiz.question: Who acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
quiz.explanation: The Vice-President of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

quiz.question: Who acts as the constitutional head of a State executive in India?
quiz.explanation: The Governor serves as the constitutional head of the state executive.

quiz.question: Which constitutional amendment introduced provisions for urban local self-governments (Municipalities)?
quiz.explanation: The 74th Amendment Act 1992 introduced Part IX-A regulating Municipalities.

quiz.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution grants the Election Commission authority to superintend and conduct elections?
quiz.explanation: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission.

subjects.name: Disaster Management and Preparedness
objectives: CO1: Identify hazards, vulnerabilities, and risks at individual, institutional, and community levels.
CO2: Outline legal and institutional frameworks of DRR in India and globally (DM Act 2005, Sendai Framework).
CO3: Demonstrate life-saving skills, emergency communication, disaster response, and risk mitigation techniques.
CO4: Utilize basic tools and technologies for risk assessment, preparedness, and resilience-building.
CO5: Prepare disaster management plans and design community awareness activities.

syllabus.unit: Unit 1: Understanding Disaster Risk Reduction and Management
syllabus.topics: Basic terminology: Hazard, Vulnerability, Capacity, Exposure, Disaster, Risk, DRR. Types of natural and man-made disasters. Disaster Management Cycle (Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Relief, Recovery, Rehabilitation). Policy Frameworks: DM Act 2005, DM Amendment Act 2025, National Policy, PM 10 Point Agenda. International Frameworks: Sendai Framework, Paris Agreement, SDGs. Institutional roles: NDMA, NIDM, IMD, SDMA, DDMA.

syllabus.unit: Unit 2: Preparedness, Mitigation and Response Planning
syllabus.topics: HVCR Assessment tools (Hazard mapping, Transect walk, Problem tree). Evacuation planning, mock drills, Incident Response System (IRS). Roles of NDRF, SDRF, Police, Fire Services. Emerging Tech: Drones, SAFAR, Meghdoot, UMANG, Sachet, CWC Flood Alerts. Structural and nonstructural audit exercises.

First Aid essentials: CPR, choking, burns, fractures, animal bites, tourniquet, triage. 72-hour emergency kit, WASH and IPC practices. Search and rescue methods, Fire safety, Gas leakage protocols. Disaster-specific responses (Floods, Earthquakes, Cyclones). Psychosocial support & Public Health preparedness.

syllabus.unit: Unit 4: Field Exposure and Community Engagement
syllabus.topics: Field visits to Emergency Operations Centres, SDRF/NDRF units, Fire Stations. Community engagement projects: Street plays (nukkad natak), awareness campaigns, DRR clubs, household/institutional DM plan preparation, budget-friendly survival kit prototypes.

notes.title: Disaster Risk Concepts & Institutional Frameworks
notes.explanation: Disaster Risk is defined as Risk = (Hazard x Vulnerability x Exposure) / Capacity. The Disaster Management Act 2005 establishes statutory authorities like NDMA, SDMA, and DDMA.
definitions: National Disaster Management Authority: Apex statutory body in India headed by the Prime Minister.
International voluntary agreement (2015-2030) aiming to reduce global disaster risk and mortality.
notes.example: IMD provides early weather warning alerts, while NDMA issues national mitigation guidelines.
exam_points: DM Act 2005 created a multi-tiered disaster response framework: NDMA (National), SDMA (State), DDMA (District).
Disaster Management Cycle comprises Pre-Disaster (Mitigation, Preparedness) and Post-Disaster (Response, Recovery) phases.

notes.title: HVCR Risk Assessment & Incident Response System
notes.explanation: HVCR (Hazard, Vulnerability, Capacity, Risk) tools map community vulnerabilities. The Incident Response System (IRS) provides a standardized administrative structure for emergency management operations.
definitions: A standardized organizational framework managing emergency incident operations across multi-agency responders.
National early warning dissemination platform delivering geo-targeted disaster alerts to citizens.
notes.example: Using drone surveillance and CWC alerts to monitor floodwater levels along rivers.
exam_points: NDRF (National Disaster Response Force) provides specialized response during natural and man-made disasters.
Structural audits evaluate building seismic stability; nonstructural audits secure unanchored furniture.

notes.title: First Aid, 72-Hour Survival Kit & Triage
notes.explanation: Life-saving skills like CPR, tourniquet application, and triage prioritize casualties during disasters. A 72-hour survival kit sustains individuals until official relief arrives.
definitions: A self-contained survival kit containing water, non-perishable food, first aid, flashlight, radio, and hygiene items.
The process of sorting injured victims into categories based on medical urgency (Red, Yellow, Green, Black).
notes.example: CPR delivers 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths during sudden cardiac arrest.
exam_points: Triage color coding: Red (Immediate/Life-threatening), Yellow (Delayed), Green (Minor/Walking wounded), Black (Deceased).
During earthquakes: Drop, Cover, and Hold On.

notes.title: Community Engagement & Field Preparedness
notes.explanation: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction (CBDRR) engages citizens via street plays, mock drills, and local DM plans to build grassroots resilience.
definitions: A simulated emergency exercise testing evacuation readiness and response protocols.
Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction: Grassroots approach empowering local communities to manage disaster risks.
notes.example: Conducting street plays (Nukkad Natak) to educate village residents on earthquake safety.
exam_points: Field visits to EOC (Emergency Operations Centres) demonstrate real-time disaster monitoring.
Institutional DM plans require annual mock drills and designated safety warden teams.

questions: Explain the stages of the Disaster Management Cycle with a neat block diagram.
Discuss the institutional framework under the DM Act 2005 (NDMA, SDMA, DDMA, NDRF).
Define Hazard, Vulnerability, Capacity, and Risk. Explain the Disaster Risk equation.
Explain the tools used in Hazard, Vulnerability, Capacity, and Risk (HVCR) Assessment.
Describe the Incident Response System (IRS) organizational structure during emergency operations.
Discuss the role of emerging digital technologies (Drones, Sachet, CWC Alerts) in disaster warning.
Explain First Aid procedures for CPR, severe bleeding control, and fracture immobilization.
Describe the composition of a standard 72-Hour Household Emergency Survival Kit.
Explain the START Triage system used to categorize disaster casualties by medical urgency.
Outline the steps to prepare a comprehensive Institutional Disaster Management Plan.
Explain how community awareness campaigns (Street plays, DRR clubs) enhance grassroots resilience.
Discuss the role and operational readiness of Fire Services and SDRF during urban structural fires.

quiz.question: Which statutory apex body handles national disaster management policies in India under the DM Act 2005?
quiz.explanation: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) is the apex statutory body headed by the Prime Minister.

quiz.question: What is the correct mathematical relationship for Disaster Risk?
options: Risk = (Hazard x Vulnerability x Exposure) / Capacity
quiz.explanation: Risk is directly proportional to Hazard, Vulnerability, and Exposure, and inversely proportional to Capacity.

quiz.question: Which operational management system provides a standardized administrative structure for disaster response in India?
quiz.explanation: Incident Response System (IRS) organizes disaster response administration.

quiz.question: In medical Triage during mass casualty incidents, which color code represents immediate life-threatening injuries requiring priority care?
quiz.explanation: Red tag indicates immediate life-threatening condition requiring urgent medical intervention.

quiz.question: What is the recommended personal survival duration covered by a household emergency kit?
quiz.explanation: Standard disaster survival kits are designed to sustain individuals for at least 72 hours.

subjects.name: Data Structures- II
objectives: CO1: Implement various searching and sorting algorithms.
CO2: Discuss various advanced data structures.
CO3: Implement non-linear Data Structures.

syllabus.topics: Trees: Definition, Terminologies, Binary Trees, Memory representation using Array and Linked List, Recursive and non-recursive Traversal of Binary Tree, Threaded Binary Tree, Binary Search Tree (BST), Insertion, Deletion and Searching in BST.
Advanced Trees: Height Balanced Trees (AVL Trees), Insertion and Deletion in AVL Tree, M-way Tree, B Tree, B+ Tree, Red-Black Tree, Heap Tree.
Graphs: Definition, Terminologies, Types of graphs, Memory representation, Graph Traversal (DFS and BFS), Shortest Path algorithm (Dijkstra’s Algorithm).

Searching: Linear Search, Binary Search, Hashing, Hash Tables, Hash Functions, Collision Resolution (Open Addressing and Chaining). Sorting: Bubble, Selection, Insertion, Quick Sort, Comparative study.

notes.title: Trees, Binary Trees & BST Operations
notes.explanation: Trees are hierarchical non-linear data structures. Binary Search Trees (BST) maintain order where left subtree values are smaller and right subtree values are larger than the parent node.
definitions: A binary tree where each node satisfies the ordering property: left child < parent < right child.
A binary tree where unused null pointers are replaced with threads pointing to in-order predecessor or successor nodes.
notes.example: Tree Traversals: Inorder (Left, Root, Right), Preorder (Root, Left, Right), Postorder (Left, Right, Root).
exam_points: Inorder traversal of a BST yields elements in strictly ascending sorted order.
Deleting a node with two children in a BST requires replacing it with its in-order predecessor or successor.

notes.title: Advanced Self-Balancing Trees & Heaps
notes.explanation: Advanced trees like AVL trees, B-trees, and Red-Black trees maintain balanced heights to ensure logarithmic time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion operations.
definitions: A self-balancing binary search tree where the balance factor (height(left) - height(right)) of every node is between -1 and +1.
A self-balancing multi-way search tree optimized for systems that read and write large blocks of data.
notes.example: AVL balance restoration uses single (LL, RR) and double (LR, RL) rotations.
exam_points: AVL tree height is strictly maintained at O(log n), guaranteeing efficient search performance.
Min-Heap and Max-Heap satisfy the heap property where parent nodes are smaller or larger than their children respectively.

notes.title: Graph Representations, Traversals & Shortest Path
notes.explanation: Graphs model pairwise relationships using vertices and edges. They are stored using Adjacency Matrices or Adjacency Lists, and explored using BFS (Queue) or DFS (Stack).
definitions: A collection of unordered lists used to represent a graph, where each list describes the set of neighbors of a vertex.
A greedy graph search algorithm that solves the single-source shortest path problem for a graph with non-negative edge path costs.
notes.example: BFS uses a Queue for level-order traversal, whereas DFS uses a Stack (or recursion) for depth-first exploration.
exam_points: Adjacency matrix representation takes O(V^2) space, whereas adjacency list takes O(V + E) space.
Dijkstra's algorithm fails when graphs contain negative edge weights.

notes.title: Hashing, Collision Resolution & Advanced Sorting
notes.explanation: Hashing maps keys to table indices using hash functions. Collisions are resolved using Open Addressing (linear/quadratic probing) or Chaining (linked lists).
definitions: A mathematical algorithm that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size hash table index values.
A collision resolution technique where all elements hashing to the same index are stored in a linked list.
notes.example: Division method hash function: h(k) = k mod m, where m is the table size.
exam_points: Open addressing techniques include linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing.
Quick sort has an average time complexity of O(n log n) and sorts arrays in-place.

questions: Write recursive and non-recursive algorithms for Inorder, Preorder, and Postorder binary tree traversals.
Explain Binary Search Tree (BST) operations: Insertion, Deletion, and Searching with code algorithms.
What is a Threaded Binary Tree? Explain its advantages over standard binary trees.
Explain AVL tree rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) with diagrams and insert a given sequence of numbers into an initially empty AVL tree.
Compare B-Trees and B+ Trees in terms of structure, search efficiency, and disk storage.
Explain Heap sort algorithm and construct a Max-Heap from an unsorted array.
Explain Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) graph traversal algorithms with step-by-step traces.
State Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a weighted directed graph.
Differentiate between Directed and Undirected graphs, and Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List memory representations.
Explain Hash Functions and collision resolution techniques: Open Addressing and Chaining.
Compare Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, and Quick Sort in terms of time complexity and stability.
Explain Binary Search algorithm and prove its O(log n) time complexity.

quiz.question: Which tree traversal technique visits the root node AFTER visiting both its left and right subtrees?
quiz.explanation: Postorder traversal follows the sequence: Left Subtree -> Right Subtree -> Root.

quiz.question: What is the allowable balance factor range for any node in an AVL tree?
quiz.explanation: AVL tree balance factor (height(left) - height(right)) must strictly remain within {-1, 0, 1}.

quiz.question: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a Queue data structure?
quiz.explanation: BFS explores graph levels iteratively using a FIFO Queue.

quiz.question: Which collision resolution technique stores colliding hash keys in linked lists at table indices?
quiz.explanation: Chaining resolves hash collisions by maintaining a linked list of elements at each hash table bucket.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
quiz.explanation: Quick Sort has a worst-case time complexity of O(n^2) when poor pivot elements are consistently chosen.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems- I
objectives: CO1: Explain Core Concepts of DBMS.
CO2: Design data models for real life problems.
CO3: Design real life Databases and write SQL queries.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Databases: Data, Database, DBMS, Advantages/Disadvantages, Users and DBAs. Data Models: Types of Data Models (Hierarchical, Network, Relational, Object-oriented).

Database Design: Keys (Primary, Candidate, Super, Foreign, Composite, Alternate, Unique, Surrogate), Table Constraints. ER Model: Entities, Attributes, Relationships, ER Diagrams, Key Constraints, Weak Entity Sets, Relational Schema mapping.

Relational Algebra: Selection, Projection, Set Operations, Joins, Division. SQL Basics: DDL, DML, DCL, Aggregate Functions, Logical Operators, Predicates, Clauses (Group By, Having, Order By), Joins (Inner, Outer, Natural). Advanced SQL: Views, Cursors, Stored Procedures, Triggers, Recursive Queries.
Normalization: Functional Dependencies, Armstrong's Axioms, Closure, Normal Forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF), Denormalization.

notes.title: Introduction to DBMS & Data Models
notes.explanation: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software designed to store, retrieve, and manage data efficiently while ensuring security and ACID compliance.
definitions: An organized collection of structured information, or data, typically stored electronically in a computer system.
The logical structure of a database designed and represented in a formal language supported by the DBMS.
notes.example: Relational data model stores data in two-dimensional tables with rows and columns.
exam_points: DBMS eliminates data redundancy and maintains data consistency compared to traditional file systems.
Database Administrator (DBA) manages system security, backups, and user access control.

notes.title: ER Modeling & Database Keys
notes.explanation: Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling provides a graphical representation of real-world entities, attributes, and relationships.
definitions: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each record in a database relation.
An entity set that does not have sufficient attributes to form a primary key on its own.
notes.example: Foreign key creates a referential integrity link between two related tables.
exam_points: Super key is a superset of candidate keys; Candidate key is minimal; Primary key is the chosen candidate key.
ER diagrams map entity sets to tables and relationship sets to foreign key constraints.

notes.title: Relational Algebra & SQL Queries
notes.explanation: Relational algebra is a procedural query language that takes relation instances as input and yields relation instances as output.
definitions: Data Definition Language (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) used to define database structures.
Data Manipulation Language (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) used to query and modify table data.
notes.example: SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Salary > 50000; filters records using relational predicates.
exam_points: Inner Join returns records with matching values in both tables; Outer Joins include unmatched rows.
Group By clause aggregates data using aggregate functions like SUM, AVG, and COUNT.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization organizes database columns and tables to minimize data redundancy and dependency anomalies.
definitions: A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies for non-prime attributes.
Boyce-Codd Normal Form: A stricter version of 3NF where every determinant must be a candidate key.
notes.example: First Normal Form (1NF) eliminates repeating groups and requires atomic attribute values.
exam_points: 2NF removes partial functional dependencies.
3NF and BCNF remove transitive and functional determinant anomalies.

questions: Explain the architecture of a DBMS and discuss the role of a Database Administrator (DBA).
Compare Hierarchical, Network, and Relational data models with diagrams.
Explain different types of database keys (Primary, Candidate, Foreign, Alternate) with examples.
Construct an ER Diagram for a University Library Management System and map it to a relational schema.
Explain basic relational algebra operations: Selection, Projection, Cartesian Product, and Joins.
Write SQL queries demonstrating GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, and Inner/Outer Joins.
Differentiate between 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF with suitable relational examples.
Explain functional dependencies and Armstrong's axioms for relational database design.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a core property of database transactions (ACID)?
quiz.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Concurrency is a property of scheduling, not an ACID acronym letter.

quiz.question: Which key uniquely identifies each record in a relation and cannot contain null values?
quiz.explanation: Primary Key uniquely identifies tuples in a relation and enforces entity integrity (no nulls).

quiz.question: Which SQL clause is used to filter grouped rows aggregated by GROUP BY?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters aggregated groups, whereas WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

quiz.question: Which normal form removes partial functional dependencies from a relation?
quiz.explanation: 2NF requires the relation to be in 1NF and have no non-prime attribute dependent on a proper subset of any candidate key.

quiz.question: In BCNF, every determinant must be a:
quiz.explanation: Boyce-Codd Normal Form strictly dictates that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a candidate key.

subjects.name: Python Programming
objectives: CO1: Develop modular Python programs.
CO2: Apply suitable Python programming constructs, built-in data structures using libraries to solve problems.
CO3: Implement Data visualization and File handling in Python.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: History, Applications, Structure, Identifiers, Operators, Data Types, Type Conversion, I/O. Strings: Formatting, Slicing, Built-in functions. Control Flow: Conditional statements, Loops, break, continue, pass.
Functions: Built-in, user-defined, scope, default arguments, lambda functions, modules. Mutable and Immutable Objects: Lists, Tuples, Dictionaries and associated methods. NumPy and Math modules.
Files: Text and Binary files, Pickle module, CSV and JSON files. Exception Handling: try-except-else-finally, raise. Data Visualization: 2D/3D plots, histograms, pie charts, curves using Matplotlib.

notes.title: Python Basics & Control Flow
notes.explanation: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language emphasizing code readability and dynamic typing.
definitions: Variable data types are checked and bound at runtime rather than compile time.
notes.example: text = 'Python'[0:3] yields 'Pyt'.
exam_points: Control flow statements include if-elif-else, for loops, and while loops.
Break exits a loop immediately; continue skips the current iteration.

notes.title: Lists, Tuples, Dictionaries & Functions
notes.explanation: Python provides powerful built-in collections: Lists are mutable sequences, Tuples are immutable sequences, and Dictionaries store key-value mappings.
definitions: An anonymous inline function defined using the 'lambda' keyword.
An object whose state or value can be modified after creation (e.g., list, dict).
notes.example: squares = [x**2 for x in range(5)] generates list [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].
exam_points: Tuples use parentheses () and are immutable; Lists use square brackets [] and are mutable.
Dictionaries store unique keys mapped to values.

notes.title: File Handling, Exceptions & Matplotlib Visualization
notes.explanation: Python handles external files using open() and modules like csv, json, and pickle. Errors are managed robustly using try-except blocks.
definitions: A mechanism to handle runtime errors gracefully using try, except, else, and finally blocks.
A comprehensive 2D/3D plotting library for creating static, animated, and interactive visualizations.
notes.example: plt.plot(x, y) creates a 2D line plot using Matplotlib.
exam_points: Always close files after I/O operations or use context managers ('with open(...) as f:').
Matplotlib provides pyplot functions like scatter(), hist(), and bar() for data visualization.

questions: Explain Python data types, type conversion functions, and basic input/output operations.
Discuss string manipulation and slicing with practical examples.
Differentiate between mutable (Lists, Dictionaries) and immutable (Tuples, Strings) objects in Python.
Explain user-defined functions, default arguments, scope rules, and lambda functions.
Write a Python script to handle ZeroDivisionError and FileNotFoundError using exception handling blocks.
Explain file handling operations for Text and CSV files, and create a 2D line plot using Matplotlib.

quiz.question: Which keyword is used to define a function in Python?
quiz.explanation: Functions in Python are defined using the 'def' keyword.

quiz.question: Which Python data collection type stores key-value pairs?
quiz.explanation: Dictionaries map unique keys to corresponding values in curly braces {}.

quiz.question: Which of the following collections is immutable in Python?
quiz.explanation: Tuples are immutable sequences defined with parentheses () and cannot be modified in-place.

quiz.question: Which block in Python exception handling always executes regardless of whether an exception occurred?
quiz.explanation: The 'finally' block executes unconditionally, making it ideal for cleanup actions like closing files.

quiz.question: Which Python library is primarily used for 2D and 3D data visualization and plotting?
quiz.explanation: Matplotlib is the standard Python plotting library used for generating charts, curves, and histograms.

subjects.name: Software Engineering
objectives: CO1: Acquire comprehensive understanding of software development lifecycles (SDLC).
CO2: Develop proficiency in project management methodologies and strategic decision-making.
CO3: Master software design, development, and testing to produce robust solutions.

syllabus.topics: Software role, Layered technology, Process models (Waterfall, Incremental, Evolutionary, Unified Process). Agile Software Development: Agility Principles, Scrum, Extreme Programming (XP).

Requirements Engineering: Functional/Non-functional requirements, SRS document, Elicitation, Analysis, Validation. Risk Management: Reactive vs Proactive, RMMM plan. Project Planning: Pricing, Scheduling, Estimation techniques.

Design Concepts: Architecture, Data design, UML Diagrams (Class, Sequence, Use Case, Activity). Testing Strategies: Black-box, White-box testing, Validation, System testing, Debugging. Product Metrics.
Quality Management: SQA, Reviews, Reliability. Release Management & Product Sustenance: Maintenance, updates, End of life.

notes.title: SDLC Process Models & Agile Scrum
notes.explanation: Software engineering provides systematic methodologies to build reliable software through structured life cycle phases.
definitions: A linear, sequential software development approach where each phase must be completed before the next begins.
An Agile framework managing complex software development through iterative Sprints and daily standups.
notes.example: Agile methodologies deliver working software incrementally in short 2-4 week Sprints.
exam_points: Waterfall model is rigid and non-adaptive to changing requirements.
Agile emphasizes customer collaboration and rapid response to change over rigid documentation.

notes.title: Requirements Engineering & Project Planning
notes.explanation: Requirements engineering gathers, analyzes, and validates functional and non-functional specifications documented in the SRS.
definitions: Software Requirements Specification: A comprehensive description of software behavior and constraints.
Identifying, analyzing, and mitigating potential project risks using RMMM (Risk Mitigation, Monitoring, and Management) plans.
notes.example: Functional requirements define system inputs and calculations; non-functional requirements govern performance and security.
exam_points: Proactive risk management anticipates risks before they occur; reactive risk management responds after problems arise.

notes.title: UML Design & Testing Strategies
notes.explanation: Software design models system architecture and behavior using UML diagrams, followed by systematic black-box and white-box testing.
definitions: Testing internal code logic, branches, and execution paths with visibility into source code.
Testing system functionality against specifications without knowing internal code implementation.
notes.example: Use case diagrams model user interactions with system features.
exam_points: Black-box testing ensures user requirements are met; white-box testing ensures code branch coverage.

notes.title: Software Quality Assurance & Maintenance
notes.explanation: SQA ensures software products meet quality standards and reliability benchmarks throughout their operational lifecycle.
definitions: Modifying software after delivery to fix faults, improve performance, or adapt to a changing environment.
The probability that software will execute without failure over a specified time period.
notes.example: Corrective, adaptive, and perfective maintenance sustain software systems post-release.
exam_points: Maintenance accounts for the largest share of total software lifecycle costs.

questions: Compare Waterfall Model and Agile Scrum Methodology in detail.
Explain Evolutionary and Incremental process models.
Explain the phases of Requirements Engineering and the key components of an SRS document.
Discuss project estimation techniques and RMMM risk management plans.
Differentiate between Black-Box testing and White-Box testing with examples.
Explain UML Class diagrams and Use Case diagrams with suitable illustrations.
Explain Software Quality Assurance (SQA) and software reliability models.
Discuss different types of software maintenance (Corrective, Adaptive, Perfective, Preventive).

quiz.question: Which software development process model is strictly linear and sequential?
quiz.explanation: The Waterfall model follows a rigid, sequential flow from requirements to maintenance.

quiz.question: What does SRS stand for in software engineering?
quiz.explanation: SRS stands for Software Requirements Specification, detailing all functional and non-functional criteria.

quiz.question: Which software testing technique validates internal code logic, paths, and branches?
quiz.explanation: White-box testing requires visibility into source code structures and internal logic paths.

quiz.question: Which type of software maintenance involves modifying software to adapt to a changing operating environment?
quiz.explanation: Adaptive maintenance updates software to run in new OS environments, hardware, or third-party platforms.

quiz.question: What does SQA stand for?
quiz.explanation: SQA stands for Software Quality Assurance, establishing processes to ensure software reliability and standards.

subjects.name: Feature Engineering
objectives: CO1: Understand the importance of features in machine learning and differentiate between various types of data and features (structured vs. unstructured, categorical, numerical, text, and date-time).
CO2: Apply basic feature preprocessing techniques such as handling missing data, data cleaning, and feature scaling and normalization.
CO3: Implement feature engineering techniques for numerical data, including binning, discretization, polynomial and interaction features, and log transformation.
CO4: Utilize categorical data techniques, such as one-hot encoding and label encoding, and understand feature selection methods, including filter and wrapper methods.
CO5: Perform feature transformation using techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and understand its application in machine learning.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Data and Features: Importance of Features in Machine Learning. Data types and features: Numerical, Categorical, Ordinal, Discrete, Continuous, Interval and Ratio. Basic Feature Preprocessing: Handling Missing Data, Data Cleaning, Feature Scaling, Normalization, and Transformation.

Techniques for Numerical Data: Binning and Discretization, Polynomial and Interaction Features. Categorical Data Techniques: One Hot Encoding, Label Encoding. Feature extraction vs. feature selection, Steps in feature selection. Feature Selection Methods: Filter, Wrapper, and Hybrid. Feature Reduction: Introduction and application of Principal Components Analysis.

notes.title: Data Types & Feature Preprocessing
notes.explanation: Feature engineering transforms raw input data into structured representations optimized for machine learning algorithms through scaling, cleaning, and normalization.
definitions: A scaling technique rescaling feature values into a fixed range [0, 1] using: X_norm = (X - X_min) / (X_max - X_min).
Rescaling features so they have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1: Z = (X - μ) / σ.
notes.example: Applying StandardScaler from Scikit-Learn on numerical feature vectors before feeding into distance-based models like KNN or SVM.
exam_points: Interval data has arbitrary zeros (e.g., Celsius), whereas Ratio data has absolute zero points (e.g., Kelvin, Weight).
Missing data can be handled via Mean/Median/Mode imputation, KNN imputation, or dropping corrupted rows.

notes.title: Numerical & Categorical Encoding and Selection
notes.explanation: Advanced feature creation includes non-linear interactions, mapping categorical strings into dynamic numeric vectors, and pruning redundant features using statistical selection algorithms.
definitions: Converting a categorical feature with N unique categories into N binary dummy columns (0 or 1).
An unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction method projecting high-dimensional features onto orthogonal variance-maximizing axes.
notes.example: Constructing PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) to capture non-linear relationship interaction terms (X1 * X2).
exam_points: Filter methods evaluate features independently using statistical metrics (ANOVA, Chi-Square, Correlation).
Wrapper methods (Recursive Feature Elimination) use model feedback to evaluate feature subsets.

questions: Differentiate between Interval and Ratio data types with real-world machine learning dataset examples.
Compare Min-Max Scaling and Z-score Standardization. Under what dataset conditions would you choose one over the other?
Explain different techniques for handling missing numerical and categorical data in raw datasets.
Explain One-Hot Encoding and Label Encoding. What is the 'Dummy Variable Trap' and how can it be avoided?
Differentiate between Feature Selection and Feature Extraction with appropriate algorithms.
Describe the step-by-step mathematical working of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction.

quiz.question: Which data type has a true, non-arbitrary zero point permitting ratio comparisons?
quiz.explanation: Ratio data possesses an absolute natural zero point (e.g., height, weight, absolute temperature).

quiz.question: Which encoding technique transforms a categorical column with 5 unique values into 5 binary indicator columns?
quiz.explanation: One-Hot Encoding generates distinct binary (0 or 1) dummy columns for every unique categorical class.

quiz.question: Which feature selection technique evaluates subset performance by directly training a predictive machine learning model?
quiz.explanation: Wrapper methods (e.g., RFE) evaluate feature subsets based on the accuracy output of a predictive model.

quiz.question: What is the primary objective of Principal Component Analysis (PCA)?
options: Handling missing values in categorical fields
Dimensionality reduction by finding orthogonal components that maximize variance
Standardizing nominal data features to zero mean
quiz.explanation: PCA projects high-dimensional data onto orthogonal principal components to maximize preserved variance in fewer dimensions.

quiz.question: Which pre-processing technique scales feature values strictly into a bounding range between 0 and 1?
quiz.explanation: Min-Max Normalization rescales numerical variables linearly into the explicit range [0, 1].

subjects.name: Entrepreneurship and Startup Ecosystem
objectives: CO1: Understand entrepreneurial mindset, startup ideation, and business model validation.
CO2: Master venture funding, financial planning, and pitch deck preparation.
CO3: Navigate intellectual property, legal structures, and scaling strategies.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Entrepreneurship: Evolution, Characteristics of Entrepreneurs, Intrapreneurship, Idea Generation, Opportunity Recognition, Design Thinking, Lean Startup Methodology.
Business Model & Market Validation: Business Model Canvas (BMC), Value Proposition Design, Customer Discovery, Minimum Viable Product (MVP), Market Research, Competitor Analysis.
Startup Financing & Funding: Bootstrapping, Angel Investors, Venture Capital, Crowdfunding, Seed Funding, Pitch Deck Creation, Financial Projections, Unit Economics (CAC, LTV).

Legal, IP & Scaling: Forms of Business Ownership (Sole Proprietorship, LLP, Private Limited), Intellectual Property Rights (Patents, Trademarks, Copyrights), Startup India Initiatives, Scaling and Exit Strategies.

notes.title: Entrepreneurial Mindset & Lean Startup
notes.explanation: Entrepreneurship involves identifying market gaps and building scalable ventures through iterative learning and validated experimentation.
definitions: The act of behaving like an entrepreneur while working within a large organization.
A methodology for developing businesses and products by combining experimental product releases with validated learning.
notes.example: Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop allows startups to pivot quickly based on customer feedback.
exam_points: Entrepreneurs take calculated risks and convert problems into commercial innovations.
Design thinking emphasizes empathy with end-users to prototype effective solutions.

notes.title: Business Model Canvas & Market Validation
notes.explanation: The Business Model Canvas (BMC) provides a strategic template for developing, describing, and pivoting new or existing business models.
definitions: A 9-block strategic management template visualizing key partners, activities, value propositions, and revenue streams.
A version of a new product with just enough features to satisfy early customers and test product hypotheses.
notes.example: Value proposition canvas matches customer jobs, pains, and gains with products and services.
exam_points: Customer discovery validates whether real market demand exists before heavy capital investment.
Competitor analysis identifies unique selling propositions (USPs) and market positioning.

notes.title: Startup Financing & Unit Economics
notes.explanation: Startups require capital from diverse funding stages ranging from bootstrapping and angel investment to institutional venture capital.
definitions: The total cost of marketing and sales efforts required to acquire a new customer.
The total net profit a business expects to generate from a single customer over their entire relationship.
notes.example: A healthy startup strives for an LTV to CAC ratio greater than 3:1.
exam_points: Pitch decks must succinctly communicate problem, solution, market size, business model, and team expertise.
Seed funding and Series A/B rounds fuel rapid market expansion and product development.

notes.title: Legal Frameworks, Intellectual Property & Scaling
notes.explanation: Protecting intellectual property and establishing robust legal entities are critical prerequisites for long-term venture sustainability.
definitions: Legal rights protecting creations of the mind such as inventions, literary works, designs, and symbols.
A corporate legal structure limiting liability of shareholders and separating personal assets from business debt.
notes.example: Patents protect novel technical inventions from unauthorized commercial replication.
exam_points: Startup India initiatives offer tax exemptions, compliance simplification, and funding support.
Scaling strategies involve operational expansion, strategic partnerships, and planned exit routes.

questions: Explain the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs and discuss the Lean Startup methodology.
How does Design Thinking drive innovation and opportunity recognition in startups?
Explain the 9 blocks of the Business Model Canvas (BMC) with a practical startup example.
What is an MVP (Minimum Viable Product)? Explain its role in customer discovery and validation.
Compare Bootstrapping, Angel Investing, and Venture Capital as startup financing options.
Explain key startup financial metrics including CAC, LTV, and burn rate with formulas.
Discuss various forms of business ownership (Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, Private Limited) and their legal implications.
What are Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)? Explain the importance of patents and trademarks for tech startups.

quiz.question: What is the primary core feedback loop in Eric Ries's Lean Startup methodology?
quiz.explanation: The Lean Startup core loop is Build-Measure-Learn, focusing on rapid validated learning.

quiz.question: How many building blocks make up Alexander Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas?
quiz.explanation: The Business Model Canvas consists of 9 fundamental building blocks covering value proposition, customers, infrastructure, and finances.

quiz.question: What does CAC stand for in startup financial unit economics?
quiz.explanation: CAC stands for Customer Acquisition Cost, measuring total sales and marketing expenses to acquire a user.

quiz.question: Which legal form of business ownership offers limited liability protection to its shareholders?
quiz.explanation: A Private Limited Company legally separates personal liability from corporate liabilities.

quiz.question: Which intellectual property right legally protects novel, non-obvious technical inventions and processes?
quiz.explanation: A patent grants exclusive legal rights for novel inventions, preventing others from making or selling them.

subjects.name: Computer Networks-I
objectives: CO1: Understand network architectures, topologies, and reference models.
CO2: Master physical and data link layer protocols, framing, error control, and MAC mechanisms.
CO3: Configure IPv4 addressing, subnetting, and network routing fundamentals.

syllabus.topics: Network Fundamentals: Topologies (Star, Mesh, Bus, Ring), OSI Reference Model, TCP/IP Suite, Network Hardware (Hub, Switch, Router, Gateway).
Physical & Data Link Layer: Transmission Media, Modulation, Framing, Error Detection (CRC, Checksum), Flow Control (Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window).
Medium Access Control: CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, Ethernet Standards (IEEE 802.3), Wireless LAN (IEEE 802.11), Switching (Circuit, Packet, Message).
Network Layer Basics: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, Classful vs Classless (CIDR) Addressing, ARP, RARP, ICMP.

notes.title: Network Topologies & OSI Model
notes.explanation: Computer networks connect autonomous computing devices to share resources using layered reference models like OSI (7 layers) and TCP/IP (4 layers).
definitions: A conceptual 7-layer framework standardizing network communication functions (Physical to Application).
A network setup where every device is connected to every other device, ensuring high fault tolerance.
notes.example: Routers operate at the Network layer (Layer 3) to forward packets across distinct networks.
exam_points: Data Link layer uses MAC addresses; Network layer uses logical IP addresses.
TCP/IP suite combines OSI session, presentation, and application layers into a single Application layer.

notes.title: Data Link Layer: Framing, Error Control & Flow Control
notes.explanation: The Data Link layer ensures reliable node-to-node data transfer, managing framing, error detection (CRC), and flow control (Sliding Window).
definitions: An error-detecting code using polynomial division to detect accidental data corruption in transit.
A flow control method allowing multiple frames to be sent in transit before awaiting acknowledgments.
notes.example: Stop-and-Wait protocol requires the sender to await an acknowledgment before transmitting the next frame.
exam_points: Checksum and CRC verify frame integrity at the receiver end.
Flow control prevents fast senders from overwhelming slow receivers.

notes.title: Medium Access Control & Switching
notes.explanation: MAC protocols coordinate shared channel access in broadcast networks, preventing collisions using CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA.
definitions: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection, used in wired Ethernet (IEEE 802.3).
Data routing method dividing messages into packets transmitted independently across switched paths.
notes.example: Wireless LANs use CSMA/CA to avoid collisions because hidden nodes cannot detect collisions directly.
exam_points: Circuit switching establishes dedicated physical connection paths; packet switching shares links dynamically.
IEEE 802.3 governs wired Ethernet standards.

notes.title: Network Layer: IPv4 Addressing & Subnetting
notes.explanation: The Network layer handles logical addressing and packet routing across interconnected subnets using IPv4 and routing protocols.
definitions: The strategy of dividing a large IP network into smaller, manageable sub-networks using subnet masks.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing: Flexible IP address allocation using variable-length subnet masks (VLSM).
notes.example: IP address 192.168.1.10 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0 designates network ID 192.168.1.0.
exam_points: ARP resolves logical IP addresses to physical MAC addresses.
ICMP handles network error reporting and diagnostic utilities like ping.

questions: Explain the 7 layers of the OSI Reference Model and compare them with the TCP/IP suite.
Discuss network topologies (Star, Mesh, Bus, Ring) with their respective advantages and disadvantages.
Explain error detection mechanisms: CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) and Checksum with examples.
Compare Stop-and-Wait flow control protocol with Sliding Window flow control.
Explain CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA medium access control protocols in wired and wireless networks.
Differentiate between Circuit Switching, Packet Switching, and Message Switching.
Perform IPv4 subnetting on a Class C network given subnetwork host requirements.
Explain Classful vs Classless (CIDR) IP addressing, and the working of ARP and ICMP protocols.

quiz.question: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for end-to-end reliable message delivery and flow control?
quiz.explanation: The Transport Layer (Layer 4) ensures reliable end-to-end data delivery using TCP or UDP.

quiz.question: Which error detection method uses polynomial division to generate a remainder attached to data frames?
quiz.explanation: CRC uses binary polynomial division to compute robust checksum remainders for error detection.

quiz.question: Which medium access control protocol is utilized in wired Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) to handle frame collisions?
quiz.explanation: CSMA/CD (Collision Detection) is used in legacy wired Ethernet networks to detect and recover from collisions.

quiz.question: Which protocol resolves a logical IP address to its corresponding physical MAC address on a local area network?
quiz.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) queries the local network to map IPv4 addresses to MAC hardware addresses.

quiz.question: How many bits comprise an IPv4 address?
quiz.explanation: IPv4 addresses consist of 32 bits, typically represented in dotted-decimal notation across 4 octets.

subjects.name: Design and Analysis of Algorithm
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithmic efficiency using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Design algorithms using Divide and Conquer, Greedy, and Dynamic Programming paradigms.
CO3: Explore backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Algorithm Analysis: Asymptotic Notations (Big-O, Omega, Theta), Recurrence Relations, Substitution Method, Recursion Tree, Master Theorem.
Divide and Conquer: Binary Search, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Strassen's Matrix Multiplication. Greedy Method: Knapsack Problem, Job Sequencing, Prim's & Kruskal's.
Dynamic Programming: 0/1 Knapsack, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), All-Pairs Shortest Path (Floyd-Warshall).
Backtracking & Branch-Bound: N-Queens Problem, Graph Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycles, NP-Completeness (P, NP, NP-Hard, NP-Complete).

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Recurrences
notes.explanation: Algorithmic efficiency is evaluated mathematically using asymptotic growth notations (Big-O, Omega, Theta) and recurrence relation solving techniques.
definitions: An asymptotic upper bound bounding function growth rate from above by $c \cdot g(n)$.
A formula used to determine asymptotic runtime bounds for divide-and-conquer recurrences of form $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$.
notes.example: Binary search has a logarithmic time complexity of $O(\log n)$.
exam_points: Theta notation ($\Theta$) provides tight asymptotic bounds (both upper and lower).
Recursion trees and substitution methods solve divide-and-conquer recurrence equations.

notes.title: Divide and Conquer & Greedy Algorithms
notes.explanation: Divide and conquer breaks problems into independent subproblems, while greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each stage.
definitions: A paradigm breaking problems into smaller subproblems, solving them recursively, and combining solutions.
Making the locally optimal choice at each decision step with the hope of finding a global optimum.
notes.example: Merge sort and Quick sort use divide and conquer principles with $O(n \log n)$ average times.
exam_points: Fractional knapsack is solved optimally via greedy value/weight ratio strategy.
Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms use greedy approaches to find minimum spanning trees (MST).

notes.title: Dynamic Programming
notes.explanation: Dynamic programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, storing results in memoization tables.
definitions: An algorithmic technique solving optimization problems by caching overlapping subproblem results.
Storing results of expensive function calls and returning the cached result when the same inputs occur again.
notes.example: 0/1 Knapsack problem uses dynamic programming tables with $O(nW)$ time complexity.
exam_points: Unlike greedy algorithms, 0/1 knapsack cannot be solved fractionally; dynamic programming guarantees optimality.
Floyd-Warshall algorithm computes all-pairs shortest paths in weighted graphs.

notes.title: Backtracking, Branch-Bound & NP-Completeness
notes.explanation: Backtracking constructs solution spaces incrementally, abandoning paths that fail constraints, while NP-completeness classifies computational hardness.
definitions: A algorithmic technique for finding all solutions by exploring paths and undoing choices when dead ends are reached.
A class of decision problems that are both in NP and NP-hard, with no known polynomial-time solution.
notes.example: N-Queens problem places $N$ non-attacking queens on an $N \times N$ chessboard using backtracking.
exam_points: P class problems are solvable in polynomial time; NP problems are verifiable in polynomial time.
Branch-and-bound optimizes state-space search by bounding optimal cost branches.

questions: Define asymptotic notations ($O$, $\Omega$, $\Theta$) with mathematical proofs and graphical representations.
State Master Theorem and apply it to solve recurrences like $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$ and $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^2$.
Explain Merge Sort and Quick Sort algorithms using divide-and-conquer, analyzing their time complexities.
Compare Greedy method and Dynamic Programming, solving the Fractional Knapsack vs 0/1 Knapsack.
Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem using Dynamic Programming with an illustrative numerical table.
Explain Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm and Matrix Chain Multiplication.
Explain the N-Queens problem and solve it using backtracking state-space trees.
Define P, NP, NP-Hard, and NP-Complete complexity classes with examples.

quiz.question: Which asymptotic notation represents the tight asymptotic bound (both upper and lower) of an algorithm's running time?
quiz.explanation: Theta notation ($\Theta$) bounds running time strictly from above and below by constant multiples.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm is optimal for solving the Fractional Knapsack problem?
quiz.explanation: Fractional Knapsack yields optimal results by greedily selecting items with the highest value-to-weight ratio.

quiz.question: Why must the 0/1 Knapsack problem be solved using Dynamic Programming rather than a Greedy approach?
options: Because items can be divided into fractions
Because items cannot be divided and greedy choice property fails
Because greedy is faster than dynamic programming
Because 0/1 knapsack has linear time complexity
quiz.explanation: In 0/1 knapsack, items are indivisible, and taking items greedily by value/weight fails to yield global optimums.

quiz.question: Which problem-solving strategy builds solutions incrementally and abandons branches that violate constraints?
quiz.explanation: Backtracking explores state-space search trees recursively, pruning branches violating constraints.

quiz.question: What does NP stand for in algorithmic complexity theory?
quiz.explanation: NP stands for Non-Deterministic Polynomial time, representing problems verifiable by a Turing machine in polynomial time.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence
objectives: CO1: Formulate state-space search problems and apply uninformed and heuristic search algorithms.
CO2: Represent knowledge using propositional and first-order logic, and inference rules.
CO3: Reason under uncertainty using probabilistic models, fuzzy logic, and machine learning fundamentals.

syllabus.topics: AI Foundations, Problem Formulations, State Space Search, Uninformed Search (BFS, DFS, Uniform Cost Search), Heuristic Search (A*, Greedy Best-First Search).
Knowledge Representation: Propositional Logic, First-Order Logic, Resolution Refutation, Forward and Backward Chaining, Ontologies.
Reasoning Under Uncertainty: Probabilistic Reasoning, Bayes' Theorem, Bayesian Networks, Fuzzy Logic and Fuzzy Sets.
Machine Learning Fundamentals: Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement Learning, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, Expert Systems.

notes.title: State Space Search & Heuristics
notes.explanation: Artificial Intelligence agents explore state spaces to achieve goal states using uninformed search or heuristic functions ($f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$).
definitions: A heuristic $h(n)$ that never overestimates the actual minimal cost to reach the goal state.
An informed search algorithm combining path cost $g(n)$ and heuristic estimate $h(n)$ to find optimal paths efficiently.
notes.example: A* search guarantees finding the shortest path when the heuristic function is admissible and consistent.
exam_points: BFS is optimal and complete on unweighted graphs; DFS is not optimal and may get trapped in infinite paths.
Greedy best-first search expands nodes closest to the goal based solely on $h(n)$.

notes.title: Knowledge Representation & Inference
notes.explanation: Knowledge representation encodes expert information using logic (Propositional and First-Order) and inference rules like resolution refutation.
definitions: A formal logical system employing objects, predicates, functions, and quantifiers ($\forall, \exists$).
A data-driven inference mechanism starting from known facts to derive new conclusions.
notes.example: Modus ponens inference rule: Given $P$ and $P \implies Q$, derive $Q$.
exam_points: Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-driven.
Resolution refutation proves theorem validity by deriving contradictions from negated goal clauses.

notes.title: Reasoning Under Uncertainty & Fuzzy Logic
notes.explanation: Real-world reasoning often deals with incomplete or probabilistic data managed via Bayes' theorem, Bayesian networks, and fuzzy logic sets.
definitions: A mathematical formula calculating conditional probability: $P(A|B) = \frac{P(B|A)P(A)}{P(B)}$.
A mathematical logic handling partial truth values ranging continuously between 0 and 1.
notes.example: Bayesian networks model probabilistic conditional dependencies among random variables in a directed acyclic graph.
exam_points: Fuzzy sets allow fractional degrees of membership rather than strict binary True/False logic.
Bayes' theorem updates probability estimates as new evidence becomes available.

notes.title: Machine Learning Fundamentals & Neural Networks
notes.explanation: Machine learning enables systems to learn from data via supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement algorithms, alongside artificial neural networks.
definitions: Machine learning paradigm where models are trained using labeled input-output training data.
A computing system inspired by biological neural networks, consisting of layered interconnected perceptrons.
notes.example: Decision trees classify data points by recursively splitting features based on entropy and information gain.
exam_points: Unsupervised learning discovers hidden patterns in unlabeled data (e.g., K-means clustering).
Reinforcement learning trains agents through rewards and penalties in dynamic environments.

questions: Explain A* search algorithm and prove its optimality conditions under admissible heuristics.
Compare uninformed search strategies (BFS, DFS, Uniform Cost Search) with heuristic search.
Differentiate between Propositional Logic and First-Order Logic with examples.
Explain Forward Chaining and Backward Chaining inference mechanisms with suitable rule-based scenarios.
State Bayes' Theorem and solve a medical diagnosis probabilistic reasoning problem.
Explain Bayesian Networks and Fuzzy Logic systems with comparative advantages.
Compare Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning paradigms.
Explain Artificial Neural Networks, activation functions, and Decision Tree induction algorithms.

quiz.question: What property must a heuristic function $h(n)$ possess to guarantee A* search optimality?
quiz.explanation: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the actual minimum cost to reach the goal, ensuring A* optimality.

quiz.question: Which inference mechanism in AI starts from known facts and applies rules to extract new conclusions in a data-driven manner?
quiz.explanation: Forward chaining is data-driven, firing rules whose premises are satisfied until a goal is reached.

quiz.question: Which mathematical theorem is fundamental for probabilistic reasoning and updating belief given new evidence?
quiz.explanation: Bayes' Theorem computes conditional probabilities $P(A|B)$ given prior beliefs and observed evidence.

quiz.question: Which machine learning paradigm trains models using labeled datasets containing both inputs and desired outputs?
quiz.explanation: Supervised learning algorithms (like regression and classification) train on explicitly labeled input-output pairs.

quiz.question: In fuzzy logic, what is the allowable range of truth values for set membership?
options: Any real number between 0 and 1 inclusive
quiz.explanation: Fuzzy logic permits continuous truth membership degrees anywhere between 0.0 (completely false) and 1.0 (completely true).

subjects.name: Database Management System-II
objectives: CO1: Master transaction processing, ACID properties, and conflict serializability.
CO2: Implement concurrency control protocols (2PL, timestamp ordering) and recovery mechanisms.
CO3: Explore distributed databases, two-phase commit, and NoSQL document databases like MongoDB.

syllabus.topics: Transaction Processing: ACID Properties, Transaction States, Schedules, Serializability (Conflict & View Serializability).
Concurrency Control: Lock-Based Protocols (2PL, Strict 2PL), Timestamp Ordering Protocols, Deadlock Handling in Databases.
Database Recovery: Failure Classification, Log-Based Recovery (Deferred and Immediate Update), Checkpoints, Shadow Paging.
Distributed Databases & NoSQL: Distributed DBMS Architecture, 2-Phase Commit Protocol, NoSQL Databases (Document, Key-Value, Graph, Column-Family), MongoDB Basics.

notes.title: Transactions & Serializability
notes.explanation: DBMS-II focuses on transaction processing, guaranteeing ACID compliance and conflict serializability across concurrent database transactions.
definitions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability: Core guarantees ensuring reliable transaction execution.
A schedule is conflict serializable if it is conflict equivalent to some serial schedule.
notes.example: Precedence graphs determine whether a concurrent transaction schedule is conflict serializable.
exam_points: Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution; Durability ensures committed updates survive system crashes.
View serializability is more general than conflict serializability but NP-complete to check.

notes.title: Concurrency Control & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Concurrency control protocols like Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Timestamp Ordering prevent interference among concurrent transactions.
definitions: A locking protocol with a growing phase (acquiring locks) followed by a shrinking phase (releasing locks).
A state where two or more transactions are permanently blocked waiting for locks held by each other.
notes.example: Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until the transaction commits, preventing cascading aborts.
exam_points: Deadlocks are handled via deadlock prevention (wait-die, wound-wait) or deadlock detection (wait-for graphs).
Timestamp ordering protocols serialize transactions based on transaction arrival timestamps.

notes.title: Database Recovery Systems
notes.explanation: Recovery mechanisms restore database consistency after system crashes using write-ahead logs (WAL) and checkpointing.
definitions: A recovery technique requiring log records for any database modification to be written to disk before the actual data.
A recovery scheme maintaining two page tables during transaction execution to ensure atomicity without logs.
notes.example: Deferred update logs changes and applies them to the database only after transaction commits successfully.
exam_points: Checkpoints reduce recovery search overhead by flushing modified buffer blocks to disk periodically.
Immediate update modifies database items during transaction execution, requiring UNDO and REDO recovery passes.

notes.title: Distributed Databases & NoSQL (MongoDB)
notes.explanation: Distributed databases spread data across multiple physical sites, coordinated via Two-Phase Commit, while NoSQL databases handle unstructured data.
definitions: An atomic commitment protocol ensuring all participating nodes commit or abort in a distributed transaction.
Non-relational databases designed for unstructured, high-velocity data storage (Document, Key-Value, Graph).
notes.example: MongoDB stores data in flexible, schema-less BSON (Binary JSON) documents.
exam_points: CAP theorem states a distributed system can simultaneously provide at most two of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.
MongoDB provides rich querying, indexing, and horizontal scaling via sharding.

questions: Explain the ACID properties of database transactions with real-world examples.
Define conflict serializability and explain how precedence graphs test schedule serializability.
Explain Two-Phase Locking (2PL), Strict 2PL, and Rigorous 2PL concurrency protocols.
Discuss deadlock handling mechanisms in databases, comparing deadlock prevention and detection.
Explain Log-Based Recovery (Deferred and Immediate update) and the role of Checkpoints.
Compare Log-Based Recovery with Shadow Paging techniques.
Explain Distributed Database Architecture and the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol.
Compare Relational RDBMS with NoSQL databases and discuss MongoDB document data models.

quiz.question: Which ACID property ensures that transaction modifications are permanent and survive system crashes?
quiz.explanation: Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, its updates will not be lost due to subsequent failures.

quiz.question: During which phase of Two-Phase Locking (2PL) are locks allowed to be released by a transaction?
quiz.explanation: In the Shrinking Phase of 2PL, transactions can release existing locks but are forbidden from acquiring new ones.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) in database recovery?
options: To speed up SQL query execution
To ensure log records are safely persisted on disk before database modifications are written
quiz.explanation: WAL requires log records of changes to be written to stable storage before data pages, enabling reliable crash recovery.

quiz.question: Which protocol guarantees atomic transaction commitment across multiple distributed database nodes?
quiz.explanation: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) ensures all nodes in a distributed network agree to commit or abort a transaction.

quiz.question: Which data format is natively used by MongoDB to store flexible document records?
quiz.explanation: MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents encoded in BSON (Binary JSON) for efficiency and schema flexibility.

subjects.name: Design Thinking and Innovation
objectives: CO1: Understand design thinking philosophy, human-centric empathy, and problem framing.
CO2: Master ideation techniques, rapid prototyping, and iterative user testing.
CO3: Apply innovation frameworks to solve real-world complex problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Design Thinking: Philosophy, Mindset, Empathy, Human-Centered Design, Problem Statement Definition (Point of View), Stakeholder Mapping.
Ideation & Divergent Thinking: Brainstorming Techniques, Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, How Might We (HMW) Questions, Concept Selection.
Prototyping & User Testing: Low-fidelity vs High-fidelity prototypes, Storyboarding, Paper Prototyping, Usability Testing, Feedback Loops.
Innovation & Implementation: Business Innovation Models, Case Studies, Pitching Ideas, Scaling Creative Solutions in Organizations.

notes.title: Human-Centered Design & Empathy
notes.explanation: Design thinking is a human-centric problem-solving framework starting with deep empathy for user needs and experiential observation.
definitions: A collaborative visualization tool capturing user behaviors and attitudes (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels).
An approach putting human needs, capabilities, and behaviors first in the design of products and services.
notes.example: Conducting qualitative user interviews uncovers latent needs that quantitative surveys miss.
exam_points: The 5 core stages of design thinking are: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test.
Defining a clear Point of View (POV) problem statement guides effective ideation.

notes.title: Ideation & Divergent Thinking
notes.explanation: Ideation encourages expansive, divergent thinking through brainstorming, SCAMPER, and mind-mapping to generate diverse creative solutions.
definitions: An ideation technique prompting innovation through Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse.
A group creativity technique generating a large volume of ideas without premature criticism.
notes.example: How Might We (HMW) questions transform identified user pain points into actionable creative prompts.
exam_points: Divergent thinking expands solution options; convergent thinking narrows them down to the best concept.

notes.title: Prototyping & User Testing
notes.explanation: Prototyping brings abstract ideas into tangible artifacts, enabling rapid usability testing and iterative feedback collection.
definitions: A quick, inexpensive mock-up (like paper sketches or wireframes) used to test early concepts.
Evaluating a prototype by observing real users interacting with it to identify friction points.
notes.example: Paper prototyping lets designers test user workflows within minutes before writing any code.
exam_points: Prototypes should be built with the user in mind to answer specific testable questions.
Feedback loops refine solutions iteratively based on user reactions.

notes.title: Innovation Frameworks & Implementation
notes.explanation: Translating innovative designs into sustainable real-world impact requires strategic storytelling, pitching, and organizational scaling.
definitions: The successful implementation of creative ideas to generate economic or social value.
A concise presentation providing investors an overview of a business innovation and value proposition.
notes.example: Successful innovation balances desirability (user needs), feasibility (technical capability), and viability (business model).
exam_points: Storytelling connects emotionally with stakeholders during innovation pitches.

questions: Explain the 5 stages of Design Thinking and the importance of empathy in problem framing.
How do empathy maps and stakeholder interviews help define accurate Point of View (POV) problem statements?
Discuss divergent thinking techniques: Brainstorming, Mind Mapping, and the SCAMPER method.
Explain how 'How Might We' (HMW) questions bridge problem definition and ideation.
Differentiate between low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototypes with examples of when to use each.
Explain the process of usability testing and gathering actionable user feedback.
Discuss the three lenses of innovation: Desirability, Feasibility, and Viability.
How do you structure an effective innovation pitch deck to present creative solutions to stakeholders?

quiz.question: What is the first fundamental stage in the Design Thinking process framework?
quiz.explanation: Design Thinking begins with Empathize to understand user needs, emotions, and pain points.

quiz.question: What does the acronym SCAMPER stand for in ideation and creative problem-solving?
options: Speed, Cost, Analysis, Management, Planning, Execution, Review
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse
Scale, Create, Assess, Measure, Pivot, Evaluate, Refine
System, Concept, Algorithm, Model, Process, Engine, Routine
quiz.explanation: SCAMPER is a powerful ideation checklist prompting creative modifications to existing products or concepts.

quiz.question: Which type of prototype is typically quick, inexpensive, and built using paper sketches or wireframes?
quiz.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes use simple materials like paper to test concepts rapidly without heavy investment.

quiz.question: What are the three core lenses required for successful innovation according to design thinking?
quiz.explanation: Innovation sits at the intersection of user desirability, technical feasibility, and business viability.

quiz.question: What is the primary objective of a pitch presentation for an innovative project?
options: To communicate the value proposition, problem, and solution concisely to stakeholders
quiz.explanation: A pitch deck communicates the core innovation, market opportunity, and feasibility clearly to secure support.

subjects.name: Programming in PHP
objectives: CO1: Master PHP syntax, server-side scripting constructs, and dynamic variables.
CO2: Implement user-defined functions, string manipulation, and array operations.
CO3: Handle HTML forms, superglobals, file I/O operations, and MySQL database connectivity.

syllabus.topics: Evolution of PHP & its comparison, Interfaces to External systems, Hardware and Software requirements, PHP Scripting, Basic PHP Development, Working of PHP scripts, Basic PHP syntax, PHP data types. Displaying type information: Testing for a specific data type, Changing type with settype(), Operators, Variable manipulation, Dynamic variables, Variable scope.

Control Statements: if() and elseif() condition Statement, The switch statement, Using the ternary (?) Operator, Using the while() Loop, The do-while statement, Using the for() Loop. Functions: Function definition, Creation, Returning values, Library Functions, User-defined functions, Dynamic function, default arguments, Passing arguments by value. String Manipulation: Formatting String for Presentation, Formatting String for Storage, Joining and Splitting String, Comparing String. Array: Anatomy of an Array, Creating index based and Associative array, Looping array using each() and foreach() loop.

Forms: Working with Forms, Super global variables, Super global array, Importing user input, Accessing user input, Combine HTML and PHP code, Using hidden fields, Redirecting the user. Working with File and Directories: Understanding file & directory, Opening and closing a file, Copying, renaming and deleting a file, Working with directories, File Uploading & Downloading. Generating Images with PHP: Basic computer Graphics, Creating Image.
Database Connectivity with MySQL: Introduction to RDBMS, Connection with MySQL Database, Performing basic database operations (DML) (Insert, Delete, Update, Select).

notes.title: PHP Syntax & Variable Fundamentals
notes.explanation: PHP is a server-side scripting language executed on the web server. PHP scripts are embedded inside HTML documents using standard open and close tags, outputting rendered HTML to client browsers.
definitions: Variables whose names are dynamically set and evaluated using double dollar signs ($$var_name).
A built-in PHP function used to explicitly convert or cast the data type of an existing variable.
notes.example:
<?php
  $var = 'college';
  $$var = 'CGC Landran';
  echo $college; // Prints: CGC Landran
?>
exam_points: Variable scope in PHP includes local, global, and static keywords.
Function is_type() (e.g., is_int(), is_string()) tests for specific data types.

notes.title: Control Structures, Functions & Arrays
notes.explanation: PHP provides flexible control structures, modular user-defined functions, and robust associative arrays to manage data collection and processing.
definitions: An array using named key identifiers mapped to corresponding values rather than standard numeric indexes.
Passing function arguments by copying their values, leaving the original variable unchanged outside the function.
notes.example: $grades = array('Math' => 90, 'Science' => 85); creates an associative array in PHP.
exam_points: foreach() is the most efficient loop construct for iterating through associative and indexed arrays.
String manipulation functions like strlen(), strpos(), and explode() format text for presentation and storage.

notes.title: Form Handling & File Operations
notes.explanation: PHP handles HTTP POST and GET user input securely via superglobal arrays ($_POST, $_GET, $_FILES) and manages server-side file systems.
definitions: Built-in PHP associative arrays accessible from any scope without global declarations (e.g., $_POST, $_SESSION).
Mechanism using fopen(), fread(), fwrite(), and fclose() to manipulate external text and binary files.
notes.example: $username = $_POST['user']; retrieves form input securely.
exam_points: Always validate and sanitize user inputs to prevent XSS and SQL injection vulnerabilities.
File uploading requires proper form attribute enctype='multipart/form-data'.

notes.title: MySQL Database Connectivity & DML Operations
notes.explanation: PHP connects seamlessly with relational MySQL databases using MySQLi extensions to execute DML queries (Insert, Select, Update, Delete).
definitions: MySQL Improved extension providing procedural and object-oriented interfaces to interact with MySQL databases.
Acronym for Create, Read, Update, and Delete database operations performed via SQL queries.
notes.example: $conn = mysqli_connect('localhost', 'root', '', 'db'); establishes a MySQL connection.
exam_points: Always check connection errors using mysqli_connect_error().
Use prepared statements to secure database queries against malicious SQL injections.

questions: Explain dynamic variables in PHP with a code example.
Differentiate between settype() and gettype() functions.
Explain indexed and associative arrays in PHP with code snippets.
Discuss user-defined functions and passing arguments by value versus reference.
Explain form handling in PHP using $_POST and $_GET superglobal arrays.
Write a PHP script to open, read, write, and close a text file on the server.
Explain MySQL database connection establishment in PHP using MySQLi.
Write a complete PHP script to execute INSERT and SELECT queries on a MySQL table.

quiz.question: Which function is used to change the data type of an existing variable in PHP?
quiz.explanation: settype() dynamically modifies the type of a given variable.

quiz.question: Which array type in PHP uses named string keys to access stored values?
quiz.explanation: Associative arrays use custom named keys mapped to values.

quiz.question: Which superglobal array is used to collect form data submitted via HTTP POST method?
quiz.explanation: $_POST collects form data passed through HTTP POST requests.

quiz.question: Which function opens a connection to a MySQL database server in PHP MySQLi extension?
quiz.explanation: mysqli_connect() establishes a new connection to the MySQL database server.

quiz.question: Which SQL statement is used to retrieve records from a database table via PHP?
quiz.explanation: SELECT is the DML query used to query and retrieve records from database tables.

subjects.name: Java Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming principles and Java architecture.
CO2: Implement classes, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, and packages.
CO3: Master exception handling, multithreading, and I/O streams in Java.

syllabus.topics: Java Programming Fundamentals: Introduction to Java, Stage for Java, Origin, Challenges of Java, Java Features, Java Program Development, Object Oriented Programming. Java Essentials: Elements of Java Program, Java API, Variables and Literals, Primitive Data Types, The String class, Variables, Constants, Operators, Scope of Variables & Blocks, Types of Comment in Java.

Control Statements: Decision making statements (if, if-else, nested if, else if ladder, switch, conditional operator), Looping statements (while, do-while, for, nested loops), Jumping statements (Break and Continue). Classes and Objects: Basic concepts of OOPS, Classes and Objects, Modifiers, Passing arguments, Constructors, Overloaded Constructors, Overloaded Operators, Static Class Members, Garbage Collection. Inheritance: Basics of inheritance, Inheriting and Overriding Superclass methods, Calling Superclass Constructor, Polymorphism, Abstract Classes, Final Class.

Arrays and Strings: Introduction to array, Processing Array Contents, Passing array as argument, Returning array from methods, Array of objects, 2D arrays, Array with three or more dimensions. String class, string concatenation, Comparing strings, Substring, Difference between String and String Buffer class, String Tokenizer class. Interface and Packages: Basics of interface, Multiple Interfaces, Multiple Inheritance Using Interface, Multilevel Interface, Packages, Create and Access Packages, Static Import and Package Class, Access Specifiers. Exception Handling: Introduction, Try and Catch Blocks, Multiple Catch, Nested Try, Finally, Throw Statement, Built-In Exceptions.

Multithreading: Introduction, Threads in Java, Thread Creation, Lifecycle of Thread, Joining a Thread, Thread Scheduler, Thread Priority, Thread Synchronization. Applets: Introduction, Applet Class, Applet Life Cycle, Graphics in Applet, Event-Handling. File and I/O Streams: File Class, Streams, Byte Streams, Filtered Byte Streams, Random Access File Class, Character Streams.

notes.title: Java Architecture & Features
notes.explanation: Java is a platform-independent, object-oriented language. Source code is compiled into platform-neutral bytecode (.class) and executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
definitions: Highly optimized set of instructions designed to be executed by the JVM.
Java's 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' capability enabled by the JVM across operating systems.
notes.example: public class Hello { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello"); } }
exam_points: Primitive data types include byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean.
JDK includes JRE and development tools like javac.

notes.title: OOPs, Classes, Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Java enforces object-oriented principles through classes, objects, inheritance, method overloading, method overriding, and abstract classes.
definitions: The ability of an object to take on many forms, implemented via method overloading (compile-time) and overriding (run-time).
A restricted class that cannot be used to create objects directly and may contain abstract methods.
notes.example: extends keyword implements single inheritance in Java classes.
