notes.explanation: Optimizing industrial microbial yields requires precise control over batch and continuous growth kinetics alongside genetic strain selection.
definitions: The time required for a microbial population to double in cell number during exponential growth.
notes.example: Using chemostats to maintain steady-state continuous microbial culture growth for continuous metabolite harvest.
exam_points: Mutagenesis and recombinant screening enhance hyper-producing microbial strains for antibiotic synthesis.

notes.title: Host-Pathogen Interactions & Quorum Sensing
notes.explanation: Pathogenic microbes utilize virulence factors and cell-density signaling mechanisms to establish infections and evade host immunity.
definitions: A cell-density dependent regulatory mechanism where bacteria communicate via secreted autoinducer signaling molecules.
notes.example: Regulating biofilm formation and toxin secretion in Pseudomonas aeruginosa via quorum sensing circuits.
exam_points: Pathogenicity islands are distinct genetic loci encoding clusters of virulence genes acquired via horizontal gene transfer.

notes.title: Industrial Fermentation & Food Microbiology
notes.explanation: Applied microbiology utilizes controlled fermentations to produce industrial solvents, organic acids, antibiotics, and safe food products.
definitions: A compound produced during the active exponential growth phase of a microorganism (e.g., ethanol, citric acid).
notes.example: Industrial production of penicillin antibiotics using submerged cultures of Penicillium chrysogenum.
exam_points: Food preservation techniques (pasteurization, refrigeration, irradiation) inhibit spoilage microbial proliferation.

questions: Compare the cellular ultrastructure of Archaea and Eubacteria with unicellular yeasts.
Describe the structural classification and replication cycle of animal and bacterial viruses.
Explain microbial growth kinetics under batch, fed-batch, and continuous cultivation systems.
Discuss strain improvement strategies using chemical mutagenesis and recombinant screening.
What are pathogenicity islands? Discuss their role in bacterial virulence and host-pathogen interactions.
Explain quorum sensing mechanisms and their significance in bacterial biofilm coordination.
Discuss industrial fermentation processes for producing commercial ethanol and organic acids.
Explain food preservation methods and the role of beneficial microbes in food additive manufacturing.

quiz.question: What cell-density dependent communication mechanism do bacteria use to coordinate collective behaviors like biofilm formation?
quiz.explanation: Quorum sensing enables bacteria to monitor population density via autoinducer signaling molecules.

quiz.question: What term describes a virus that specifically infects and replicates within bacterial cells?
quiz.explanation: Bacteriophages are specialized viruses targeting bacterial hosts.

quiz.question: During which microbial growth phase do secondary metabolites like antibiotics typically accumulate?
quiz.explanation: Secondary metabolites are usually synthesized during the stationary phase when nutrient limitation occurs.

quiz.question: What device is used to maintain continuous microbial culture by constantly adding fresh nutrient medium while removing spent culture?
quiz.explanation: A chemostat is a continuous culture bioreactor maintaining constant microbial growth rates.

subjects.name: Introduction to Microbiology
objectives: CO1: Understand historical developments in microbiology, biogenesis vs. abiogenesis, and Koch's postulates.
CO2: Master microbial classification, morphology, cell wall structure (Gram-positive vs. Gram-negative), and sporulation.
CO3: Analyze microbial growth kinetics, nutritional biodiversity, extremophiles, and sterilization techniques.

syllabus.topics: History of microbiology: Leeuwenhoek, Pasteur, Koch, Lister, Tyndall, biogenesis vs. abiogenesis, Koch's postulates, antibiotic discovery. Microscopy principles: Bright field, dark field, phase contrast, fluorescent, and electron microscopy.

Microbial classification (bacteria, fungi, algae). Morphology and bacterial cell wall structure (Gram-positive and Gram-negative). Microbial spores, sporulation, germination, and agricultural nitrogen-fixing microbes.

Microbial growth, nutritional biodiversity, growth phases, generation time, growth rates, monoauxic, diauxic, and synchronous growth, chemostat. Extremophiles (high temperature, extreme pH). Sterilization and pasteurization.
Normal human microflora, microbial pathogens and diseases. Microbial interactions (symbiosis, antibiosis). Aerobic/anaerobic fermentation and heterologous protein production.

notes.title: Historical Milestones & Microscopy
notes.explanation: Microbiology emerged through foundational experiments disproving spontaneous generation and establishing germ theory via Koch's postulates.
definitions: A series of four scientific criteria established to identify the causative microorganism of a specific infectious disease.
notes.example: Utilizing bright field and phase contrast microscopy to observe unstained live bacterial wet mounts.
exam_points: Louis Pasteur developed pasteurization and attenuated vaccines for anthrax and rabies.

notes.title: Bacterial Structure & Cell Walls
notes.explanation: Bacterial architecture is distinguished by peptidoglycan cell wall composition, differentiating Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms.
definitions: A rigid polymer matrix of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by peptide chains forming bacterial cell walls.
notes.example: Performing Gram staining to distinguish thick peptidoglycan Gram-positive cells from thin Gram-negative cells.
exam_points: Endospores formed by Bacillus and Clostridium species confer extreme resistance against thermal and chemical stress.

notes.title: Microbial Growth Kinetics & Extremophiles
notes.explanation: Microbial populations multiply via binary fission, exhibiting predictable batch growth phases and adapting to extreme environmental niches.
definitions: A continuous culture bioreactor that maintains exponential microbial growth by continuously supplying fresh nutrients.
notes.example: Culturing thermophilic bacteria in hot springs operating at temperatures exceeding 80 degrees Celsius.
exam_points: Autoclaving utilizes pressurized steam at 121 degrees Celsius for complete sterilization of laboratory media.

notes.title: Pathogens & Microbial Interactions
notes.explanation: Human microflora coexist symbiotically, whereas pathogenic microbes deploy virulence factors causing infectious diseases.
definitions: A close and long-term biological interaction between two different biological organism species.
notes.example: Mutualistic nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria inhabiting legume plant root nodules.
exam_points: Recombinant microbes are engineered industrially to express therapeutic heterologous human proteins.

questions: Discuss the contributions of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in establishing the germ theory of disease.
Compare bright field, phase contrast, and electron microscopy in resolving microbial ultrastructure.
Differentiate between the cell wall ultrastructure of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
Describe the mechanism of bacterial endospore formation, sporulation, and subsequent germination.
Explain the phases of microbial batch growth and define generation time and specific growth rate.
Discuss physiological adaptations of extremophilic microorganisms thriving in high temperature and pH extremes.
Explain the significance of normal human microflora and evaluate common pathogenic mechanisms.
Discuss microbial symbiosis and the industrial production of heterologous proteins using bacterial hosts.

quiz.question: Which scientific criteria established by Robert Koch prove that a specific organism causes a specific disease?
quiz.explanation: Koch's postulates define experimental criteria linking specific infectious agents to specific diseases.

quiz.question: What primary polymer constitutes the rigid cell wall matrix of bacteria?
quiz.explanation: Peptidoglycan provides structural rigidity and shape to bacterial cell walls.

quiz.question: What standard temperature and pressure conditions are utilized in an autoclave for effective sterilization?
quiz.explanation: Autoclaving uses saturated steam under 15 psi pressure reaching 121°C to kill all microbial life and spores.

quiz.question: What term describes continuous culture systems that maintain constant cell density by regulating nutrient inflow?
quiz.explanation: A chemostat maintains continuous logarithmic microbial growth by balancing nutrient input and waste removal.

Bachelor of Science (Hons) in Nutrition.full_name: Bachelor of Science (Hons) in Nutrition and Dietetics

subjects.name: Principles of Human Nutrition
objectives: CO1: Understand fundamental concepts of human nutrition, food groups, malnutrition, and nutritional status assessment methods.
CO2: Develop knowledge of metabolism, functions, sources, and deficiencies of water, energy, carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
CO3: Gain proficiency in formulating Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA) and balanced diet guidelines.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Human Nutrition: Concept of nutrition, food groups and functions, history and scope, malnutrition types and health impact, assessment methods (dietary surveys, anthropometry, clinical signs, biochemistry), balanced diet, RDA, dietary guidelines, nutrition education, policies, non-conventional foods, water functions, metabolism, sources, and deficiency.
Energy, Carbohydrates, and Fat Metabolism: Detailed functions, metabolism, sources, and deficiency of energy and carbohydrates in the human body.
Proteins and Fats: Functions, metabolism, sources, and deficiencies of proteins focusing on growth, repair, and bodily functions, alongside detailed analysis of dietary fats.
Vitamins and Minerals: Functions, metabolism, sources, and deficiencies of essential vitamins and minerals maintaining physiological balance.

notes.title: Introduction to Human Nutrition
notes.explanation: Human nutrition studies physiological utilization of food nutrients to maintain health, prevent deficiency diseases, and sustain optimal growth.
definitions: The daily dietary intake level considered sufficient to meet nutrient requirements of nearly all healthy individuals.
notes.example: Assessing community nutritional status using anthropometric measurements such as BMI and mid-upper arm circumference.
exam_points: Malnutrition encompasses both undernutrition (protein-energy malnutrition) and overnutrition (obesity and micronutrient excess).

notes.title: Energy & Carbohydrate Metabolism
notes.explanation: Carbohydrates serve as the primary dietary energy source, metabolizing through glycolysis and cellular respiration into ATP.
definitions: A relative ranking of carbohydrate in foods according to how much they raise blood glucose levels after eating.
notes.example: Comparing complex polysaccharides (dietary fiber, starch) against simple sugars in metabolic energy provision.
exam_points: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) represents the minimum energy expenditure required to sustain vital organ functioning at rest.

notes.title: Proteins & Dietary Fats
notes.explanation: Proteins provide essential amino acids for tissue synthesis, whereas dietary lipids supply concentrated energy and essential fatty acids.
definitions: Amino acids that cannot be synthesized de novo by human metabolism and must be obtained through dietary intake.
notes.example: Combining cereal and legume proteins to achieve mutual complementation of essential amino acids.
exam_points: Unsaturated fatty acids (omega-3 and omega-6) play critical roles in reducing cardiovascular disease risks.

notes.title: Vitamins & Minerals
notes.explanation: Vitamins and minerals act as vital cofactors, coenzymes, and structural electrolytes regulating human metabolic homeostasis.
definitions: Essential dietary nutrients required in small quantities (vitamins and minerals) for vital physiological functions.
notes.example: Preventing iron-deficiency anemia by consuming iron-rich foods combined with vitamin C enhancers.
exam_points: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in hepatic and adipose tissues, whereas water-soluble vitamins require regular intake.

questions: Discuss methods used for assessing nutritional status in individuals and communities.
Explain the concept of a balanced diet and the formulation of Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA).
Explain the classification, digestion, and metabolic utilization of dietary carbohydrates.
Discuss factors influencing Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) and total daily energy expenditure.
What are essential amino acids? Discuss protein quality evaluation methods and nitrogen balance.
Classify dietary lipids and evaluate the health implications of saturated versus unsaturated fatty acids.
Classify vitamins into fat-soluble and water-soluble categories, detailing deficiency disorders for each.
Discuss the physiological functions and dietary sources of major macro-minerals and trace elements.

quiz.question: What term describes amino acids that cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be acquired through diet?
quiz.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized endogenously and must be supplied by dietary protein sources.

quiz.question: Which fat-soluble vitamin deficiency leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin A is essential for visual pigment synthesis in retinal photoreceptor cells; deficiency causes night blindness.

quiz.question: What index measures how rapidly blood glucose levels rise following carbohydrate ingestion?
quiz.explanation: The Glycemic Index ranks carbohydrates based on their immediate postprandial blood glucose response.

quiz.question: Which mineral is a core structural component of hemoglobin enabling oxygen transport in red blood cells?
quiz.explanation: Iron is the central transition metal in heme molecules binding oxygen molecules within erythrocytes.

B.Sc. ATHM(2020 onwards).full_name: Bachelor of Science in Airlines, Tourism and Hospitality Management (B.Sc. ATHM )

subjects.name: Mathematics
objectives: CO1: Represent data using various mathematical notions and set theory operations.
CO2: Explain logical connectives, truth tables, tautologies, and contradictions.
CO3: Apply matrix algebra and arithmetic/geometric progression formulas to solve mathematical problems.

syllabus.topics: Set Introduction, objectives, representation of sets (Roster, Set Builder), types of sets (null, singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent, disjoint, subset, power set, universal), and set operations (union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference, complement).
Logic Statement, connectives, basic logic operations (conjunction, disjunction, negation), logical equivalence, tautologies, and contradictions.

Matrices Introduction, types of matrices (row, column, rectangular, square, diagonal, scalar, unit, null, comparable, equal), scalar multiplication, addition, subtraction, multiplication, and transpose of matrices.
Progressions: Arithmetic Progression (A.P.), sum of finite number of quantities in A.P., arithmetic means, Geometric Progression (G.P.), and geometric means.

notes.title: Set Theory & Operations
notes.explanation: Set theory provides the fundamental mathematical framework for organizing discrete data collections and logical relations.
definitions: The set of all subsets of a given set, including the empty set and the set itself.
notes.example: Calculating the union and intersection of sets A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}.
exam_points: De Morgan's laws govern complement relations over union and intersection operations in set theory.

notes.title: Mathematical Logic & Propositional Calculus
notes.explanation: Propositional logic evaluates truth values of logical statements connected via logical operators.
definitions: A propositional formula that is true under all possible truth value assignments.
notes.example: Constructing truth tables to prove logical equivalence between conditional propositions and their contrapositives.
exam_points: Conjunction ($\land$) is true only when both constituent propositions are true.

notes.title: Matrix Algebra
notes.explanation: Matrices organize multidimensional numerical data arrays essential for linear transformations and machine learning feature representations.
definitions: A square matrix in which all elements outside the main diagonal are zero.
notes.example: Multiplying two compatible matrices to yield a resultant transformation matrix.
exam_points:
Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive, but generally not commutative ($AB 
eq BA$).

notes.title: Progressions & Series
notes.explanation: Arithmetic and geometric progressions model discrete sequential numerical growth patterns and iterative algorithms.
definitions: A sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero common ratio.
notes.example: Finding the sum of the first 10 terms of a geometric progression with common ratio 2.
exam_points: The nth term of an arithmetic progression is given by $a_n = a + (n-1)d$.

questions: Define power set and universal set. Illustrate set difference and symmetric difference using Venn diagrams.
Verify De Morgan's laws using illustrative set examples.
Construct truth tables to determine whether the proposition $(p \land q) \to p$ is a tautology.
Define logical equivalence and explain conjunction, disjunction, and negation operators.
Perform matrix multiplication on two given 3x3 matrices and find their transpose.
Classify different types of matrices with mathematical examples for each.
Find the sum of n terms of an arithmetic progression whose first term is 'a' and common difference is 'd'.
Explain geometric progression and calculate the geometric mean between two numbers.

quiz.question: What is a propositional formula that evaluates to true under every possible truth value assignment called?
quiz.explanation: A tautology is a compound statement that is unconditionally true regardless of the truth values of its atomic propositions.

quiz.question: What matrix type is a square matrix with zeros everywhere except along the main diagonal?
quiz.explanation: A diagonal matrix has non-zero elements exclusively on its principal diagonal.

quiz.question: If set A has 3 elements, how many elements reside in its power set $P(A)$?
quiz.explanation: The number of elements in the power set of a set with n elements is $2^n$. Here $2^3 = 8$.

quiz.question: What is the common ratio of the geometric progression 2, 6, 18, 54, ...?
quiz.explanation: Dividing any term by its preceding term ($6/2 = 3$) yields the common ratio 3.

subjects.name: Fundamentals of Computer and IT
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware components, input/output devices, and data representation systems.
CO2: Learn functional units of computer architecture and operating system interface functions.
CO3: Understand basic office productivity software and responsible internet usage.

syllabus.topics: Human-Computer Interface: Hardware and software, data vs. information. Functional units of computer systems (CPU, registers, system bus, main memory, cache). Devices: Input and output devices. Memory: Primary, secondary, auxiliary memory, RAM, ROM, hard disks, optical disks. Data representation: Binary, decimal, hexadecimal, octal systems, conversions, binary arithmetic.
Concept of computing, language types (machine, assembly, high-level). Operating systems as user interfaces, utility programs, file management, and system booting.
Office Productivity Software: Basic word processing, spreadsheet calculations, and presentation graphics software tools.
Internet and Information Technology: Networking fundamentals, World Wide Web, web browsers, electronic mail, cybersecurity basics, and safe, legal, responsible internet utilization.

notes.title: Computer Hardware & Data Representation
notes.explanation: Computer systems process data by translating human input into binary machine code executed through hardware functional units.
definitions: The primary electronic circuitry within a computer carrying out instructions of computer programs.
notes.example: Converting decimal integers into hexadecimal and binary representations for computer memory storage.
exam_points: Primary memory (RAM) is volatile, whereas secondary storage (HDD/SSD) provides persistent data retention.

notes.title: Software & Operating Systems
notes.explanation: Operating systems manage computer hardware resources and provide common services for application software execution.
definitions: System software managing computer hardware, software resources, and providing common services for computer programs.
notes.example: Booting up a computer system and managing file directories through graphical user interfaces (GUI).
exam_points: High-level programming languages require compilers or interpreters to translate source code into machine executable binary.

notes.title: Office Productivity Applications
notes.explanation: Productivity software suites streamline document creation, tabular data analysis, and professional presentations.
definitions: An interactive computer application for organization, analysis, and storage of data in tabular form.
notes.example: Using spreadsheet formulas and charts to analyze experimental dataset metrics.
exam_points: Word processors format textual documents, while presentation software utilizes slide decks for visual communication.

notes.title: Internet & Cybersecurity
notes.explanation: Global networking infrastructure connects computers worldwide, necessitating safe, ethical, and secure digital communication practices.
definitions: An information space where documents and web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators (URLs).
notes.example: Navigating web browsers securely using HTTPS encrypted protocols.
exam_points: Cyber hygiene practices protect against malware, phishing attacks, and unauthorized network intrusions.

questions: Describe the functional units of a computer system and explain the role of the CPU and cache memory.
Perform binary arithmetic: add binary numbers 101102 and 11012, and convert decimal 255 into hexadecimal.
Explain the role of an operating system as a user interface and resource manager.
Distinguish between machine language, assembly language, and high-level programming languages.
Discuss the key features and applications of word processing and electronic spreadsheet software.
Explain how presentation graphics software enhances professional communication.
Explain internet fundamentals, URL structures, and the role of web browsers.
Discuss cybersecurity best practices and safe, responsible internet utilization.

quiz.question: Which memory type is volatile and loses its stored data when computer power is turned off?
quiz.explanation: RAM is volatile primary memory requiring electrical power to maintain stored data.

quiz.question: What system software manages computer hardware resources and provides user interface services?
quiz.explanation: An operating system acts as the intermediary bridge between computer hardware and user applications.

quiz.question: What is the binary equivalent of the decimal number 5?
quiz.explanation: Decimal 5 in binary is represented as $4 + 1 = 101_2$.

quiz.question: Which protocol secures web browsing traffic through encrypted communication channels?
quiz.explanation: HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts web data using SSL/TLS protocols.

B.Sc. Graphics and Web Designing.full_name: Bachelor of Science in Graphics and Web Designing (B.Sc. Graphics and Web Designing)

subjects.name: Mathematics for Design
objectives: CO1: Apply mathematical principles and algebraic methods to graphic and web design problems.
CO2: Use geometric and trigonometric concepts for visual composition, golden ratio, and layout design.
CO3: Perform calculations involving digital measurements, pixels, resolution (PPI/DPI), and color systems (RGB, CMYK, Hex).

syllabus.topics: Number systems, scale factors, dimensional calculations, golden ratio, mathematical proportions in design, patterns and symmetry in visual communication.
Basic geometric shapes and properties, angles, polygons, circles, coordinate geometry fundamentals, trigonometric functions, angles and distances in computer graphics.

Vectors and vector notation, vector addition/subtraction, dot product, geometric interpretation, matrix concepts, determinants, inverse matrices, and matrix representation of geometric transformations.

Digital units (pixels, points, picas, inches, centimeters), image dimensions, aspect ratios, screen resolution (PPI and DPI), file size estimation, storage calculations, RGB, CMYK, hexadecimal color values, 2D transformations (translation, rotation, scaling, reflection).
Mathematical modeling in computer graphics, parametric representation of curves, Bézier curves, spline concepts, surface representations, 3D coordinate systems, projection and viewing concepts.

notes.title: Proportions & Golden Ratio in Design
notes.explanation: Mathematical proportions and the golden ratio provide harmonious structural foundations for visual aesthetics and graphic layouts.
definitions: A mathematical ratio approximately equal to 1.618, often used to create aesthetically pleasing compositions in art and design.
notes.example: Applying the golden spiral grid structure to frame web UI layout components and typography hierarchy.
exam_points: Proportional scaling maintains visual balance across varying display aspect ratios.

notes.title: Coordinate Geometry & Trigonometry
notes.explanation: Coordinate geometry and trigonometric functions govern spatial positioning and vector calculations in digital graphics software.
definitions: A system using one or more numbers (coordinates) to uniquely determine the position of points in geometric space.
notes.example: Calculating vector angles and distances when plotting geometric shapes on digital canvas coordinates.
exam_points: Trigonometric functions calculate rotational trajectories and angular alignments in vector graphic editors.

notes.title: Matrix Transformations in Computer Graphics
notes.explanation: Linear algebra and transformation matrices manipulate digital objects through translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.
definitions: A matrix that performs linear transformations on coordinate vectors in computer graphics rendering.
notes.example: Multiplying a 2D coordinate vector by a scaling matrix to resize a graphic asset proportionally.
exam_points: Homogeneous coordinates allow translation and rotation to be combined into unified matrix multiplications.

notes.title: Digital Units, Resolution & Color Models
notes.explanation: Digital design requires mastering pixel measurements, screen resolution standards, and additive/subtractive color models.
definitions: A measurement of pixel density on digital display screens and electronic monitors.
notes.example: Converting a print graphic design from RGB color mode to CMYK mode prior to press publication.
exam_points: Hexadecimal color codes define web color values using base-16 numerical representations.

questions: Explain the application of the golden ratio and mathematical proportions in visual composition.
Discuss the role of scale factors and dimensional calculations in desktop publishing.
How are coordinate geometry and trigonometric functions applied in computer graphics?
Describe the geometric properties of polygons and circles used in digital vector art.
Explain how transformation matrices execute translation, scaling, and rotation in 2D graphics.
Discuss the geometric interpretation of dot products and vector addition in graphics rendering.
Differentiate between PPI and DPI, explaining their significance in digital displays versus print resolution.
Compare RGB and CMYK color models, detailing their respective use cases in digital media and print.

quiz.question: What numerical value represents the golden ratio commonly utilized in aesthetic visual design?
quiz.explanation: The golden ratio is approximately 1.618, valued for creating balanced visual proportions.

quiz.question: What does PPI stand for in digital image resolution measurement?
quiz.explanation: PPI stands for Pixels Per Inch, measuring digital screen display resolution.

quiz.question: Which color model is additive and primarily used for electronic display screens and web design?
quiz.explanation: RGB (Red, Green, Blue) is an additive color model used for emitting light on digital display monitors.

quiz.question: What type of mathematical matrix is used to resize digital objects proportionally or disproportionately?
quiz.explanation: A scaling matrix multiplies coordinates by scaling factors along X and Y axes to resize objects.

subjects.name: Web Design Fundamentals
objectives: CO1: Understand core web architecture, internet protocols, and web page markup principles.
CO2: Master HTML5 semantic tags, structuring web documents, and embedding media elements.
CO3: Apply CSS3 styling, responsive grid layouts, Flexbox, and modern web design aesthetics.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Web Design: World Wide Web architecture, web servers, browsers, HTTP/HTTPS protocols, IP addresses, domain names, and responsive web design concepts.
HTML5 Fundamentals: Document structure, semantic tags, headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, tables, forms, input types, audio, and video embedding.
CSS3 Styling: Syntax, selectors, colors, typography, box model (margin, border, padding, content), positioning, display properties, background styling, and gradients.
Advanced Layouts & Responsiveness: CSS Flexbox, Grid layouts, media queries, mobile-first design philosophy, and responsive navigation menus.

notes.title: Web Architecture & Protocols
notes.explanation: Web design begins by understanding client-server interactions, Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), and internet communication protocols.
definitions: The underlying protocol used by the World Wide Web to define how messages are formatted and transmitted.
notes.example: Resolving a domain name through DNS servers to establish secure HTTPS connections with a web hosting server.
exam_points: Responsive web design ensures web pages render well across a variety of devices and window screen sizes.

notes.title: HTML5 Semantic Structure
notes.explanation: HTML5 provides semantic structural elements (<header>, <nav>, <article>, <section>, <footer>) that improve accessibility and SEO.
definitions: HTML tags that clearly describe their meaning to both the browser and the developer.
notes.example: Structuring a multi-column blog web page using semantic HTML5 article and section tags.
exam_points: HTML5 forms support native client-side validation attributes like required, email, and pattern matching.

notes.title: CSS3 Styling & Box Model
notes.explanation: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS3) control visual presentation, color schemes, typography, and element positioning in web layouts.
definitions: A box that wraps around every HTML element, consisting of margins, borders, padding, and the actual content.
notes.example: Applying box-sizing: border-box to ensure padding and borders are included within element width calculations.
exam_points: CSS selectors target HTML elements by tag name, class attributes, ID selectors, and pseudo-classes.

notes.title: Flexbox, Grid & Media Queries
notes.explanation: Modern CSS layout modules like Flexbox and Grid, combined with media queries, enable fluid responsive web designs.
definitions: A CSS technique adapting web page styles based on device characteristics such as screen resolution and viewport width.
notes.example: Designing a flexible navigation bar that collapses into a hamburger menu on mobile viewports using media queries.
exam_points: CSS Flexbox excels at one-dimensional layouts, while CSS Grid manages complex two-dimensional grid structures.

questions: Explain the client-server architecture of the World Wide Web and the role of HTTP/HTTPS protocols.
Discuss the core principles of responsive web design and cross-browser compatibility.
What are semantic elements in HTML5? Explain their importance in web accessibility and search engine optimization.
Describe how to design complex HTML5 form layouts with various input types and validation attributes.
Explain the CSS Box Model in detail, highlighting the differences between padding, border, and margin.
Discuss various CSS selectors and methods of applying style sheets (inline, internal, external).
Compare CSS Flexbox with CSS Grid layout systems, providing appropriate use cases for each.
Explain how media queries implement mobile-first responsive design across multiple device screen sizes.

quiz.question: Which HTML5 tag is semantically designated for introductory content or navigation links at the top of a page?
quiz.explanation: The <header> element represents introductory content or a group of navigational links.

quiz.question: What are the four components of the CSS Box Model from innermost to outermost?
quiz.explanation: The CSS Box Model consists of content directly surrounded by padding, border, and outermost margin.

quiz.question: Which CSS layout module is primarily designed for one-dimensional row or column alignments?
quiz.explanation: CSS Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout model optimized for distributing space along a single axis.

quiz.question: What CSS feature enables adaptive styling based on device screen width and resolution?
quiz.explanation: Media queries apply conditional CSS rules depending on device viewport dimensions and media characteristics.

B.Sc. Multimedia.full_name: Bachelor of Science in Multimedia (B.Sc. Multimedia)

subjects.name: Introduction to Multimedia & Digital Creativity
objectives: CO1: Understand the foundational concepts, elements, and historical evolution of multimedia systems.
CO2: Master digital media types including text, graphics, audio, video, and animation principles.
CO3: Explore digital creativity workflows, hardware/software requirements, and multimedia authoring tools.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Multimedia: Definition, historical evolution, elements of multimedia (text, graphics, audio, video, animation), applications in education, entertainment, advertising, and digital communication.

Digital Media & Data Representation: Text formatting, fonts, typography basics, digital audio principles (sampling rate, bit depth, compression), digital video standards, codecs, and container formats.
Animation Principles: 12 basic principles of animation, traditional frame-by-frame animation, keyframing, timing, spacing, squash and stretch, anticipation, and staging.
Multimedia Authoring & Workflows: Authoring tools, user interface design, storyboarding, scriptwriting, production pipeline stages (pre-production, production, post-production), and copyright ethics.

notes.title: Multimedia Foundations & Elements
notes.explanation: Multimedia integrates multiple continuous and discrete digital media types to convey interactive information and engaging visual stories.
definitions: The integration of text, graphics, audio, video, and animation delivered via computer or digital electronic devices.
notes.example: Developing interactive multimedia learning modules combining audio voiceovers, animated graphics, and text captions.
exam_points: Discrete media include text and still images, whereas continuous media include audio and video streams.

notes.title: Digital Audio & Video Standards
notes.explanation: Digital media representation converts analog sound and visual waves into discrete binary digital data streams using specialized codecs.
definitions: The number of samples taken per second to convert analog audio waveforms into digital audio signals.
notes.example: Encoding uncompressed digital video footage using H.264 codecs to optimize file size for web streaming.
exam_points: Higher audio sampling rates and bit depths increase fidelity while expanding digital storage requirements.

notes.title: Principles of Animation
notes.explanation: The 12 basic principles of animation established by Disney animators guide weight, timing, and emotional realism in motion design.
definitions: An animation principle giving a sense of weight and flexibility to objects by distorting their shape during motion.
notes.example: Applying anticipation and follow-through mechanics when animating a bouncing ball or character jump.
exam_points: Timing and spacing dictate the perceived speed and mass of animated digital objects.

notes.title: Production Pipeline & Storyboarding
notes.explanation: Multimedia projects follow a structured production pipeline moving from initial creative conceptualization to final rendering.
definitions: A sequential series of visual panel sketches outlining camera shots and action flow in video and animation production.
notes.example: Drafting comprehensive storyboards and script outlines prior to digital animation production.
exam_points: Pre-production planning prevents costly revisions during final post-production rendering phases.

questions: Define multimedia and discuss its primary components and applications in modern digital industries.
Differentiate between discrete and continuous media types in digital communication.
Explain digital audio principles including sampling rate, bit depth, and quantization.
Discuss digital video standards, codecs, and container formats used in multimedia production.
Detail at least five of the 12 basic principles of animation with illustrative examples.
Explain the role of timing and spacing in creating natural movement in character animation.
Describe the stages of the multimedia production pipeline from pre-production to post-production.
Explain the importance of storyboarding and scriptwriting in multimedia project development.

quiz.question: Which animation principle gives a flexible object a sense of weight and volume during impact?
quiz.explanation: Squash and stretch creates the illusion of weight and volume deformation when an object moves or collides.

quiz.question: What does audio sampling rate measure in digital sound recording?
options: The amplitude of sound waves per second
The number of audio samples captured per second
The frequency range of human hearing
quiz.explanation: Sampling rate measures how many times per second an analog sound wave is sampled into digital values.

quiz.question: Which stage of the multimedia production pipeline involves storyboarding, scriptwriting, and concept art?
quiz.explanation: Pre-production encompasses initial planning, budgeting, scriptwriting, and storyboarding.

quiz.question: Which media classification includes textual documents and still photographs?
quiz.explanation: Discrete media consist of independent, time-independent information elements like text and still images.

subjects.name: Photography & Audio-Video Production Basics
objectives: CO1: Master photographic exposure principles, camera operations, lens optics, and lighting techniques.
CO2: Understand audio recording, microphone types, acoustic principles, and sound editing workflows.
CO3: Explore digital video production, camera movements, editing fundamentals, and post-production workflows.

syllabus.topics: Fundamentals of Photography: Camera anatomy, DSLR/mirrorless cameras, exposure triangle (aperture, shutter speed, ISO), depth of field, lens focal lengths, composition rules (rule of thirds).
Lighting & Studio Photography: Natural versus artificial lighting, three-point lighting setup, softboxes, reflectors, flash photography, color temperature, and white balance.
Audio Production Principles: Sound waves, frequency, amplitude, microphone polar patterns (dynamic, condenser, lavalier), field recording, audio mixing, and digital editing.
Video Production & Editing: Video camera operation, framing, camera movements (pan, tilt, dolly, zoom), editing terminology (cuts, transitions, timeline), and post-production workflows.

notes.title: Photographic Exposure & Composition
notes.explanation: Photographic exposure relies on balancing aperture, shutter speed, and ISO to capture optimal light on digital sensors.
definitions: The interrelationship between aperture, shutter speed, and ISO determining overall image exposure.
notes.example: Adjusting a wide aperture (low f-number) to create shallow depth of field in portrait photography.
exam_points: Shutter speed controls motion blur, whereas aperture controls depth of field and light quantity.

notes.title: Studio Lighting Techniques
notes.explanation: Professional lighting shapes subject contours, mood, and dimensionality using structured three-point lighting setups.
definitions: A standard lighting arrangement utilizing key, fill, and backlight sources to illuminate a subject.
notes.example: Deploying key lights and reflectors to eliminate harsh facial shadows during studio interviews.
exam_points: Kelvin color temperature scales distinguish warm tungsten indoor lighting from cool daylight conditions.

notes.title: Audio Recording & Microphones
notes.explanation: Clean audio capture requires understanding acoustic properties, microphone directionality, and signal-to-noise ratios.
definitions: A directional microphone that picks up sound primarily from the front while rejecting ambient sound from the sides and rear.
notes.example: Using lavalier clip-on microphones during documentary dialogue recording to isolate speech from background noise.
exam_points: Condenser microphones offer high acoustic sensitivity requiring phantom power supplies.

notes.title: Video Production & Editing
notes.explanation: Video editing assembles raw visual and auditory clips into cohesive narrative sequences using professional timeline editors.
definitions: Advanced editing transitions where audio from the preceding or upcoming clip plays before or after the visual cut.
notes.example: Executing smooth continuity cuts to maintain seamless narrative flow across camera angles.
exam_points: Camera movements such as panning and tilting add dynamic visual energy to cinematic sequences.

questions: Explain the exposure triangle in photography, detailing the roles of aperture, shutter speed, and ISO.
Discuss composition rules including the rule of thirds, leading lines, and framing techniques.
Describe the three-point lighting setup and explain the functions of key, fill, and back lights.
How does color temperature affect photography? Explain the importance of white balance settings.
Classify microphone polar patterns and discuss applications for cardioid and omnidirectional microphones.
Explain basic acoustic principles and techniques for reducing unwanted background noise in field recording.
Describe essential camera movements (pan, tilt, dolly, trucking) used in professional video production.
Explain video editing fundamentals including continuity cutting, transitions, and timeline arrangement.

quiz.question: Which element of the exposure triangle controls the physical duration that light strikes the camera sensor?
quiz.explanation: Shutter speed controls the length of time the camera shutter remains open to expose light.

quiz.question: What lighting source in a three-point setup illuminates the subject from behind to separate them from the background?
quiz.explanation: The backlight illuminates the subject from behind, creating a glowing outline that separates them from the backdrop.

quiz.question: Which microphone polar pattern is heart-shaped, picking up sound primarily from the front?
quiz.explanation: A cardioid microphone exhibits heart-shaped directional sensitivity rejecting sound from behind.

quiz.question: What camera movement involves rotating the camera horizontally on a fixed tripod axis?
quiz.explanation: Panning rotates the camera horizontally left or right from a stationary pivot point.

B.Tech.CSE.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering (B.Tech. CSE)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for solving linear systems and transformations in engineering.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations (matrix equation) such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for a 2x2 system matrix.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations (fopen, fread, fwrite, fclose).

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal, reference passing, and dynamic heap memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate and deallocate dynamic memory for arrays in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation (Newton's, Lagrange's formulas).
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration (Trapezoidal rule, Simpson's 1/3 and 3/8 rules), numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying engineering system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving second-order spring-mass damper differential equations using Laplace transform tables.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Engineering Physics
objectives: CO1: Understand quantum mechanics principles, wave-particle duality, and Schrödinger equations.
CO2: Master laser physics, fiber optics communication, and semiconductor physics.
CO3: Explore electromagnetism and Maxwell's equations.

syllabus.topics: Quantum Mechanics: Wave-particle duality, de Broglie waves, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, wave function physical significance, time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger wave equations.

Laser & Fiber Optics: Spontaneous and stimulated emission, Einstein coefficients, He-Ne laser, semiconductor laser. Optical fibers: Propagation mechanism, acceptance angle, numerical aperture, attenuation, and dispersion.

Electromagnetism & Dielectrics: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral forms, electromagnetic wave propagation in free space. Dielectric polarization, types of polarization, Clausius-Mossotti relation.
Band Theory of Solids: Free electron theory, Kronig-Penney model, energy bands in solids, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, Fermi-Dirac distribution function.

notes.title: Quantum Mechanics
notes.explanation: Quantum mechanics explains atomic and subatomic phenomena where classical mechanics fails.
definitions: A mathematical function describing the quantum state of an isolated quantum system.
notes.example: Solving the Schrödinger equation for an electron confined in a 1D potential well box.
exam_points: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle sets fundamental limits on simultaneously measuring position and momentum.

questions: Derive time-independent and time-dependent Schrödinger wave equations.
State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and explain its physical consequences.

quiz.question: What does Heisenberg's uncertainty principle restrict simultaneous measurement of?
quiz.explanation: Position and conjugate momentum cannot be simultaneously measured with arbitrary precision.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts (objects, classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism). C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading (unary and binary operators), friend functions.

Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers (public, private, protected), types of inheritance (single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid), virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling (try, catch, throw), file I/O streams (ifstream, ofstream, fstream).

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS (batch, multiprogrammed, time-sharing, real-time), system calls, system programs. Process Management: Process concept, process control block, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Priority, Round Robin).

Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, Peterson's solution, semaphores, classical synchronization problems (producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers). Deadlocks: System model, deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection, and recovery.

Memory Management: Logical vs. physical address space, swapping, contiguous memory allocation, paging, structure of page table, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal), thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk structure, disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN).

notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem, substitution and recursion tree methods.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees (Kruskal's, Prim's algorithms), Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem, sum of subsets, graph coloring.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using the fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problem.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, data abstraction, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets, mapping cardinalities. Relational Model: Relational algebra, tuple and domain relational calculus.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers, and stored procedures.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition, and dependency preservation.

Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, conflict and view serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols, deadlock handling. Recovery System: Log-based recovery, checkpoints.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Computer Networks
objectives: CO1: Understand OSI and TCP/IP reference models and physical layer transmission media.
CO2: Master data link layer protocols, error detection/correction, and MAC sublayer protocols.
CO3: Explore network layer routing, IP addressing, transport layer protocols, and application layer services.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Data communication components, OSI and TCP/IP reference models, physical layer transmission media, analog vs. digital signals, bandwidth, and multiplexing.

Data Link Layer: Design issues, framing, error detection and correction (Hamming code, CRC), sliding window protocols (Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat). MAC Sublayer: Multiple access protocols (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), Ethernet standards.
Network Layer: Routing algorithms (distance vector, link state), congestion control algorithms, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, subnetting, NAT, routers, and routing protocols (OSPF, BGP).
Transport Layer: Process-to-process communication, UDP, TCP reliable data transfer, congestion control, flow control. Application Layer: DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, and DHCP.

notes.title: Network Layer Routing & IP Addressing
notes.explanation: The network layer manages packet forwarding across interconnected networks using IP addressing and routing algorithms.
definitions: The practice of dividing a single physical network into multiple smaller logical sub-networks.
notes.example: Calculating network and broadcast addresses using CIDR netmask notations.
exam_points: Distance vector routing utilizes the Bellman-Ford algorithm, whereas link state routing uses Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions: Compare distance vector routing with link-state routing algorithms.
Explain IPv4 subnetting and calculate subnet masks for given host requirements.

quiz.question: Which protocol provides reliable, connection-oriented data transmission at the transport layer?
quiz.explanation: TCP ensures reliable, connection-oriented stream delivery with error checking and flow control.

subjects.name: Compiler Design
objectives: CO1: Understand phases of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, and finite automata.
CO2: Master parsing techniques including top-down (LL(1)) and bottom-up (LR, LALR) parsers.
CO3: Explore syntax-directed translation, intermediate code generation, and code optimization.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Compilers: Phases of compilation, compiler construction tools. Lexical Analysis: Role of lexical analyzer, input buffering, specification of tokens, regular expressions, finite automata, NFA to DFA conversion, Lex tool.

Syntax Analysis: Role of parser, context-free grammars, parse trees, ambiguity. Top-down parsing: Recursive descent parsing, LL(1) grammars. Bottom-up parsing: Shift-reduce parsing, SLR, CLR, and LALR parsers, Yacc tool.

Syntax-Directed Translation & Intermediate Code: Syntax-directed definitions, evaluation orders, intermediate languages (three-address code, quadruples, triples), translation of declarations and control statements.

Run-Time Environments & Code Optimization: Storage organization, activation records. Code Optimization: Principal sources of optimization, optimization of basic blocks, loop optimization, code generation.

notes.title: Syntax Analysis & Parsing
notes.explanation: Parsers validate token streams against grammar rules, constructing parse trees for semantic analysis.
definitions: A top-down parser that parses input from Left to right, constructs a Leftmost derivation, using 1 lookahead token.
notes.example: Constructing FIRST and FOLLOW sets to build predictive parsing tables for LL(1) grammars.
exam_points: LR parsers are more powerful than LL parsers and handle bottom-up shift-reduce parsing efficiently.

questions: Explain the construction of FIRST and FOLLOW sets for a given context-free grammar.
Differentiate between LL(1) top-down parsing and LR bottom-up parsing.

quiz.question: What parsing table construction method is used for bottom-up LALR parsers?
quiz.explanation: LALR parsers merge LR(1) states having identical LR(0) items and different lookaheads to reduce table size.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence
objectives: CO1: Understand AI foundations, intelligent agents, and uninformed/informed search strategies.
CO2: Master knowledge representation, propositional logic, first-order logic, and inference.
CO3: Explore probabilistic reasoning, machine learning basics, and natural language processing.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to AI: History, intelligent agents, PEAS framework. Uninformed Search: BFS, DFS, Depth-Limited Search, Iterative Deepening. Informed Search: Greedy Best-First Search, A* search, heuristic functions.
Adversarial Search & Games: Game theory, minimax algorithm, alpha-beta pruning. Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs): Constraint propagation, backtracking search.
Knowledge Representation: Propositional logic, inference rules, first-order logic, unification, resolution. Ontologies and semantic networks.
Probabilistic Reasoning: Uncertainty, conditional probability, Bayes' rule. Introduction to Machine Learning: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, neural networks basics.

notes.title: Heuristic Search Strategies
notes.explanation: Informed search algorithms utilize domain-specific heuristic functions to guide search spaces efficiently toward goal states.
definitions: A heuristic that never overestimates the actual cost to reach the goal.
notes.example: Applying A* search with Euclidean distance heuristics for optimal robot pathfinding.
exam_points: A* search guarantees optimal solutions if the heuristic function is admissible and consistent.

questions: Explain A* search algorithm and prove that an admissible heuristic guarantees optimality.
Discuss minimax game tree search with alpha-beta pruning optimization.

quiz.question: What condition must an evaluation heuristic satisfy in A* search to guarantee finding an optimal path?
quiz.explanation: An admissible heuristic ensures A* never overestimates true remaining path costs, guaranteeing optimality.

subjects.name: Network Security and Cryptography
objectives: CO1: Understand classical ciphers, symmetric encryption standards (AES, DES), and block cipher modes.
CO2: Master asymmetric cryptography (RSA, Diffie-Hellman), hash functions, and digital signatures.
CO3: Explore network security protocols (IPsec, SSL/TLS) and firewall architectures.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Security goals (CIA triad), classical encryption techniques (substitution, transposition ciphers). Symmetric Ciphers: Data Encryption Standard (DES), Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), block cipher modes of operation (CBC, ECB, CTR).
Asymmetric Cryptography: Principles of public-key cryptography, RSA algorithm, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC).
Cryptographic Data Integrity: Message authentication codes, secure hash functions (SHA-256, MD5), digital signature standards (DSS), public key infrastructure (PKI), and X.509 certificates.
Network Security & Applications: Kerberos authentication, IPsec architecture, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) and Transport Layer Security (TLS), firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), and malware.

notes.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
notes.explanation: Public-key cryptography utilizes key pairs (public and private keys) to secure communications without prior shared secrets.
definitions: A public-key cryptosystem based on the practical difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers.
notes.example: Encrypting secret session keys using recipient public keys during SSL handshakes.
exam_points: Diffie-Hellman key exchange allows two parties to establish a shared secret over insecure communication channels.

questions: Explain the RSA public-key encryption and decryption algorithm with mathematical steps.
Discuss the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol and its vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks.

quiz.question: What mathematical hardness assumption underpins the security of the RSA public-key cryptosystem?
options: Integer factorization of large composite numbers
quiz.explanation: RSA relies on the computational difficulty of factoring large composite integers into original prime factors.

subjects.name: Data Mining and Data Warehousing
objectives: CO1: Understand data warehouse architecture, OLAP operations, and multidimensional data models.
CO2: Master data preprocessing, data cleaning, integration, reduction, and transformation.
CO3: Explore association rule mining (Apriori), classification, clustering (K-Means), and outlier detection.

syllabus.topics: Data Warehousing: Introduction, multidimensional data model, data warehouse architecture, OLAP operations (roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice, pivot), schemas (star, snowflake, fact constellation).
Data Mining Fundamentals: Data mining task primitives, data preprocessing (cleaning, integration, reduction, transformation), data discretization.
Association Rule Mining: Market basket analysis, frequent itemsets, Apriori algorithm, generating association rules, FP-growth algorithm.
Classification & Clustering: Decision tree induction, Bayesian classification, k-nearest neighbor. Clustering: Partitioning methods (k-means, k-medoids), hierarchical methods, outlier detection.

notes.title: Association Rule Mining
notes.explanation: Association rule mining discovers interesting correlation relationships and frequent itemsets in transactional databases.
definitions: Support measures itemset frequency, while confidence measures rule reliability given antecedent presence.
notes.example: Applying the Apriori algorithm to identify frequently co-purchased retail merchandise items.
exam_points: The Apriori property states that all non-empty subsets of a frequent itemset must also be frequent.

questions: Explain the Apriori algorithm for mining frequent itemsets with an illustrative example.
Define support and confidence in association rule mining.

quiz.question: What property does the Apriori algorithm use to prune candidate itemsets during frequent pattern mining?
options: Any subset of a frequent itemset must be frequent
Any superset of an infrequent itemset must be frequent
quiz.explanation: The Apriori downward-closure property ensures all subsets of frequent itemsets are themselves frequent.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech CSE engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry software problems.
CO2: Collaborate within multidisciplinary teams adhering to professional software development lifecycles.
CO3: Demonstrate technical communication, documentation, and project defense skills.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or software development placement in approved IT organizations or technology startups.
Capstone Project: Design, development, testing, and deployment of a comprehensive software engineering project.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Preparation of technical documentation, code repositories, system architecture diagrams, and final project presentation defense.

notes.title: Industrial Software Engineering
notes.explanation: Industrial training bridges academic theory with practical enterprise software development methodologies.
definitions: An iterative software development methodology emphasizing team collaboration, customer feedback, and rapid releases.
notes.example: Developing full-stack web applications using version control (Git), CI/CD pipelines, and cloud deployment.
exam_points: Comprehensive project documentation and code modularity ensure maintainability in enterprise environments.

questions: Describe the system architecture, database schema, and technology stack utilized in your capstone project.
Discuss challenges faced during software integration and how they were resolved during industrial training.

quiz.question: What software development methodology emphasizes iterative sprints, continuous feedback, and adaptive planning?
quiz.explanation: Agile methodology promotes collaborative iterative development through flexible sprints and continuous feedback.

B,Tech.IT.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Information Technology (B.Tech. IT)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for solving linear systems and transformations in engineering.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations (matrix equation) such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for a 2x2 system matrix.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations (fopen, fread, fwrite, fclose).

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal, reference passing, and dynamic heap memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate and deallocate dynamic memory for arrays in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.
