quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation (Newton's, Lagrange's formulas).
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration (Trapezoidal rule, Simpson's 1/3 and 3/8 rules), numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying engineering system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving second-order spring-mass damper differential equations using Laplace transform tables.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts (objects, classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism). C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading (unary and binary operators), friend functions.

Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers (public, private, protected), types of inheritance (single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid), virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling (try, catch, throw), file I/O streams (ifstream, ofstream, fstream).

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Computer Networks
objectives: CO1: Understand OSI and TCP/IP reference models and physical layer transmission media.
CO2: Master data link layer protocols, error detection/correction, and MAC sublayer protocols.
CO3: Explore network layer routing, IP addressing, transport layer protocols, and application layer services.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Data communication components, OSI and TCP/IP reference models, physical layer transmission media, analog vs. digital signals, bandwidth, and multiplexing.

Data Link Layer: Design issues, framing, error detection and correction (Hamming code, CRC), sliding window protocols (Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat). MAC Sublayer: Multiple access protocols (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), Ethernet standards.
Network Layer: Routing algorithms (distance vector, link state), congestion control algorithms, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, subnetting, NAT, routers, and routing protocols (OSPF, BGP).
Transport Layer: Process-to-process communication, UDP, TCP reliable data transfer, congestion control, flow control. Application Layer: DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, and DHCP.

notes.title: Network Layer Routing & IP Addressing
notes.explanation: The network layer manages packet forwarding across interconnected networks using IP addressing and routing algorithms.
definitions: The practice of dividing a single physical network into multiple smaller logical sub-networks.
notes.example: Calculating network and broadcast addresses using CIDR netmask notations.
exam_points: Distance vector routing utilizes the Bellman-Ford algorithm, whereas link state routing uses Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions: Compare distance vector routing with link-state routing algorithms.
Explain IPv4 subnetting and calculate subnet masks for given host requirements.

quiz.question: Which protocol provides reliable, connection-oriented data transmission at the transport layer?
quiz.explanation: TCP ensures reliable, connection-oriented stream delivery with error checking and flow control.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS (batch, multiprogrammed, time-sharing, real-time), system calls, system programs. Process Management: Process concept, process control block, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Priority, Round Robin).

Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, Peterson's solution, semaphores, classical synchronization problems (producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers). Deadlocks: System model, deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection, and recovery.

Memory Management: Logical vs. physical address space, swapping, contiguous memory allocation, paging, structure of page table, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal), thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk structure, disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN).

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, data abstraction, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets, mapping cardinalities. Relational Model: Relational algebra, tuple and domain relational calculus.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers, and stored procedures.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition, and dependency preservation.

Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, conflict and view serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols, deadlock handling. Recovery System: Log-based recovery, checkpoints.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Programming in Java
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming principles in Java, classes, objects, and packages.
CO2: Master exception handling, multithreading, and I/O streams in Java.
CO3: Explore GUI development using Swing, AWT, and database connectivity via JDBC.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Java: Java features, JVM, bytecode, data types, control structures, classes, objects, methods, constructors, inheritance, polymorphism, packages, and interfaces.

Exception Handling & Multithreading: Exception handling mechanism (try, catch, throw, throws, finally), creating custom exceptions. Multithreading: Thread life cycle, creating threads (Thread class, Runnable interface), synchronization.
Collections & I/O Streams: Collections framework (List, Set, Map, ArrayList, HashSet, HashMap), generics, byte streams, character streams, serialization.
GUI & JDBC: AWT and Swing components, event handling (listeners, adapters), JDBC architecture, connecting to databases, executing SQL queries.

notes.title: Multithreading in Java
notes.explanation: Multithreading allows concurrent execution of multiple instruction threads to maximize CPU utilization.
definitions: A mechanism ensuring that two or more concurrent threads do not simultaneously access critical shared resources.
notes.example: Using synchronized blocks to prevent race conditions during multithreaded bank account balance updates.
exam_points: Threads can be created by extending the Thread class or implementing the Runnable interface.

questions: Explain the thread life cycle in Java and compare extending Thread vs implementing Runnable.
Discuss exception handling mechanisms in Java with try, catch, and finally blocks.

quiz.question: Which interface must be implemented to create a thread by passing an instance to a Thread object in Java?
quiz.explanation: The Runnable interface defines the run() method executed by separate threads.

subjects.name: Big Data
objectives: CO1: Understand big data characteristics (Vs), Hadoop ecosystem, and HDFS architecture.
CO2: Master MapReduce programming framework, data processing, and cluster deployment.
CO3: Explore NoSQL databases, Apache Spark, and real-time big data analytics.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Big Data: Characteristics (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity), big data challenges, Hadoop ecosystem overview, Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) architecture, NameNode, DataNode.
MapReduce Framework: MapReduce programming model, mappers, reducers, shuffle and sort phase, writing MapReduce jobs in Java, YARN architecture.
NoSQL Databases: Introduction to NoSQL, CAP theorem, key-value stores, document databases (MongoDB), column-family stores (Hbase), graph databases.
Apache Spark: Spark architecture, Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs), Spark SQL, DataFrame, Spark streaming, and real-time analytics.

notes.title: Hadoop & HDFS Architecture
notes.explanation: HDFS provides distributed fault-tolerant file storage across commodity server clusters.
definitions: The master node in HDFS managing file system namespace, directory tree, and block location metadata.
notes.example: Storing petabytes of log data across distributed DataNode block servers with replication.
exam_points: Default block size in HDFS is large (typically 128MB or 256MB) to optimize sequential disk read performance.

questions: Explain HDFS architecture and the roles of NameNode and DataNodes.
Discuss the 5 Vs of big data and architectural challenges in processing unstructured data.

quiz.question: What master node component in HDFS manages file system namespace and metadata?
quiz.explanation: The NameNode maintains the directory tree and metadata for all files in HDFS.

subjects.name: Web Technologies
objectives: CO1: Understand client-server web architecture, HTML5, CSS3, and responsive design.
CO2: Master JavaScript, DOM manipulation, asynchronous programming, and AJAX.
CO3: Explore server-side scripting (Node.js/PHP), RESTful APIs, and database integration.

syllabus.topics: Web Fundamentals: Internet protocols, HTML5 semantic tags, CSS3 selectors, box model, Flexbox, Grid, responsive design principles.
Client-Side Scripting (JavaScript): Syntax, objects, functions, DOM manipulation, event handling, ES6 features, asynchronous JavaScript (Promises, async/await), AJAX.
Server-Side Development: Node.js introduction, Express.js framework, routing, middleware, RESTful API design, connecting applications to databases (MongoDB/MySQL).
Web Security & Deployment: Authentication, authorization, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), web security vulnerabilities (XSS, CSRF), cloud hosting and deployment.

notes.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
notes.explanation: Asynchronous JavaScript handles non-blocking operations like network requests using Promises and async/await syntax.
definitions: An object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.
notes.example: Fetching JSON data from a REST API using async/await syntax in JavaScript.
exam_points: The JavaScript event loop manages callback execution queues in single-threaded runtime environments.

questions: Explain Promises and async/await in JavaScript for handling asynchronous operations.
Discuss DOM manipulation and event delegation in client-side web applications.

quiz.question: What object represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous JavaScript operation?
quiz.explanation: A Promise represents an asynchronous operation's eventual settled state (fulfilled or rejected).

subjects.name: Software Testing and Quality Assurance
objectives: CO1: Understand software testing principles, V-model, bug life cycle, and quality assurance.
CO2: Master black-box and white-box testing techniques, boundary value analysis, and path testing.
CO3: Explore integration, system, regression, and automated testing tools.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Testing: Software testing principles, bug life cycle, testing lifecycle (STLC), verification vs. validation, quality assurance vs. quality control.

Black-Box Testing: Boundary value analysis, equivalence partitioning, decision table testing, state transition testing. White-Box Testing: Statement coverage, branch coverage, path testing, cyclomatic complexity.
Levels of Testing: Unit testing, integration testing (top-down, bottom-up), system testing, acceptance testing, regression testing, performance and security testing.
Test Management & Automation: Test planning, test case design, test metrics, defect tracking tools (Jira), introduction to test automation frameworks.

notes.title: White-Box Testing & Cyclomatic Complexity
notes.explanation: White-box testing examines internal code logic paths and control flow structures to ensure thorough test coverage.
definitions: A software metric measuring the number of linearly independent paths through a program's source code.
notes.example: Calculating McCabe's cyclomatic complexity for a method containing multiple nested if-else conditional branches.
exam_points: Cyclomatic complexity formula is V(G) = E - N + 2P, where E is edges, N is nodes, and P is connected components.

questions: Explain cyclomatic complexity and calculate it for a given control flow graph.
Differentiate between black-box and white-box testing techniques with examples.

quiz.question: What software metric measures the number of linearly independent paths through a program control flow graph?
quiz.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity quantifies code logical test coverage requirements.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech IT engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry software problems.
CO2: Collaborate within multidisciplinary teams adhering to professional software development lifecycles.
CO3: Demonstrate technical communication, documentation, and project defense skills.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or software development placement in approved IT organizations or technology startups.
Capstone Project: Design, development, testing, and deployment of a comprehensive software engineering project.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Preparation of technical documentation, code repositories, system architecture diagrams, and final project presentation defense.

notes.title: Industrial Software Engineering
notes.explanation: Industrial training bridges academic theory with practical enterprise software development methodologies.
definitions: An iterative software development methodology emphasizing team collaboration, customer feedback, and rapid releases.
notes.example: Developing full-stack web applications using version control (Git), CI/CD pipelines, and cloud deployment.
exam_points: Comprehensive project documentation and code modularity ensure maintainability in enterprise environments.

questions: Describe the system architecture, database schema, and technology stack utilized in your capstone project.
Discuss challenges faced during software integration and how they were resolved during industrial training.

quiz.question: What software development methodology emphasizes iterative sprints, continuous feedback, and adaptive planning?
quiz.explanation: Agile methodology promotes collaborative iterative development through flexible sprints and continuous feedback.

B.Tech. Robotics & AI.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Robotics & Artificial Intelligence (B.Tech. Robotics & AI)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for solving linear systems and transformations in robotics coordinate geometry.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for transformation matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory for sensor data buffers in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying robotic control system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving actuator motor transfer function differential equations using Laplace transforms.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts. C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading, friend functions.
Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers, inheritance types, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling, file I/O streams.

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS, system calls. Process Management: Process concept, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms.
Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, semaphores, classical synchronization problems. Deadlocks: Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Memory Management: Contiguous memory allocation, paging, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk scheduling algorithms.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets. Relational Model: Relational algebra.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition.
Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Robotics Kinematics & Dynamics
objectives: CO1: Understand spatial descriptions, transformations, and homogeneous coordinate systems in robotics.
CO2: Master forward and inverse kinematics of robotic manipulators using Denavit-Hartenberg parameters.
CO3: Explore manipulator velocity kinematics, Jacobians, and dynamic equations of motion.

syllabus.topics: Spatial Descriptions & Transformations: Position, orientation, frames, mappings, operator rotations, translations, homogeneous transformations, roll-pitch-yaw angles, Euler angles.
Manipulator Forward Kinematics: Link description, Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention, joint variables, link transformation matrices, forward kinematics equations for standard robot arms.
Manipulator Inverse Kinematics: Solvability, algebraic vs. geometric approaches, tool configuration, inverse kinematics solutions for typical 3-axis and 6-axis manipulators.
Velocity Kinematics & Dynamics: Linear and angular velocity of links, manipulator Jacobian matrix, singularities, Lagrangian mechanics, equations of motion for robotic manipulators.

notes.title: Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Parameters
notes.explanation: DH convention standardizes coordinate frame assignments between adjacent links of a robotic manipulator.
definitions: Four kinematic parameters (link length, link twist, link offset, joint angle) defining spatial relationships between joint axes.
notes.example: Assigning coordinate frames and deriving transformation matrices for a 3-DOF articulated robot arm.
exam_points: The z-axis of each coordinate frame is aligned with the joint axis of motion.

questions: Explain the Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention for establishing link coordinate frames.
Derive forward kinematics equations for a 2-DOF planar robotic arm.

quiz.question: What convention is standardly used to systematically assign coordinate frames to robot manipulator links?
quiz.explanation: The DH convention uses four parameters to define spatial transformations between joint links.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence & Expert Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand AI agent architectures, uninformed and informed heuristic search algorithms.
CO2: Master knowledge representation, propositional and first-order predicate logic, and inference.
CO3: Explore machine learning fundamentals, neural networks, and expert system design.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to AI: Intelligent agents, PEAS framework. Uninformed search strategies: BFS, DFS. Informed search: Greedy best-first search, A* search, heuristic admissibility.
Knowledge Representation & Logic: Propositional logic, inference rules, first-order predicate logic, unification, resolution refutation, semantic networks.
Machine Learning Foundations: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, evaluation metrics.
Neural Networks & Expert Systems: Artificial neural networks, perceptron, multi-layer perceptrons, backpropagation. Expert systems architecture, inference engines, rule-based systems.

notes.title: A* Search & Heuristics
notes.explanation: A* search combines path cost g(n) and heuristic estimate h(n) to find optimal paths efficiently.
definitions: A heuristic function that never overestimates the actual cost to reach the goal.
notes.example: Using Euclidean distance as an admissible heuristic for robot path planning grids.
exam_points: A* search guarantees finding optimal paths when the heuristic is both admissible and consistent.

questions: Explain A* search algorithm and prove that an admissible heuristic guarantees optimality.
Compare BFS and DFS search strategies with respect to completeness and time complexity.

quiz.question: What property must a heuristic function possess in A* search to guarantee optimal path finding?
quiz.explanation: An admissible heuristic ensures A* never overestimates the remaining cost to the goal.

subjects.name: Mobile Robot Navigation & SLAM
objectives: CO1: Understand mobile robot kinematics, differential drive models, and sensor suites.
CO2: Master localization, probabilistic sensor models, and Monte Carlo localization (Particle Filters).
CO3: Explore Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), graph-based SLAM, and ROS navigation stacks.

syllabus.topics: Mobile Robot Kinematics: Differential drive robots, unicycle kinematics, bicycle models, forward kinematics, odometry calculations, sensor modeling (LiDAR, IMU, sonar).
Robot Localization: The localization problem, probabilistic kinematics, occupancy grid maps, Kalman filters, Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) for localization.
Monte Carlo Localization: Particle filtering, resampling algorithms, Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) algorithm implementation for mobile robots.
SLAM & Navigation: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping formulation, Graph-based SLAM, pose graph optimization, Robot Operating System (ROS) navigation stack architecture.

notes.title: Monte Carlo Localization (MCL)
notes.explanation: MCL uses particle filters to represent probability distributions of robot poses in known maps.
definitions: A recursive Bayesian filter that estimates probability density functions using discrete weighted particles.
notes.example: Tracking a warehouse mobile robot's position using laser rangefinder measurements and particle resampling.
exam_points: Particle resampling prevents weight degeneracy by eliminating low-weight particles and replicating high-weight ones.

questions: Explain the Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) algorithm and particle filter steps.
Discuss differential drive robot kinematics and odometry error propagation.

quiz.question: What algorithmic filtering approach does Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) utilize?
quiz.explanation: MCL implements particle filtering to represent non-Gaussian belief distributions of robot poses.

subjects.name: Computer Vision & Deep Learning for Robotics
objectives: CO1: Understand digital image processing fundamentals, filtering, edge detection, and feature extraction.
CO2: Master convolutional neural networks (CNNs), object detection (YOLO), and image segmentation.
CO3: Explore vision-based robot control, visual servoing, and autonomous navigation pipelines.

syllabus.topics: Image Processing Basics: Image acquisition, sampling, quantization, color spaces, spatial filtering, edge detection (Sobel, Canny), feature extraction (SIFT, SURF, ORB).
Deep Learning for Vision: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), architecture layers (convolution, pooling, fully connected), activation functions, training optimization.
Object Detection & Segmentation: Region-based CNNs, YOLO (You Only Look Once) architecture, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN).
Visual Servoing & Applications: Image-based visual servoing (IBVS), position-based visual servoing (PBVS), camera calibration, hand-eye calibration for robotic arms.

notes.title: Object Detection with YOLO
notes.explanation: YOLO frames object detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly.
definitions: A rectangular coordinate envelope enclosing a detected object instance within an image frame.
notes.example: Detecting and localizing assembly parts on a factory conveyor belt in real-time using YOLOv8.
exam_points: YOLO divides images into grid cells where each cell predicts bounding boxes and confidence scores.

questions: Explain the architecture and working principle of the YOLO object detection framework.
Differentiate between image-based visual servoing (IBVS) and position-based visual servoing (PBVS).

quiz.question: How does YOLO approach object detection compared to traditional region-proposal methods?
options: As a single regression problem across grid cells
Using exhaustive sliding window template matching
quiz.explanation: YOLO frames object detection as a single regression problem evaluated directly across image grid cells.

aliases: computer vision & deep learning for robotics

subjects.name: Reinforcement Learning & Autonomous Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), value functions, and Bellman equations.
CO2: Master dynamic programming, Monte Carlo methods, and Temporal Difference learning (Q-learning, SARSA).
CO3: Explore deep reinforcement learning (DQN, Policy Gradients) and autonomous robotic control applications.

syllabus.topics: Markov Decision Processes: Introduction to reinforcement learning, agent-environment interaction, MDP formulation, policies, value functions, Bellman optimality equations.
Model-Free Learning: Monte Carlo methods for prediction and control, Temporal Difference (TD) learning, SARSA, Q-learning algorithm.
Deep Reinforcement Learning: Function approximation, Deep Q-Networks (DQN), experience replay, target networks, policy gradient methods.
Robotic Control Applications: Reinforcement learning for simulated and physical robot locomotion, obstacle avoidance, grasping manipulation tasks.

notes.title: Q-Learning Algorithm
notes.explanation: Q-learning is an off-policy temporal difference learning algorithm that learns action-value functions without requiring environment models.
definitions: The expected discounted reward of taking a given action in a specific state under policy pi.
notes.example: Training a mobile robot to navigate mazes by updating Q-table values based on reward feedback.
exam_points: Q-learning updates action values using the maximum expected reward of subsequent states.

questions: Explain the Q-learning update rule and contrast off-policy Q-learning with on-policy SARSA.
Derive the Bellman optimality equation for Markov Decision Processes.

quiz.question: Is Q-learning an on-policy or off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Q-learning is an off-policy algorithm because it learns the optimal policy independently of the agent's actions.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / Robotics Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech Robotics & AI engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry automation problems.
CO2: Design, prototype, and test robotic hardware-software integrated systems adhering to engineering standards.
CO3: Demonstrate technical documentation, presentation, and project defense proficiency.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or research placement in robotics, automation, or artificial intelligence firms.
Capstone Project: Design, fabrication, programming, and testing of an autonomous robotic system or AI-driven automation pipeline.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Comprehensive technical documentation, CAD models, ROS package repositories, system testing logs, and final defense presentation.

notes.title: Robotics System Integration
notes.explanation: Capstone projects integrate mechanical design, electronic sensors, actuator control, and AI software stacks.
definitions: A flexible framework for writing robot software providing hardware abstraction and inter-process message passing.
notes.example: Deploying autonomous mobile robot navigation nodes on ROS 2 Humble across Ubuntu Linux environments.
exam_points: Robust system calibration and sensor fusion are critical for reliable autonomous robotic operation.

questions: Describe the hardware architecture, sensor suite, and AI software stack of your capstone robotics project.
Discuss engineering challenges encountered during ROS integration and hardware debugging.

quiz.question: What meta-operating system framework is standardly used for modular robot software development?
quiz.explanation: ROS provides standardized middleware, hardware abstraction, and messaging libraries for robotics.

aliases: semester industrial training / robotics capstone project
