syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying data modeling systems.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving differential equations using Laplace transform tables.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts. C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading, friend functions.
Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers, inheritance types, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling, file I/O streams.

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS, system calls. Process Management: Process concept, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms.
Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, semaphores, classical synchronization problems. Deadlocks: Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Memory Management: Contiguous memory allocation, paging, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk scheduling algorithms.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Programming in Python
objectives: CO1: Master Python programming fundamentals, control flows, data structures, and functions.
CO2: Implement object-oriented programming, file handling, and exception management in Python.
CO3: Explore scientific computing libraries including NumPy, Pandas, and data visualization tools.

syllabus.topics: Python Basics: Variables, data types, operators, conditional statements, loops, functions, scope, modules, packages, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets.
OOP & File I/O: Classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, exception handling, file reading and writing operations.
Data Science Libraries - NumPy & Pandas: NumPy arrays, indexing, slicing, vectorization, mathematical operations. Pandas Series, DataFrames, data cleaning, grouping, and merging.
Data Visualization: Matplotlib and Seaborn libraries, line plots, scatter plots, histograms, box plots, heatmaps, and exploratory data analysis.

notes.title: NumPy & Pandas for Data Science
notes.explanation: NumPy provides high-performance multidimensional array operations, while Pandas offers tabular data structures for data manipulation.
definitions: A two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different types in Pandas.
notes.example: Handling missing values and calculating summary statistics on datasets using Pandas DataFrames.
exam_points: Vectorized operations in NumPy execute significantly faster than standard Python loops by running compiled C code.

questions: Explain the difference between NumPy arrays and standard Python lists.
Discuss data cleaning and handling missing values using Pandas.

quiz.question: What primary data structure in Pandas represents a two-dimensional labeled tabular dataset?
quiz.explanation: A DataFrame is a 2-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different data types.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets. Relational Model: Relational algebra.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition.
Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Machine Learning for Data Science
objectives: CO1: Understand supervised and unsupervised machine learning paradigms and data preprocessing.
CO2: Master regression, classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, SVM, Decision Trees), and evaluation metrics.
CO3: Explore clustering, dimensionality reduction (PCA), and ensemble learning methods.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to ML: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, training/testing splits, cross-validation, feature scaling, handling categorical variables, bias-variance tradeoff.

Supervised Learning - Regression & Classification: Linear regression, multiple linear regression, logistic regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees, Random Forests.
Model Evaluation & Optimization: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC curves, hyperparameter tuning using Grid Search and Random Search.
Unsupervised Learning: Clustering algorithms (k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN), Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

notes.title: Supervised Classification Models
notes.explanation: Classification algorithms predict categorical class labels based on input feature vectors.
definitions: A classifier that finds an optimal hyperplane maximizing the margin between data classes in feature space.
notes.example: Training a Support Vector Machine to classify spam versus non-spam emails.
exam_points: Kernel tricks in SVM allow mapping non-linear separable data into higher dimensional spaces.

questions: Explain the working principle of Support Vector Machines and kernel functions.
Compare precision, recall, and F1-score as evaluation metrics for imbalanced classification.

quiz.question: What evaluation metric harmonic mean combines both precision and recall?
quiz.explanation: The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics.

subjects.name: Big Data Analytics
objectives: CO1: Understand big data characteristics, Hadoop architecture, and HDFS distributed file systems.
CO2: Master MapReduce distributed computing paradigms and data processing jobs.
CO3: Explore Apache Spark resilient distributed datasets (RDDs), Spark SQL, and big data streaming.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Big Data: 5 Vs of big data, Hadoop ecosystem overview, Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) architecture, NameNode, DataNode blocks.
MapReduce Framework: MapReduce programming model, mappers, reducers, shuffle and sort phase, YARN resource manager.
Apache Spark: Spark architecture, Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs), transformations and actions, lazy evaluation.
Spark SQL & Analytics: Spark DataFrames, SQL queries on big data, introduction to NoSQL databases (MongoDB/HBase).

notes.title: Apache Spark RDDs
notes.explanation: Spark RDDs provide fault-tolerant distributed memory abstractions enabling parallel data processing across clusters.
definitions: An execution strategy where Spark does not compute transformations immediately until an action is called.
notes.example: Applying map and filter transformations on distributed RDD datasets followed by count actions.
exam_points: Transformations are lazy (e.g., map, filter), whereas actions trigger actual pipeline execution (e.g., collect, count).

questions: Explain transformations and actions in Apache Spark RDDs with examples.
Compare MapReduce with Apache Spark processing architectures.

quiz.question: What type of operation triggers actual execution of a computation pipeline in Apache Spark?
quiz.explanation: Actions (like collect() or count()) trigger the execution of lazy transformations in Spark.

subjects.name: Data Warehousing and Mining
objectives: CO1: Understand data warehouse architecture, OLAP operations, and multidimensional data modeling schemas.
CO2: Master data preprocessing, cleaning, transformation, and reduction techniques.
CO3: Explore association rule mining (Apriori), classification, and cluster analysis algorithms.

syllabus.topics: Data Warehousing: Data warehouse architecture, multidimensional data model, star schema, snowflake schema, fact constellation schema, OLAP operations (roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice, pivot).
Data Mining Preprocessing: Data cleaning, data integration, data reduction (dimensionality reduction, numerosity reduction), data transformation and discretization.
Association Rule Mining: Market basket analysis, frequent itemsets, Apriori algorithm, generating association rules, FP-growth algorithm.
Classification & Clustering: Decision tree induction, Bayesian classification, k-means clustering, hierarchical clustering.

notes.title: Multidimensional Data Models & OLAP
notes.explanation: Data warehouses organize enterprise data into multidimensional cubes to facilitate fast online analytical processing.
definitions: A database schema where a central fact table is connected to multiple dimensional tables without further normalization.
notes.example: Executing drill-down OLAP queries from yearly sales summaries down to daily store transactions.
exam_points: Star schemas optimize read-heavy analytical queries by minimizing table joins compared to fully normalized operational databases.

questions: Compare star schema with snowflake schema in data warehouse design.
Explain OLAP operations including roll-up, drill-down, slice, and dice.

quiz.question: What data warehouse schema features a central fact table surrounded by unnormalized dimensional tables?
quiz.explanation: A star schema consists of a central fact table directly linked to unnormalized dimension tables.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / Data Science Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech Data Science engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry analytics problems.
CO2: Design, build, train, and deploy end-to-end data science pipelines and machine learning models.
CO3: Demonstrate technical documentation, code repositories, and project presentation defense.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or data science placement in approved IT organizations or analytics firms.
Capstone Project: End-to-end data science project execution covering exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, machine learning modeling, and web deployment.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Technical documentation, GitHub code repositories, Jupyter notebooks, system architecture diagrams, and final defense presentation.

notes.title: End-to-End Data Science Pipelines
notes.explanation: Capstone projects integrate data ingestion, cleaning, predictive modeling, and cloud deployment into cohesive enterprise applications.
definitions: A practice for collaborating and managing the end-to-end machine learning lifecycle in production.
notes.example: Deploying a trained machine learning classification model as a REST API using Flask or FastAPI.
exam_points: Clean code modularity, robust data preprocessing, and reproducibility are paramount for production-grade data science systems.

questions: Describe the dataset, exploratory data analysis findings, and machine learning models utilized in your capstone project.
Discuss challenges faced during model evaluation, hyperparameter tuning, and deployment.

quiz.question: What acronym describes the practices for collaboration and automation of machine learning lifecycles in production?
quiz.explanation: MLOps combines machine learning, DevOps, and data engineering to deploy and maintain models reliably in production.

aliases: semester industrial training / data science capstone project

B.Tech. ECE.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Electronics and Communication Engineering (B.Tech. ECE)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations in electronic signals.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric waveforms using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for solving linear circuit equations and state-space control systems.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for network admittance matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation in embedded firmware.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory for signal processing buffers in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying electronic circuit analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving RLC circuit transient differential equations using Laplace transforms.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Electronic Devices
objectives: CO1: Understand semiconductor physics, energy bands, carrier transport, and p-n junction diode characteristics.
CO2: Master Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs), biasing, small-signal models, and hybrid parameters.
CO3: Explore Field Effect Transistors (FETs, MOSFETs), optoelectronic devices, and power semiconductor devices.

syllabus.topics: Semiconductor Physics: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, Fermi level, carrier concentration, drift and diffusion current, continuity equation, Hall effect. P-N Junction Diode: Diode equation, V-I characteristics, capacitance effects, breakdown mechanisms (Zener and avalanche), diode applications (rectifiers, clippers, clampers).
Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT): Construction, operation, transistor configurations (CB, CE, CC), current gains, V-I characteristics, BJT biasing, stability factors, thermal runaway.

Small-Signal BJT Amplifiers: Hybrid-pi model, h-parameter equivalent circuit of BJT amplifiers in CE configuration. Field Effect Transistors (FET): JFET construction, pinch-off voltage, transfer characteristics. MOSFET: Enhancement and depletion MOSFETs, CMOS inverter basics.
Optoelectronic & Special Devices: Photodiodes, LEDs, solar cells, laser diodes, Schottky diodes, tunnel diodes, varactor diodes, SCR, TRIAC, DIAC, and UJT characteristics.

notes.title: Semiconductor Physics & P-N Junction
notes.explanation: Semiconductors exhibit electrical conductivity between conductors and insulators, governed by thermal carrier excitation and doping.
definitions: An insulating zone around a p-n junction depleted of mobile charge carriers due to electron-hole recombination.
notes.example: Analyzing forward and reverse bias diode V-I characteristics using the Shockley diode equation.
exam_points: Zener breakdown occurs in heavily doped diodes at low reverse voltages via quantum tunneling.

questions: Derive the Shockley diode equation and explain Zener versus avalanche breakdown mechanisms.
Discuss carrier drift, diffusion currents, and the Einstein relation in semiconductors.

quiz.question: What breakdown mechanism occurs in heavily doped p-n junctions under high reverse electric fields due to valence electron quantum tunneling?
quiz.explanation: Zener breakdown predominates in heavily doped diodes with narrow depletion regions under strong electric fields.

subjects.name: Digital System Design
objectives: CO1: Understand Boolean algebra, logic gates, Karnaugh maps, and combinational logic design.
CO2: Master sequential logic circuits, flip-flops, counters, shift registers, and finite state machines.
CO3: Explore hardware description languages (Verilog/VHDL), programmable logic devices (PLDs, FPGAs), and memory systems.

syllabus.topics: Number Systems & Boolean Algebra: Binary, octal, hexadecimal number bases, codes (BCD, Gray, ASCII), Boolean postulates, De Morgan's laws, K-map simplification (up to 4 variables), Quine-McCluskey method, logic gates.
Combinational Logic Circuits: Adders, subtractors, multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders, decoders, code converters, magnitude comparators, parity generators/checkers.

Sequential Logic Circuits: Latches, flip-flops (SR, JK, D, T), master-slave flip-flops, excitation tables, synchronous and asynchronous counters, shift registers, finite state machines (Mealy and Moore models).
Memory & Programmable Logic: ROM, RAM, PLA, PAL, FPGA architecture. Introduction to HDLs: Verilog/VHDL syntax, behavioral and structural modeling.

notes.title: Sequential Logic & Flip-Flops
notes.explanation: Sequential circuits incorporate feedback memory elements where output states depend on current inputs and past states.
definitions: A malfunction in level-triggered JK flip-flops where outputs oscillate during clock high pulses if propagation delay is less than pulse width.
notes.example: Designing synchronous modulo-10 decade counters using JK flip-flops.
exam_points: Master-slave configuration eliminates race-around conditions in flip-flops.

questions: Explain the race-around condition in JK flip-flops and how master-slave flip-flops resolve it.
Design a synchronous 4-bit binary up-counter using JK flip-flops.

quiz.question: What circuit modification eliminates the race-around condition in level-triggered JK flip-flops?
quiz.explanation: Master-slave or edge-triggered flip-flops ensure outputs change only on specific clock transitions, preventing race conditions.

subjects.name: Analog Circuits
objectives: CO1: Master BJT and MOSFET multistage amplifiers, frequency response, and cascading techniques.
CO2: Understand feedback amplifiers, stability, Barkhausen criterion, and sinusoidal oscillators.
CO3: Explore operational amplifiers (Op-Amps), active filters, tuned amplifiers, and power amplifiers.

syllabus.topics: Multistage Amplifiers: Cascading amplifiers, coupling methods (RC coupling, direct coupling, transformer coupling), differential amplifiers, common mode and differential mode gains, current sources.

Feedback Amplifiers: Feedback concepts, properties of negative feedback (gain stability, bandwidth extension, impedance modification), topologies (voltage-series, current-series, voltage-shunt, current-shunt).

Oscillators & Power Amplifiers: Barkhausen criterion, RC phase shift oscillator, Wien bridge oscillator, Hartley and Colpitts oscillators, crystal oscillators. Power amplifiers: Class A, Class B, Class AB, Class C power amplifiers, push-pull configurations, harmonic distortion.

Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps): Ideal vs. practical op-amp characteristics, inverting/non-inverting amplifiers, summing amplifiers, integrators, differentiators, active filters (Butterworth low-pass and high-pass filters).

notes.title: Feedback Amplifiers
notes.explanation: Negative feedback samples output signals and feeds them back out-of-phase to improve amplifier stability and linearity.
definitions: The factor (1 + A*beta) by which negative feedback reduces amplifier gain variations and distortion.
notes.example: Calculating closed-loop input and output impedances for voltage-series negative feedback amplifiers.
exam_points: Voltage-series feedback increases input impedance and decreases output impedance.

questions: Discuss the four feedback topologies and their effects on input and output impedances.
Derive expression for closed-loop gain of negative feedback amplifiers.

quiz.question: What effect does voltage-series negative feedback have on input impedance of an amplifier?
quiz.explanation: Voltage-series feedback samples output voltage in series, increasing the effective input impedance.

subjects.name: Microprocessors and Microcontrollers
objectives: CO1: Understand 8086 microprocessor architecture, pin diagram, bus cycles, and assembly language programming.
CO2: Master interrupts, memory interfacing, programmable peripheral interface (8255 PPI), and DMA controllers.
CO3: Explore 8051 microcontroller architecture, instruction sets, timer/counters, serial communication, and embedded interfacing.

syllabus.topics: 8086 Microprocessor: Architecture, internal registers, bus interface unit, execution unit, pin configuration, minimum and maximum modes, timing diagrams, 8086 instruction set and assembly language programming.

Interrupts & Interfacing: 8086 interrupt structure, interrupt vector table, 8259 PIC. Memory interfacing: RAM/ROM interfacing. Programmable Peripheral Interface: 8255 PPI modes, 8253 timer, 8251 USART, DMA controller 8237.
8051 Microcontroller Architecture: Microprocessor vs. microcontroller, 8051 internal architecture, memory organization, PSW, registers, I/O ports, pin diagram, addressing modes.
8051 Programming & Interfacing: 8051 instruction set, assembly programming, timers and counters, serial communication, interrupts, interfacing LED, LCD, stepper motor, and ADC/DAC.

notes.title: 8086 Architecture & Assembly
notes.explanation: The 8086 is a 16-bit microprocessor featuring pipelined instruction fetching and segmented memory architecture.
definitions: A 20-bit memory address calculated in 8086 as Segment Address * 16 + Offset Address.
notes.example: Calculating physical memory addresses given DS = 5000H and IP = 1234H.
exam_points: The 8086 instruction queue stores up to 6 pre-fetched instruction bytes to speed up execution.

questions: Explain the internal architecture of 8086 microprocessor with block diagram.
Describe memory segmentation in 8086 and calculate physical address given CS = 2000H and IP = 5000H.

quiz.question: How many bits wide is the physical address bus of the 8086 microprocessor enabling 1MB memory access?
quiz.explanation: The 8086 features a 20-bit address bus, supporting $2^{20} = 1	ext{MB}$ of physical memory.

subjects.name: Analog and Digital Communication
objectives: CO1: Understand amplitude modulation, frequency modulation, angle modulation, and demodulation systems.
CO2: Master pulse modulation, sampling theorem, PCM, DPCM, DM, and digital passband modulation (ASK, FSK, PSK).
CO3: Explore information theory, source coding, channel capacity, and error-control block codes.

syllabus.topics: Analog Communication Systems: Elements of communication systems, Amplitude Modulation (AM): DSB-SC, SSB-SC, VSB, generation and demodulation, angle modulation: Frequency Modulation (FM), Phase Modulation (PM), narrowband and wideband FM, FM modulators and demodulators, superheterodyne receiver.

Pulse Modulation & Baseband Transmission: Sampling theorem, Pulse Amplitude Modulation (PAM), Pulse Width Modulation (PWM), Pulse Position Modulation (PPM). Pulse Code Modulation (PCM), quantization noise, companding, DPCM, ADPCM, Delta Modulation, Adaptive Delta Modulation.

Digital Passband Transmission: Introduction to digital modulation, Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK), Frequency Shift Keying (FSK), Phase Shift Keying (PSK), BPSK, QPSK, Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM), constellation diagrams, probability of error.

Information Theory & Coding: Uncertainty, information rate, entropy, source coding theorem (Shannon-Fano, Huffman coding), mutual information, channel capacity theorem, Shannon limit. Error-control coding: Linear block codes, cyclic codes, convolutional codes.

notes.title: Sampling Theorem & PCM
notes.explanation: The sampling theorem governs the conversion of continuous-time analog signals into discrete digital pulse streams without aliasing.
definitions: The minimum sampling frequency $f_s \ge 2f_m$ required to faithfully reconstruct a bandlimited signal of maximum frequency $f_m$.
notes.example: Calculating bit rates for transmitting audio signals sampled at Nyquist frequency using 8-bit PCM quantizers.
exam_points: Aliasing occurs when sampling frequencies fall below the Nyquist rate, causing high-frequency components to overlap into baseband.

questions: State and prove the sampling theorem for bandlimited signals.
Explain Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) transmitter and receiver block diagrams with quantization noise analysis.

quiz.question: According to the sampling theorem, what is the minimum sampling frequency required to prevent aliasing for a signal bandlimited to f_m Hz?
quiz.explanation: The Nyquist sampling rate requires $f_s \ge 2f_m$ to prevent spectral overlap and aliasing.

subjects.name: Digital Signal Processing
objectives: CO1: Understand discrete-time signals, systems, linear convolution, correlation, and Z-transforms.
CO2: Master Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithms, and frequency analysis.
CO3: Design Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) and Finite Impulse Response (FIR) digital filters.

syllabus.topics: Discrete-Time Signals & Systems: Classification of signals and systems, linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, impulse response, linear convolution, cross-correlation, auto-correlation. Z-transform: Region of convergence (ROC), inverse Z-transform, transfer functions.

Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT): Frequency domain sampling, properties of DFT, circular convolution, linear convolution using DFT. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Radix-2 DIT and DIF algorithms, computational complexity.
Digital Filter Structures: Block diagram representation, signal flow graphs, direct form I and II, cascade and parallel structures for FIR and IIR filters.

Digital Filter Design: Butterworth and Chebyshev filter approximations, impulse invariance and bilinear transformation methods for IIR filter design. FIR filter design: Windowing techniques (Rectangular, Hamming, Hanning windows), frequency sampling method.

notes.title: DFT & Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
notes.explanation: The FFT algorithm exploits symmetry and periodicity of twiddle factors to drastically reduce DFT computational complexity.
definitions: The complex exponential coefficient $W_N^{nk} = e^{-j 2\pi nk / N}$ used in butterfly computations.
notes.example: Comparing $O(N^2)$ direct DFT computations with $O(N \log_2 N)$ Radix-2 FFT butterfly operations.
exam_points: Radix-2 DIT FFT algorithms require sample sizes $N$ to be powers of 2 ($N = 2^m$).

questions: Explain Radix-2 Decimation-In-Time (DIT) FFT algorithm and draw its butterfly flow graph for N = 4.
Compare circular convolution with linear convolution using DFT.

quiz.question: What is the computational complexity order of an N-point Radix-2 Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Radix-2 FFT algorithms reduce computational complexity from $O(N^2)$ down to $O(N \log_2 N)$.

subjects.name: Wireless Communication
objectives: CO1: Understand cellular mobile radio concepts, frequency reuse, handoff strategies, and trunking efficiency.
CO2: Master mobile radio propagation, large-scale path loss, Rayleigh and Rician fading channels, and multipath phenomena.
CO3: Explore digital cellular standards (GSM, CDMA), multiple access techniques (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, OFDM), and modern wireless systems.

syllabus.topics: Cellular Concept: Evolution of mobile radio communications, cellular concept, frequency reuse, channel assignment strategies, handoff strategies, interference and system capacity, trunking and grade of service.

Mobile Radio Propagation: Free space propagation model, large-scale path loss, reflection, diffraction, scattering, small-scale fading and multipath, Doppler shift, Rayleigh and Rician fading distributions, coherence bandwidth, delay spread.
Multiple Access Techniques: FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM), space-division multiple access (SDMA).

Wireless Systems & Standards: Second generation (2G) GSM architecture and services, CDMA digital cellular standard (IS-95), 3G wireless systems (UMTS, CDMA2000), introduction to 4G LTE and 5G networks.

notes.title: Cellular Frequency Reuse
notes.explanation: Frequency reuse allows spatial reuse of radio channels across distinct cells separated by sufficient geographical distance to limit co-channel interference.
definitions: The number of adjacent cells in a cluster that collectively use the complete available frequency spectrum.
notes.example: Calculating co-channel interference reduction factor for 7-cell and 12-cell frequency reuse patterns.
exam_points: Common cluster sizes in cellular design are $N = I^2 + IJ + J^2$ (where $I, J$ are integers), yielding standard values like 3, 4, 7, 12.

questions: Explain the cellular frequency reuse concept and derive the co-channel interference ratio formula.
Discuss handoff strategies and types of handoffs in cellular communication.

quiz.question: What parameter defines the number of adjacent cells comprising a complete frequency reuse cluster?
quiz.explanation: Cluster size N represents the number of cells sharing distinct frequency allocations before reuse.

subjects.name: Optical Fibers & Communication
objectives: CO1: Understand optical fiber propagation principles, total internal reflection, numerical aperture, and fiber types.
CO2: Master optical signal attenuation, chromatic dispersion, polarization mode dispersion, and nonlinear effects.
CO3: Explore optical transmitters (lasers, LEDs), receivers (photodetectors), optical amplifiers, and WDM networks.

syllabus.topics: Optical Fiber Propagation: Ray theory optics, total internal reflection, acceptance angle, numerical aperture (NA), step-index and graded-index fibers, single-mode and multimode fibers, electromagnetic mode theory of fibers.

Signal Degradation in Optical Fibers: Attenuation (absorption, scattering, bending losses), signal distortion in optical waveguides, chromatic dispersion, material dispersion, waveguide dispersion, intermodal dispersion, polarization mode dispersion.

Optical Sources & Detectors: Optical sources: LED and semiconductor laser diodes, structures, characteristics, quantum efficiency. Optical detectors: PIN photodiode, Avalanche Photodiode (APD), noise in optical receivers.
Optical Systems & Networks: Optical link budget design, rise time budget, Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) principles, optical amplifiers (EDFA, SOA), optical networks.

notes.title: Numerical Aperture & Fiber Modes
notes.explanation: Numerical aperture quantifies the light-gathering capacity of an optical fiber based on core and cladding refractive indices.
definitions: The sine of the maximum acceptance angle within which incident light rays enter the fiber core and propagate via total internal reflection.
notes.example: Calculating NA for step-index fibers given core refractive index $n_1 = 1.48$ and cladding index $n_2 = 1.46$.
exam_points: Formula: $NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = n_1 \sqrt{2\Delta}$ where $\Delta$ is relative refractive index difference.

questions: Define Numerical Aperture and derive its mathematical expression in terms of core and cladding refractive indices.
Differentiate between step-index and graded-index optical fibers.

quiz.question: What formula calculates the Numerical Aperture (NA) of a step-index optical fiber given core refractive index n_1 and cladding index n_2?
quiz.explanation: Numerical aperture is defined as $NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$.

subjects.name: Project-II & Report
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech ECE engineering knowledge to design and implement hardware-software electronic systems.
CO2: Conduct engineering investigations, PCB design, microcontroller programming, and testing.
CO3: Demonstrate professional technical communication, report writing, and project defense proficiency.

syllabus.topics: System Specification & Design: Literature survey, problem formulation, hardware/software selection, block diagram schematic design.
Prototype Implementation: PCB fabrication, circuit assembling, microcontroller/FPGA firmware programming, testing, and debugging.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Preparation of formal technical dissertation report, schematic diagrams, test results, and final presentation defense.

notes.title: Embedded System Prototyping
notes.explanation: Capstone projects integrate analog sensor signal conditioning, digital microcontroller processing, and wireless communication modules.
definitions: A laminated non-conductive board supporting and interconnecting electronic components using copper tracks.
notes.example: Designing IoT-based wireless sensor nodes using ESP32 microcontrollers and sensor telemetry.
exam_points: Thorough circuit grounding and decoupling capacitor placement minimize electromagnetic interference (EMI) in hardware prototypes.

questions: Describe the hardware architecture, schematic design, and firmware algorithm of your ECE capstone project.
Discuss challenges encountered during PCB layout routing and signal integrity testing.

quiz.question: What electronic design artifact provides mechanical support and electrical copper interconnections between circuit components?
quiz.explanation: PCBs provide permanent mechanical support and conductive copper pathways for electronic circuits.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training & Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech ECE engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry electronics and communication problems.
CO2: Collaborate within multidisciplinary engineering teams adhering to industrial design and manufacturing standards.
CO3: Demonstrate professional technical documentation, presentation, and evaluation defense.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training in embedded systems, VLSI design, telecommunications, or IoT companies.
Industrial Project: Execution of engineering tasks, hardware testing, software development, or network optimization assigned by industry mentors.
Training Report & Viva Voce: Compilation of industrial training logbooks, project deliverables, and formal evaluation presentation defense.

notes.title: Industrial Engineering Practices
notes.explanation: Industrial training bridges academic theory with practical manufacturing, testing, and deployment methodologies in electronics.
definitions: A systematic process verifying that manufactured electronic hardware meets established reliability and safety specifications.
notes.example: Testing radio frequency transceiver modules using spectrum analyzers in industrial R&D laboratories.
exam_points: Adherence to industrial ESD (Electrostatic Discharge) protection guidelines prevents semiconductor component damage.

questions: Describe the core technical projects and engineering responsibilities undertaken during your industrial training.
Discuss industrial testing standards and debugging tools utilized in your placement organization.

quiz.question: What safety precaution prevents electrostatic discharge (ESD) damage to sensitive semiconductor integrated circuits during handling?
options: Using grounded wrist straps and anti-static mats
quiz.explanation: Grounded wrist straps and anti-static workstations safely drain static charges away from sensitive microchips.

B.Tech. Computer Science & Engineering (.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering (Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for dimensionality reduction and linear transformations in machine learning.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for data covariance matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory for data arrays in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying engineering system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving differential equations using Laplace transform tables.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts. C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading, friend functions.
Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers, inheritance types, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling, file I/O streams.

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS, system calls. Process Management: Process concept, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms.
Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, semaphores, classical synchronization problems. Deadlocks: Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Memory Management: Contiguous memory allocation, paging, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk scheduling algorithms.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Programming in Python
objectives: CO1: Master Python programming fundamentals, control flows, data structures, and functions.
CO2: Implement object-oriented programming, file handling, and exception management in Python.
CO3: Explore scientific computing libraries including NumPy, Pandas, and data visualization tools.

syllabus.topics: Python Basics: Variables, data types, operators, conditional statements, loops, functions, scope, modules, packages, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets.
OOP & File I/O: Classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, exception handling, file reading and writing operations.
Data Science Libraries - NumPy & Pandas: NumPy arrays, indexing, slicing, vectorization, mathematical operations. Pandas Series, DataFrames, data cleaning, grouping, and merging.
Data Visualization: Matplotlib and Seaborn libraries, line plots, scatter plots, histograms, box plots, heatmaps, and exploratory data analysis.

notes.title: NumPy & Pandas for AI/ML
notes.explanation: NumPy provides high-performance multidimensional array operations, while Pandas offers tabular data structures for data manipulation.
definitions: A two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different types in Pandas.
notes.example: Handling missing values and calculating summary statistics on datasets using Pandas DataFrames.
exam_points: Vectorized operations in NumPy execute significantly faster than standard Python loops by running compiled C code.

questions: Explain the difference between NumPy arrays and standard Python lists.
Discuss data cleaning and handling missing values using Pandas.

quiz.question: What primary data structure in Pandas represents a two-dimensional labeled tabular dataset?
quiz.explanation: A DataFrame is a 2-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different data types.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence
objectives: CO1: Understand AI foundations, intelligent agents, and uninformed/informed search strategies.
CO2: Master knowledge representation, propositional logic, first-order logic, and inference.
CO3: Explore probabilistic reasoning, machine learning basics, and natural language processing.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to AI: History, intelligent agents, PEAS framework. Uninformed Search: BFS, DFS, Depth-Limited Search, Iterative Deepening. Informed Search: Greedy Best-First Search, A* search, heuristic functions.
Adversarial Search & Games: Game theory, minimax algorithm, alpha-beta pruning. Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs): Constraint propagation, backtracking search.
Knowledge Representation: Propositional logic, inference rules, first-order logic, unification, resolution. Ontologies and semantic networks.
Probabilistic Reasoning: Uncertainty, conditional probability, Bayes' rule. Introduction to Machine Learning: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, neural networks basics.

notes.title: Heuristic Search Strategies
notes.explanation: Informed search algorithms utilize domain-specific heuristic functions to guide search spaces efficiently toward goal states.
definitions: A heuristic that never overestimates the actual cost to reach the goal.
notes.example: Applying A* search with Euclidean distance heuristics for optimal robot pathfinding.
exam_points: A* search guarantees optimal solutions if the heuristic function is admissible and consistent.

questions: Explain A* search algorithm and prove that an admissible heuristic guarantees optimality.
Discuss minimax game tree search with alpha-beta pruning optimization.

quiz.question: What condition must an evaluation heuristic satisfy in A* search to guarantee finding an optimal path?
quiz.explanation: An admissible heuristic ensures A* never overestimates true remaining path costs, guaranteeing optimality.

subjects.name: Machine Learning
objectives: CO1: Understand supervised and unsupervised machine learning paradigms and data preprocessing.
CO2: Master regression, classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, SVM, Decision Trees), and evaluation metrics.
CO3: Explore clustering, dimensionality reduction (PCA), and ensemble learning methods.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to ML: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, training/testing splits, cross-validation, feature scaling, handling categorical variables, bias-variance tradeoff.

Supervised Learning - Regression & Classification: Linear regression, multiple linear regression, logistic regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees, Random Forests.
Model Evaluation & Optimization: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC curves, hyperparameter tuning using Grid Search and Random Search.
Unsupervised Learning: Clustering algorithms (k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN), Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

notes.title: Supervised Classification Models
notes.explanation: Classification algorithms predict categorical class labels based on input feature vectors.
definitions: A classifier that finds an optimal hyperplane maximizing the margin between data classes in feature space.
notes.example: Training a Support Vector Machine to classify spam versus non-spam emails.
exam_points: Kernel tricks in SVM allow mapping non-linear separable data into higher dimensional spaces.

questions: Explain the working principle of Support Vector Machines and kernel functions.
Compare precision, recall, and F1-score as evaluation metrics for imbalanced classification.

quiz.question: What evaluation metric harmonic mean combines both precision and recall?
quiz.explanation: The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics.

subjects.name: Computer Networks
objectives: CO1: Understand OSI and TCP/IP reference models and physical layer transmission media.
CO2: Master data link layer protocols, error detection/correction, and MAC sublayer protocols.
CO3: Explore network layer routing, IP addressing, transport layer protocols, and application layer services.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Data communication components, OSI and TCP/IP reference models, physical layer transmission media, analog vs. digital signals, bandwidth, and multiplexing.

Data Link Layer: Design issues, framing, error detection and correction (Hamming code, CRC), sliding window protocols. MAC Sublayer: Multiple access protocols (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), Ethernet standards.
Network Layer: Routing algorithms (distance vector, link state), congestion control algorithms, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, subnetting, NAT, routers, and routing protocols (OSPF, BGP).
Transport Layer: Process-to-process communication, UDP, TCP reliable data transfer, congestion control, flow control. Application Layer: DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, and DHCP.

notes.title: Network Layer Routing & IP Addressing
notes.explanation: The network layer manages packet forwarding across interconnected networks using IP addressing and routing algorithms.
definitions: The practice of dividing a single physical network into multiple smaller logical sub-networks.
notes.example: Calculating network and broadcast addresses using CIDR netmask notations.
exam_points: Distance vector routing utilizes the Bellman-Ford algorithm, whereas link state routing uses Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions: Compare distance vector routing with link-state routing algorithms.
Explain IPv4 subnetting and calculate subnet masks for given host requirements.

quiz.question: Which protocol provides reliable, connection-oriented data transmission at the transport layer?
quiz.explanation: TCP ensures reliable, connection-oriented stream delivery with error checking and flow control.

subjects.name: Computer Vision
objectives: CO1: Understand digital image processing fundamentals, filtering, edge detection, and feature extraction.
CO2: Master convolutional neural networks (CNNs), object detection (YOLO), and image segmentation.
CO3: Explore advanced computer vision applications including face recognition, video tracking, and optical flow.

syllabus.topics: Image Processing Basics: Image acquisition, sampling, quantization, color spaces, spatial filtering, edge detection (Sobel, Canny), feature extraction (SIFT, SURF, ORB).
Deep Learning for Vision: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), architecture layers (convolution, pooling, fully connected), activation functions, training optimization.
Object Detection & Segmentation: Region-based CNNs, YOLO (You Only Look Once) architecture, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN).
Advanced Vision Applications: Face recognition, object tracking, optical flow, video analysis, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) in computer vision.

notes.title: Object Detection with YOLO
notes.explanation: YOLO frames object detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly.
definitions: A rectangular coordinate envelope enclosing a detected object instance within an image frame.
notes.example: Detecting and localizing objects in real-time video feeds using YOLOv8 architectures.
exam_points: YOLO divides images into grid cells where each cell predicts bounding boxes and confidence scores.

questions: Explain the architecture and working principle of the YOLO object detection framework.
Differentiate between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation in computer vision.

quiz.question: How does YOLO approach object detection compared to traditional region-proposal methods?
options: As a single regression problem across grid cells
Using exhaustive sliding window template matching
quiz.explanation: YOLO frames object detection as a single regression problem evaluated directly across image grid cells.

subjects.name: Compiler Design
objectives: CO1: Understand phases of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, and finite automata.
CO2: Master parsing techniques including top-down (LL(1)) and bottom-up (LR, LALR) parsers.
CO3: Explore syntax-directed translation, intermediate code generation, and code optimization.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Compilers: Phases of compilation, compiler construction tools. Lexical Analysis: Role of lexical analyzer, tokens, regular expressions, finite automata.
Syntax Analysis: Role of parser, context-free grammars, parse trees. Top-down parsing: LL(1) grammars. Bottom-up parsing: Shift-reduce parsing, SLR, CLR, and LALR parsers.
Syntax-Directed Translation & Intermediate Code: Syntax-directed definitions, evaluation orders, intermediate languages (three-address code, quadruples, triples).
Run-Time Environments & Code Optimization: Storage organization, activation records. Code Optimization: Principal sources of optimization, basic blocks, code generation.

notes.title: Syntax Analysis & Parsing
notes.explanation: Parsers validate token streams against grammar rules, constructing parse trees for semantic analysis.
definitions: A top-down parser that parses input from Left to right, constructs a Leftmost derivation, using 1 lookahead token.
notes.example: Constructing FIRST and FOLLOW sets to build predictive parsing tables for LL(1) grammars.
exam_points: LR parsers are more powerful than LL parsers and handle bottom-up shift-reduce parsing efficiently.

questions: Explain the construction of FIRST and FOLLOW sets for a given context-free grammar.
Differentiate between LL(1) top-down parsing and LR bottom-up parsing.

quiz.question: What parsing table construction method is used for bottom-up LALR parsers?
quiz.explanation: LALR parsers merge LR(1) states having identical LR(0) items and different lookaheads to reduce table size.
