subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations in machine learning models.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating loss functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for dimensionality reduction techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for data covariance matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory for data arrays in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying engineering system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving differential equations using Laplace transform tables.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts. C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading, friend functions.
Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers, inheritance types, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling, file I/O streams.

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS, system calls. Process Management: Process concept, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms.
Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, semaphores, classical synchronization problems. Deadlocks: Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Memory Management: Contiguous memory allocation, paging, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk scheduling algorithms.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence
objectives: CO1: Understand AI foundations, intelligent agents, and uninformed/informed search strategies.
CO2: Master knowledge representation, propositional logic, first-order logic, and inference.
CO3: Explore probabilistic reasoning, machine learning basics, and natural language processing.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to AI: History, intelligent agents, PEAS framework. Uninformed Search: BFS, DFS, Depth-Limited Search, Iterative Deepening. Informed Search: Greedy Best-First Search, A* search, heuristic functions.
Adversarial Search & Games: Game theory, minimax algorithm, alpha-beta pruning. Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs): Constraint propagation, backtracking search.
Knowledge Representation: Propositional logic, inference rules, first-order logic, unification, resolution. Ontologies and semantic networks.
Probabilistic Reasoning: Uncertainty, conditional probability, Bayes' rule. Introduction to Machine Learning: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, neural networks basics.

notes.title: Heuristic Search Strategies
notes.explanation: Informed search algorithms utilize domain-specific heuristic functions to guide search spaces efficiently toward goal states.
definitions: A heuristic that never overestimates the actual cost to reach the goal.
notes.example: Applying A* search with Euclidean distance heuristics for optimal pathfinding.
exam_points: A* search guarantees optimal solutions if the heuristic function is admissible and consistent.

questions: Explain A* search algorithm and prove that an admissible heuristic guarantees optimality.
Discuss minimax game tree search with alpha-beta pruning optimization.

quiz.question: What condition must an evaluation heuristic satisfy in A* search to guarantee finding an optimal path?
quiz.explanation: An admissible heuristic ensures A* never overestimates true remaining path costs, guaranteeing optimality.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets. Relational Model: Relational algebra.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition.
Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Machine Learning
objectives: CO1: Understand supervised and unsupervised machine learning paradigms and data preprocessing.
CO2: Master regression, classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, SVM, Decision Trees), and evaluation metrics.
CO3: Explore clustering, dimensionality reduction (PCA), and ensemble learning methods.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to ML: Supervised vs. unsupervised learning, training/testing splits, cross-validation, feature scaling, handling categorical variables, bias-variance tradeoff.

Supervised Learning - Regression & Classification: Linear regression, multiple linear regression, logistic regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees, Random Forests.
Model Evaluation & Optimization: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC curves, hyperparameter tuning using Grid Search and Random Search.
Unsupervised Learning: Clustering algorithms (k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN), Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

notes.title: Supervised Classification Models
notes.explanation: Classification algorithms predict categorical class labels based on input feature vectors.
definitions: A classifier that finds an optimal hyperplane maximizing the margin between data classes in feature space.
notes.example: Training a Support Vector Machine to classify dataset samples.
exam_points: Kernel tricks in SVM allow mapping non-linear separable data into higher dimensional spaces.

questions: Explain the working principle of Support Vector Machines and kernel functions.
Compare precision, recall, and F1-score as evaluation metrics for imbalanced classification.

quiz.question: What evaluation metric harmonic mean combines both precision and recall?
quiz.explanation: The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics.

subjects.name: Big Data Analytics
objectives: CO1: Understand big data characteristics, Hadoop architecture, and HDFS distributed file systems.
CO2: Master MapReduce distributed computing paradigms and data processing jobs.
CO3: Explore Apache Spark resilient distributed datasets (RDDs), Spark SQL, and big data streaming.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Big Data: 5 Vs of big data, Hadoop ecosystem overview, Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) architecture, NameNode, DataNode blocks.
MapReduce Framework: MapReduce programming model, mappers, reducers, shuffle and sort phase, YARN resource manager.
Apache Spark: Spark architecture, Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs), transformations and actions, lazy evaluation.
Spark SQL & Analytics: Spark DataFrames, SQL queries on big data, introduction to NoSQL databases (MongoDB/HBase).

notes.title: Apache Spark RDDs
notes.explanation: Spark RDDs provide fault-tolerant distributed memory abstractions enabling parallel data processing across clusters.
definitions: An execution strategy where Spark does not compute transformations immediately until an action is called.
notes.example: Applying map and filter transformations on distributed RDD datasets followed by count actions.
exam_points: Transformations are lazy (e.g., map, filter), whereas actions trigger actual pipeline execution (e.g., collect, count).

questions: Explain transformations and actions in Apache Spark RDDs with examples.
Compare MapReduce with Apache Spark processing architectures.

quiz.question: What type of operation triggers actual execution of a computation pipeline in Apache Spark?
quiz.explanation: Actions (like collect() or count()) trigger the execution of lazy transformations in Spark.

subjects.name: Deep Learning
objectives: CO1: Understand neural network architectures, perceptrons, activation functions, and backpropagation.
CO2: Master Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for computer vision and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs, LSTMs) for sequence modeling.
CO3: Explore generative models (GANs, VAEs) and deep learning optimization techniques.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Deep Learning: Artificial neural networks, perceptrons, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), activation functions (ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh), loss functions, gradient descent, backpropagation.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): Convolutional layers, pooling layers, padding, stride, CNN architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet), object detection basics.
Sequence Modeling & RNNs: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), sequence-to-sequence models, attention mechanisms.
Generative Models & Optimization: Regularization (dropout, batch normalization), optimizers (Adam, RMSprop), Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

notes.title: Backpropagation & Neural Networks
notes.explanation: Backpropagation computes gradient errors across neural network weights using the chain rule of calculus.
definitions: A mathematical function applied to neuron outputs introducing non-linearities into neural networks.
notes.example: Applying ReLU activation functions in hidden layers to prevent vanishing gradient problems.
exam_points: The chain rule is applied recursively backward from the output layer to update weights via gradient descent.

questions: Explain the backpropagation algorithm and the role of activation functions in neural networks.
Compare vanishing gradient and exploding gradient problems in deep networks.

quiz.question: What non-linear activation function outputs zero for negative inputs and linear scaling for positive inputs?
quiz.explanation: ReLU outputs max(0, x), mitigating vanishing gradients in deep neural networks.

Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?

CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving differential equations using Laplace transform properties.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?

subjects.name: Data Structure & Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze performance of algorithms using asymptotic notations and time-space trade-offs.
CO2: Implement linear and non-linear data structures including stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees.
CO3: Apply sorting, hashing, and graph traversal algorithms to solve computational problems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Elementary data organizations, data structure operations, algorithm analysis, asymptotic notations, time-space trade-off. Searching: Linear search, binary search, complexity analysis.
Stacks and Queues: ADT stack operations, expression conversion and evaluation. ADT queue types: Simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, operations and algorithms.
Linked Lists and Trees: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists. Tree terminology, binary trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, B-trees, and B+ trees.
Sorting and Hashing: Selection sort, bubble sort, insertion sort, quick sort, merge sort, heap sort, performance comparison, and hashing.
Graph: Basic terminologies, representations, graph search, and traversal algorithms with complexity analysis.

notes.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Searching
notes.explanation: Algorithm efficiency is evaluated using asymptotic notations to measure growth rates of time and space requirements.
definitions: A mathematical notation describing the upper bound of an algorithm's running time complexity.
notes.example: Comparing linear search (O(n)) and binary search (O(log n)) search times on sorted arrays.
exam_points: Binary search requires a pre-sorted array and divides the search space in half during each iteration.

questions: Define asymptotic notations and analyze the time complexity of binary search.
Compare linear search and binary search algorithms with respect to input size.

quiz.question: What data structure operational principle characterizes a Stack?
quiz.explanation: Stacks operate on LIFO principles where the last element inserted is the first one removed.

subjects.name: Object Oriented Programming
objectives: CO1: Understand object-oriented programming paradigms, classes, and objects.
CO2: Implement inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, and operator overloading in C++.
CO3: Manage exceptions, templates, and file input/output streams.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OOP: Procedure-oriented vs. Object-oriented programming, basic concepts. C++ Basics: Data types, operators, control structures, functions, classes, and objects.
Constructors & Operator Overloading: Constructors, parameterized constructors, copy constructors, destructors. Operator overloading, friend functions.
Inheritance & Polymorphism: Derived classes, access specifiers, inheritance types, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, and abstract classes.
Templates, Exception Handling & Files: Function and class templates, exception handling, file I/O streams.

notes.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
notes.explanation: Inheritance promotes code reusability, while polymorphism enables dynamic method dispatch through virtual functions.
definitions: A member function declared within a base class and redefined by a derived class to support dynamic polymorphism.
notes.example: Using base class pointers to invoke overridden derived class methods dynamically.
exam_points: Abstract classes contain at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions: Explain constructors and destructors in C++. Why is a copy constructor required?
Discuss operator overloading in C++ with an example of overloading the binary '+' operator.

quiz.question: Which OOP feature allows creating a new class from an existing class?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance enables derivative classes to inherit attributes and methods from base classes.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand operating system structures, system calls, and process management.
CO2: Analyze CPU scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlock handling mechanisms.
CO3: Manage virtual memory, paging, segmentation, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to OS: Operating system functions, types of OS, system calls. Process Management: Process concept, CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms.
Process Synchronization: Critical section problem, semaphores, classical synchronization problems. Deadlocks: Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Memory Management: Contiguous memory allocation, paging, segmentation. Virtual Memory: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing.
File System & Secondary Storage: File concept, access methods, directory structure, disk scheduling algorithms.

notes.title: Process Synchronization & Deadlocks
notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Internet of Things
objectives: CO1: Understand IoT architecture, sensor and actuator technologies, and smart device connectivity.
CO2: Master IoT communication protocols (MQTT, CoAP, HTTP) and networking layers.
CO3: Explore cloud integration, data analytics, and IoT security applications.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to IoT: Definition, architectural overview, design principles, M2M vs. IoT, smart objects, sensors, actuators, and embedded microcontrollers.
IoT Protocols & Networking: Network and communication layers, IEEE 802.15.4, ZigBee, RFID, NFC, MQTT, CoAP, HTTP/REST protocols.
Cloud & Data Analytics: Cloud computing platforms for IoT, data ingestion, time-series databases, streaming analytics, fog computing, and edge computing.
IoT Security & Applications: Vulnerabilities in IoT, authentication, access control, smart home, smart city, and industrial IoT (IIoT) case studies.

notes.title: MQTT Protocol
notes.explanation: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and low-bandwidth networks.
definitions: A messaging pattern where senders (publishers) do not program messages to specific receivers (subscribers), but categorize them into topics.
notes.example: Transmitting temperature sensor telemetry to an AWS IoT cloud broker over MQTT topics.
exam_points: MQTT operates over TCP/IP and supports three Quality of Service (QoS) levels: 0, 1, and 2.

questions: Explain the publish-subscribe architecture of MQTT and compare QoS levels.
Discuss CoAP protocol and its suitability for constrained IoT environments.

quiz.question: What messaging pattern does the MQTT protocol utilize for lightweight device communication?
quiz.explanation: MQTT uses a publish-subscribe architecture decoupling publishers and subscribers via topic brokers.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets. Relational Model: Relational algebra.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition.
Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Blockchain Technology & Architecture
objectives: CO1: Understand cryptographic hash functions, digital signatures, distributed ledgers, and decentralized consensus.
CO2: Master Bitcoin protocol, transaction mechanics, mining, and smart contracts.
CO3: Explore Ethereum, Hyperledger Fabric, permissioned blockchains, and enterprise applications.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Blockchain: Distributed ledgers, cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256), hash pointers, digital signatures, Merkle trees, and basic consensus mechanisms.
Bitcoin Basics & Mechanics: Bitcoin protocol, transactions, script language, wallets, mining, Proof of Work (PoW), difficulty adjustment, forks, and double-spending prevention.
Ethereum & Smart Contracts: Ethereum virtual machine (EVM), accounts, gas, smart contract development in Solidity, decentralized applications (DApps), and alternative consensus (Proof of Stake).
Permissioned Blockchains & Hyperledger: Hyperledger Fabric architecture, peers, orderers, chaincode design, and enterprise blockchain use cases in supply chain and finance.

notes.title: Cryptographic Hash Functions & Merkle Trees
notes.explanation: Cryptographic hashes ensure data integrity by mapping arbitrary data inputs to fixed-size cryptographic outputs.
definitions: A binary tree where every parent node is a cryptographic hash of its child nodes, allowing efficient and secure verification of large datasets.
notes.example: Verifying transaction inclusion in a Bitcoin block using Merkle proof authentication paths.
exam_points: Collision resistance ensures it is computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs yielding identical hash outputs.

questions: Explain cryptographic hash functions and how Merkle trees ensure data integrity in blockchains.
Compare Proof of Work (PoW) with Proof of Stake (PoS) consensus mechanisms.

quiz.question: What data structure aggregates multiple transaction hashes into a single root hash in blockchain blocks?
quiz.explanation: Merkle trees summarize all transactions in a block into a single root hash for efficient verification.

subjects.name: Cyber Security & Ethical Hacking
objectives: CO1: Understand cybersecurity principles, threat landscapes, vulnerability assessment, and risk management.
CO2: Master reconnaissance, network scanning, system hacking, malware, and web application vulnerabilities.
CO3: Explore cryptography, intrusion detection systems, firewalls, and incident response frameworks.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Cybersecurity: CIA triad, attack vectors, threat modeling, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing phases (reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation).
Network & System Hacking: Port scanning (Nmap), sniffing, ARP spoofing, denial of service (DoS) attacks, password cracking, buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
Web Application Security: OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities (SQL injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), CSRF, session hijacking), web server hardening.
Defense Mechanisms & Cryptography: Symmetric/asymmetric encryption, firewall architectures, Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS), incident response, and digital forensics.

notes.title: OWASP Top 10 & SQL Injection
notes.explanation: SQL injection occurs when untrusted user input is directly concatenated into database query strings, allowing attackers to manipulate queries.
definitions: A code injection vulnerability enabling attackers to execute arbitrary SQL queries on backend databases.
notes.example: Bypassing authentication forms by injecting `' OR '1'='1` into login input fields.
exam_points: Parameterized queries and prepared statements effectively prevent SQL injection vulnerabilities.

questions: Explain SQL injection vulnerability and how parameterized statements prevent it.
Discuss Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) types and mitigation techniques.

quiz.question: What programming practice best prevents SQL injection vulnerabilities in web applications?
options: Using parameterized queries and prepared statements
Encrypting database passwords in plain text
quiz.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL code from user-supplied data parameters, neutralizing injection attacks.

subjects.name: Advanced Cryptography & Blockchain Security
objectives: CO1: Understand advanced cryptographic primitives, zero-knowledge proofs, and secure multiparty computation.
CO2: Master blockchain smart contract security auditing, reentrancy vulnerabilities, and gas optimization.
CO3: Explore privacy-preserving cryptocurrencies, ring signatures, zero-knowledge rollups, and quantum cryptography.

syllabus.topics: Advanced Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), bilinear pairings, zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP), zk-SNARKs, zk-STARKs, and homomorphic encryption.
Smart Contract Security: Common smart contract vulnerabilities (reentrancy, integer overflow/underflow, front-running, access control flaws), static analysis tools, and fuzzing.
Privacy & Anonymity in Blockchains: CoinJoin, ring signatures, Monero privacy protocols, zero-knowledge privacy coins, and blockchain forensics.
Scaling & Quantum Resistance: Layer-2 scaling solutions (State channels, Optimistic rollups, ZK-rollups), cross-chain bridges, and post-quantum cryptography.

notes.title: Smart Contract Reentrancy Vulnerability
notes.explanation: Reentrancy occurs when an untrusted contract calls back into a vulnerable contract before state variables are updated.
definitions: An exploit where a malicious contract repeatedly drains funds from a victim contract by re-entering withdraw functions before balances update.
notes.example: Analyzing the DAO hack exploit caused by recursive fallback calls during Ether withdrawals.
exam_points: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and ReentrancyGuard modifiers prevent reentrancy vulnerabilities.

questions: Explain the reentrancy vulnerability in Solidity smart contracts and how to prevent it using Checks-Effects-Interactions.
Discuss zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) and their role in blockchain privacy and scaling.

quiz.question: What design pattern prevents reentrancy attacks in Solidity smart contracts?
quiz.explanation: Performing all internal checks and state updates before interacting with external contracts prevents reentrancy.

subjects.name: Compiler Design
objectives: CO1: Understand phases of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, and finite automata.
CO2: Master parsing techniques including top-down (LL(1)) and bottom-up (LR, LALR) parsers.
CO3: Explore syntax-directed translation, intermediate code generation, and code optimization.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Compilers: Phases of compilation, compiler construction tools. Lexical Analysis: Role of lexical analyzer, tokens, regular expressions, finite automata.
Syntax Analysis: Role of parser, context-free grammars, parse trees. Top-down parsing: LL(1) grammars. Bottom-up parsing: Shift-reduce parsing, SLR, CLR, and LALR parsers.
Syntax-Directed Translation & Intermediate Code: Syntax-directed definitions, evaluation orders, intermediate languages (three-address code, quadruples, triples).
Run-Time Environments & Code Optimization: Storage organization, activation records. Code Optimization: Principal sources of optimization, basic blocks, code generation.

notes.title: Syntax Analysis & Parsing
notes.explanation: Parsers validate token streams against grammar rules, constructing parse trees for semantic analysis.
definitions: A top-down parser that parses input from Left to right, constructs a Leftmost derivation, using 1 lookahead token.
notes.example: Constructing FIRST and FOLLOW sets to build predictive parsing tables for LL(1) grammars.
exam_points: LR parsers are more powerful than LL parsers and handle bottom-up shift-reduce parsing efficiently.

questions: Explain the construction of FIRST and FOLLOW sets for a given context-free grammar.
Differentiate between LL(1) top-down parsing and LR bottom-up parsing.

quiz.question: What parsing table construction method is used for bottom-up LALR parsers?
quiz.explanation: LALR parsers merge LR(1) states having identical LR(0) items and different lookaheads to reduce table size.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / IoT, Cyber Security & Blockchain Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech CSE (IoT, Cyber Security & Blockchain) engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry security and decentralization problems.
CO2: Design, prototype, test, and deploy secure IoT devices, smart contracts, and cybersecurity defense systems.
CO3: Demonstrate technical documentation, code repositories, and project defense proficiency.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or specialized engineering placement in IoT, cybersecurity, or blockchain firms.
Capstone Project: Design, development, security auditing, and deployment of an integrated IoT, cybersecurity, or blockchain application.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Preparation of technical documentation, GitHub code repositories, smart contract audits, system architecture diagrams, and final defense presentation.

notes.title: Industrial Security & Decentralized Systems
notes.explanation: Capstone projects bridge academic theory with practical enterprise security auditing and decentralized application deployment.
definitions: An integration of security practices into every phase of the software development lifecycle.
notes.example: Deploying secure smart contracts on Ethereum testnets with automated CI/CD vulnerability scanning.
exam_points: Rigorous penetration testing, secure coding standards, and threat modeling ensure robust enterprise deployments.

questions: Describe the architecture, threat mitigation strategies, and implementation details of your capstone project.
Discuss security challenges encountered during smart contract auditing or IoT network deployment.

quiz.question: What software engineering practice integrates security controls throughout all phases of development?
quiz.explanation: DevSecOps integrates security automation and threat analysis directly into software pipelines.

Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating trigonometric functions using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for cryptography and linear transformations.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating characteristic roots and eigenvectors for transformation matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

notes.explanation: Synchronization mechanisms prevent race conditions, while deadlock avoidance algorithms ensure safe resource allocation states.
definitions: An integer variable used for signaling and synchronizing access to shared resources in concurrent processes.
notes.example: Applying Banker's algorithm to test whether allocating resource requests maintains a safe system state.
exam_points: Deadlocks occur when four conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions: Explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock occurrence and discuss Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.
What is a semaphore? Solve the classic producer-consumer problem using semaphores.

quiz.question: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance in operating systems?
quiz.explanation: Banker's algorithm tests resource allocation safety before granting requests to avoid deadlocks.

subjects.name: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
objectives: CO1: Analyze algorithm complexity using asymptotic notations and recurrence relations.
CO2: Apply divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming paradigms.
CO3: Master graph algorithms, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and NP-completeness theory.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Algorithm definition, performance analysis, space and time complexity, asymptotic notations. Recurrence relations, Master theorem.

Divide and Conquer: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen's matrix multiplication. Greedy Algorithms: Knapsack problem, job sequencing, Huffman codes, Minimum Spanning Trees, Dijkstra's shortest path.
Dynamic Programming: Principles, matrix chain multiplication, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Backtracking: N-Queens problem.
Branch and Bound: Traveling salesperson problem, 0/1 knapsack. NP-Completeness: P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard complexity classes.

notes.title: Greedy & Divide-and-Conquer
notes.explanation: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, whereas divide-and-conquer breaks problems into independent sub-problems.
definitions: A property stating that a globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making locally optimal choices.
notes.example: Constructing Minimum Spanning Trees using Kruskal's edge-sorting greedy algorithm.
exam_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and trace it on a sample weighted graph.
Compare greedy algorithms with dynamic programming using fractional versus 0/1 knapsack problems.

quiz.question: Which algorithmic paradigm builds up solutions bottom-up using optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems stored in tables.

subjects.name: Mathematics Foundations for Cryptography
objectives: CO1: Understand number theory fundamentals, divisibility, primes, and modular arithmetic.
CO2: Master congruence relations, Euler's totient function, Chinese remainder theorem, and discrete logarithms.
CO3: Explore finite fields, algebraic structures, and cryptographic math foundations.

syllabus.topics: Number Theory Basics: Divisibility, Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), Euclidean algorithm, prime numbers, fundamental theorem of arithmetic, modular arithmetic.
Congruences: Linear congruences, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat's Little Theorem, Euler's totient function, Euler's theorem.
Algebraic Structures: Groups, rings, fields, finite fields (Galois fields GF(p) and GF(2^n)), polynomial arithmetic over finite fields.
Discrete Logarithms & Cryptographic Foundations: Primitive roots, discrete logarithm problem, quadratic residues, Legendre and Jacobi symbols.

notes.title: Euler's Totient Function & RSA Math
notes.explanation: Euler's totient function counts positive integers up to a given integer n that are relatively prime to n.
definitions: The number of integers between 1 and n inclusive that are coprime to n.
notes.example: Calculating phi(p * q) = (p - 1)(q - 1) for distinct prime numbers p and q in RSA key generation.
exam_points: For any prime p, phi(p) = p - 1.

questions: State and prove Euler's theorem and calculate phi(n) for composite numbers.
Explain the Chinese Remainder Theorem and solve system of congruence equations.

quiz.question: What is the value of Euler's totient function phi(p) when p is a prime number?
quiz.explanation: Since all positive integers less than a prime p are coprime to it, phi(p) = p - 1.

subjects.name: Database Management Systems
objectives: CO1: Understand relational database models, ER modeling, and relational algebra.
CO2: Master SQL queries, integrity constraints, and database normalization (1NF to BCNF).
CO3: Explore transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction: Database system architecture, ER model, entities, attributes, relationship sets. Relational Model: Relational algebra.
Structured Query Language (SQL): DDL, DML, DCL, basic queries, nested queries, joins, views, aggregate functions, integrity constraints, triggers.
Relational Database Design: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure of attributes, normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), lossless decomposition.
Transactions & Concurrency Control: ACID properties, transaction states, schedules, serializability, lock-based protocols (2PL), timestamp-based protocols.

notes.title: Database Normalization
notes.explanation: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and insertion/deletion anomalies by decomposing relations into higher normal forms.
definitions: A stricter version of 3NF requiring that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
notes.example: Decomposing an unnormalized relation violating 2NF into relations with fully functional dependencies.
exam_points: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples are generated when joining decomposed relations.

questions: Define functional dependency and explain normalization up to BCNF with examples.
Discuss Armstrong's axioms and the computation of attribute set closures.

quiz.question: What property ensures that database transactions execute reliably adhering to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability?
quiz.explanation: ACID properties guarantee reliable transaction processing in database management systems.

subjects.name: Cryptography & Network Security
objectives: CO1: Understand classical ciphers, symmetric encryption algorithms (DES, AES), and block cipher modes.
CO2: Master asymmetric cryptography (RSA, Diffie-Hellman), digital signatures, and public key infrastructure.
CO3: Explore network security protocols (IPsec, SSL/TLS), firewalls, and intrusion detection systems.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Cryptography: Security goals (CIA triad), classical ciphers (Caesar, Playfair, Vigenere), symmetric ciphers, Data Encryption Standard (DES), Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), block cipher modes of operation (CBC, ECB, CTR).
Asymmetric Cryptography: Principles of public-key crypto, RSA algorithm, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), digital signature standard (DSS).
Key Management & PKI: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, X.509 certificate standard, key distribution centers, Kerberos authentication.
Network Security Protocols: Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL), HTTPS, IPsec architecture, Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), firewalls, and intrusion detection systems.

notes.title: RSA Asymmetric Cryptography
notes.explanation: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem based on the practical difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers.
definitions: A cryptographic key pair comprising modulus n and encryption exponent e, shared publicly for encryption.
notes.example: Encrypting plaintext message M using ciphertext formula $C = M^e \pmod n$.
exam_points: Decryption uses private exponent d computed as $d \equiv e^{-1} \pmod{\phi(n)}$.

questions: Explain the RSA algorithm for encryption and decryption with mathematical steps.
Discuss Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol and its vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks.

quiz.question: What mathematical hard problem forms the underlying security foundation of the RSA cryptographic algorithm?
quiz.explanation: RSA security relies on the computational difficulty of factoring large composite numbers into prime factors.

subjects.name: Ethical Hacking & Vulnerability Assessment
objectives: CO1: Understand ethical hacking methodologies, reconnaissance, and footprinting techniques.
CO2: Master network scanning, enumeration, vulnerability assessment tools, and system hacking.
CO3: Explore web hacking, wireless network attacks, social engineering, and penetration testing reports.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Ethical Hacking: Legal aspects, hacking phases, footprinting, reconnaissance using Google dorks, DNS enumeration, and network mapping (Nmap).
Scanning & Enumeration: Port scanning techniques, OS fingerprinting, vulnerability scanning (Nessus, OpenVAS), enumeration of SNMP, SMB, and LDAP services.
System & Web Hacking: Password cracking (John the Ripper), privilege escalation, malware analysis, OWASP Top 10 web vulnerabilities, SQL injection, and XSS exploitation.
Wireless & Social Engineering: Wi-Fi cracking (WPA/WPA2, Aircrack-ng), social engineering attacks (phishing, spear phishing), and penetration testing report writing.

notes.title: Reconnaissance & Nmap Scanning
notes.explanation: Reconnaissance gathers intelligence about target systems prior to launching security assessments.
definitions: The comprehensive collection of organization profile data, domain names, and IP address ranges.
notes.example: Executing Nmap SYN stealth scans (`nmap -sS`) to discover active network ports without completing TCP handshakes.
exam_points: SYN scans are stealthy because target servers do not log full connection sessions.

questions: Explain the phases of penetration testing and ethical hacking methodology.
Discuss various Nmap port scanning techniques (SYN scan, UDP scan, ACK scan).

quiz.question: What type of Nmap port scan sends TCP SYN packets and analyzes responses without completing the 3-way handshake?
quiz.explanation: SYN stealth scans send half-open connection probes, making them less likely to be logged by target firewalls.

subjects.name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response
objectives: CO1: Understand digital forensics process, evidence acquisition, chain of custody, and legal frameworks.
CO2: Master file system forensics (FAT, NTFS), disk imaging, memory forensics, and artifact recovery.
CO3: Explore network forensics, log analysis, malware analysis, and incident response procedures.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Digital Forensics: Forensics lifecycle, evidence acquisition principles, chain of custody, legal standards, write blockers, and forensic imaging tools (FTK, EnCase).
File System & Memory Forensics: FAT and NTFS file structures, slack space, deleted file recovery, volatile memory acquisition, Volatility framework for RAM analysis.
Network Forensics & Log Analysis: Packet analysis (Wireshark), firewall logs, IDS/IPS event logs, SIEM tools (Splunk/ELK stack), anomaly detection.
Incident Response: Incident response lifecycle (preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned), malware triage and analysis.

notes.title: Chain of Custody & Forensics
notes.explanation: Chain of custody documents the chronological seizure, custody, control, transfer, analysis, and disposition of digital evidence.
definitions: A bit-stream, sector-by-sector duplicate of a storage medium including deleted files and unallocated space.
notes.example: Using cryptographic hash functions (MD5/SHA-256) to verify bit-stream forensic disk image integrity.
exam_points: Write blockers prevent accidental modification of storage media during forensic acquisition.

questions: Explain the digital forensics process and the importance of chain of custody in legal proceedings.
Discuss volatile memory acquisition and RAM forensics using Volatility framework.

quiz.question: What hardware device ensures digital storage media cannot be modified during forensic data acquisition?
quiz.explanation: Write blockers intercept write commands, ensuring evidence remains unaltered during forensic imaging.

subjects.name: Compiler Design
objectives: CO1: Understand phases of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, and finite automata.
CO2: Master parsing techniques including top-down (LL(1)) and bottom-up (LR, LALR) parsers.
CO3: Explore syntax-directed translation, intermediate code generation, and code optimization.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Compilers: Phases of compilation, compiler construction tools. Lexical Analysis: Role of lexical analyzer, tokens, regular expressions, finite automata.
Syntax Analysis: Role of parser, context-free grammars, parse trees. Top-down parsing: LL(1) grammars. Bottom-up parsing: Shift-reduce parsing, SLR, CLR, and LALR parsers.
Syntax-Directed Translation & Intermediate Code: Syntax-directed definitions, evaluation orders, intermediate languages (three-address code, quadruples, triples).
Run-Time Environments & Code Optimization: Storage organization, activation records. Code Optimization: Principal sources of optimization, basic blocks, code generation.

notes.title: Syntax Analysis & Parsing
notes.explanation: Parsers validate token streams against grammar rules, constructing parse trees for semantic analysis.
definitions: A top-down parser that parses input from Left to right, constructs a Leftmost derivation, using 1 lookahead token.
notes.example: Constructing FIRST and FOLLOW sets to build predictive parsing tables for LL(1) grammars.
exam_points: LR parsers are more powerful than LL parsers and handle bottom-up shift-reduce parsing efficiently.

questions: Explain the construction of FIRST and FOLLOW sets for a given context-free grammar.
Differentiate between LL(1) top-down parsing and LR bottom-up parsing.

quiz.question: What parsing table construction method is used for bottom-up LALR parsers?
quiz.explanation: LALR parsers merge LR(1) states having identical LR(0) items and different lookaheads to reduce table size.

subjects.name: Semester Industrial Training / Cyber Security Capstone Project
objectives: CO1: Apply cumulative B.Tech CSE (Cyber Security) engineering knowledge to solve real-world industry security and threat mitigation problems.
CO2: Design, implement, test, and audit secure enterprise systems, intrusion detection frameworks, and penetration testing tools.
CO3: Demonstrate technical documentation, code repositories, and project defense proficiency.

syllabus.topics: Industry Internship: Full-time industrial training or cybersecurity engineering placement in approved IT organizations or security firms.
Capstone Project: Design, development, vulnerability assessment, and deployment of a secure cybersecurity application or defense system.
Project Report & Viva Voce: Preparation of technical documentation, GitHub code repositories, security audit logs, system architecture diagrams, and final defense presentation.

notes.title: Industrial Cyber Defense & SecOps
notes.explanation: Capstone projects bridge academic theory with practical enterprise security auditing and incident response automation.
definitions: Software solutions providing real-time analysis of security alerts generated by applications and network hardware.
notes.example: Deploying intrusion detection rules and automated log aggregation using ELK stack pipelines.
exam_points: Rigorous vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, and secure coding practices ensure robust enterprise deployments.

questions: Describe the architecture, threat mitigation strategies, and implementation details of your capstone cybersecurity project.
Discuss security challenges encountered during vulnerability assessment or incident response testing.

quiz.question: What enterprise software solution aggregates and analyzes log data in real time to detect security threats?
quiz.explanation: SIEM systems aggregate security telemetry across networks to detect anomalies and trigger incident alerts.

aliases: semester industrial training / cyber security capstone project

B.Tech. ME.full_name: Bachelor of Technology in Mechanical Engineering (B.Tech. Mechanical Engineering)

subjects.name: Mathematics-I (Calculus & Linear Algebra)
objectives: CO1: Apply differential and integral calculus concepts to engineering problems.
CO2: Solve ordinary differential equations of first and higher orders.
CO3: Understand matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and linear transformations.

syllabus.topics: Calculus: Limit, continuity, and differentiability, Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's series. Evaluation of definite and improper integrals.
Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, total derivative, Euler's theorem, maxima and minima, Jacobian.
Ordinary Differential Equations: First order differential equations, exact equations, linear differential equations of higher order with constant coefficients.
Matrices: Rank of a matrix, elementary transformations, system of linear equations, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

notes.title: Calculus & Series Expansions
notes.explanation: Calculus forms the foundation for analyzing continuous change, optimization, and function approximations in mechanical engineering systems.
definitions: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point.
notes.example: Approximating kinematic motion equations using Maclaurin polynomial expansions.
exam_points: Rolle's theorem requires a function to be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b).

notes.title: Matrices & Eigenvalues
notes.explanation: Matrix algebra and eigenvalue analysis are essential for solving multi-degree-of-freedom mechanical vibration systems.
definitions: A scalar lambda associated with a linear system of equations such that Av = lambda*v.
notes.example: Calculating natural frequencies and mode shapes for structural vibration matrices.
exam_points: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions: State and verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x^3 - 4x on interval [0,2].
Expand e^x * sin(x) in powers of x using Maclaurin's theorem.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]].
Verify Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a given 3x3 matrix and compute its inverse.

quiz.question: What theorem states that if f(x) is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), there exists c such that f'(c)=0?
quiz.explanation: Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point where the derivative equals zero under those conditions.

quiz.question: What does the Cayley-Hamilton theorem establish for any square matrix A?
options: A satisfies its own characteristic equation
The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: The theorem proves that replacing lambda with matrix A in its characteristic polynomial yields a zero matrix.

subjects.name: Programming for Problem Solving
objectives: CO1: Understand computer hardware, software, and basic algorithmic problem solving.
CO2: Master C programming fundamentals including control structures, arrays, and functions.
CO3: Implement pointers, structures, unions, and file handling operations in C.

syllabus.topics: Introduction to Programming: Computer system components, algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code. C fundamentals: Data types, operators, input/output statements.
Control Statements & Arrays: Conditional branching (if, switch), loops (while, for, do-while), 1D and 2D arrays, character strings and string manipulation functions.
Functions & Pointers: Function declaration, definition, recursion, parameter passing by value and reference. Pointers: Pointer arithmetic, dynamic memory allocation.
Structures, Unions & File Handling: User-defined data types, structures, arrays of structures, unions, file I/O operations.

notes.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
notes.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses, enabling efficient array traversal and dynamic memory allocation in engineering calculations.
definitions: A variable whose value is the address of another location in computer memory.
notes.example: Using malloc() and free() to allocate dynamic memory for numerical simulation data in C.
exam_points: Passing arguments by reference allows functions to modify original caller variables directly.

questions: Explain call by value versus call by reference in C functions with code examples.
Discuss dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) in C.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access the memory address of a variable in C?
quiz.explanation: The address-of operator (&) returns the memory address of a variable.

subjects.name: Mathematics-II (Differential Equations & Numerical Methods)
objectives: CO1: Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms.
CO2: Apply vector calculus including gradient, divergence, curl, and integral theorems.
CO3: Solve algebraic, transcendental, and differential equations using numerical methods.

syllabus.topics: Laplace Transforms: Definition, properties, evaluation of integrals by Laplace transform, inverse Laplace transforms, convolution theorem, solution of ordinary differential equations.
Vector Calculus: Gradient, divergence, and curl, vector identities, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems.
Numerical Methods-I: Solution of algebraic and transcendental equations (Bisection, Regula-Falsi, Newton-Raphson methods), finite differences, interpolation.
Numerical Methods-II: Numerical differentiation and integration, numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (Euler's, Runge-Kutta methods).

notes.title: Laplace Transforms
notes.explanation: Laplace transforms convert linear differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying dynamic control system analysis.
definitions: An integral transform converting a function of time t to a function of complex frequency s.
notes.example: Solving mechanical spring-mass-damper transient differential equations using Laplace transforms.
exam_points: The convolution theorem evaluates inverse transforms of products of transformed functions.

questions: Find the Laplace transform of t^2 * e^(-3t) sin(2t).
State and prove the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms.

quiz.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t-a)?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace transform of u(t-a) is e^(-as)/s by the shifting property.

subjects.name: Fluid Mechanics
objectives: CO1: Understand the concept of fluids and their physical properties.
CO2: Solve problems related to fluid statics, kinematics, and dynamics.
CO3: Apply dimensional analysis and similitude techniques to fluid flow phenomena.

syllabus.topics: Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics: Introduction, continuum concept, ideal and real fluids, fluid properties (density, viscosity, surface tension, compressibility), Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids.
Fluid Statics: Pascal's law, hydrostatic pressure, buoyant force, submerged surfaces, metacenter and metacentric height determination, liquid subjected to linear and rotational acceleration.

Fluid Kinematics: Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions, velocity and acceleration, streamlines, pathlines, streaklines, continuity equation in Cartesian and cylindrical coordinates, vorticity, stream function.

Fluid Dynamics & Internal Flows: Euler's equation, Bernoulli's equation, Navier-Stokes equations introduction, laminar and turbulent flows, Hagen-Poiseuille equation, Darcy-Weisbach equation, pipe friction losses.

notes.title: Fluid Properties & Viscosity
notes.explanation: Fluid properties dictate how fluids respond to shear stresses and pressure gradients.
definitions: A fluid's internal resistance to shear or gradual deformation by shear stress or tensile stress.
notes.example: Calculating shear stress in Newtonian lubricating oils using Newton's law of viscosity.
exam_points: Dynamic viscosity units are Pa·s or Poise, whereas kinematic viscosity is measured in Stokes.

questions: Define Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids with stress-strain rate graphs.
Explain surface tension and capillarity phenomena with mathematical derivations.

quiz.question: What law states that shear stress is directly proportional to velocity gradient in Newtonian fluids?
quiz.explanation: Newton's law of viscosity states tau = mu * (du/dy) for Newtonian fluids.

subjects.name: Theory of Machines - I
objectives: CO1: Understand constructional and working features of machine linkages and mechanisms.
CO2: Design belt, rope, and chain drives for mechanical power transmission.
CO3: Construct cam profiles for specified follower motion and analyze governors and brakes.

syllabus.topics: Basic Concepts: Link, mechanism, kinematic pair, kinematic chain, inversions of four-bar chain, slider-crank chain. Graphical and analytical displacement, velocity, and acceleration analysis.
Lower and Higher Pairs: Universal joint, steering mechanisms (Ackerman and Davis steering), straight-line mechanisms, pantograph, engine indicators.
Belts, Ropes & Chains: Flat and V-belt drives, centrifugal tension, initial tension, power transmission capacity, chain drives and rope drives.
Cams & Followers: Types of cams and followers, follower motion (SHM, uniform velocity, uniform acceleration), cam profile synthesis.

notes.title: Kinematic Chains & Mechanisms
notes.explanation: Kinematic chains translate constrained relative motion from input links to output links.
definitions: A mechanism obtained by fixing different links of a kinematic chain sequentially.
notes.example: Obtaining reciprocating engine mechanisms by fixing the cylinder block link of a slider-crank chain.
exam_points: Grubler's criterion for planar mechanisms is given by DOF = 3(n - 1) - 2j - h.

questions: State and explain Grubler's criterion for degree of freedom of mechanisms.
Discuss inversions of a single slider-crank chain with practical engineering applications.

quiz.question: What formula calculates the degree of freedom (DOF) for planar mechanisms with lower pairs?
quiz.explanation: Grubler's criterion for planar mechanisms is DOF = 3(n - 1) - 2j - h.

subjects.name: Strength of Materials - I
objectives: CO1: Understand mechanical behavior of materials under axial, shear, and torsional loads.
CO2: Calculate bending moments, shear forces, and stresses in beams.
CO3: Analyze principal stresses, strain energy, and column buckling.

syllabus.topics: Simple Stresses and Strains: Hooke's law, stress-strain diagrams for ductile and brittle materials, elastic constants (Young's modulus, shear modulus, bulk modulus, Poisson's ratio), thermal stresses.

Shear Force and Bending Moment: Shear force and bending moment diagrams for statically determinate beams under various loading conditions (point loads, udl, uvl), relation between load, shear force, and bending moment.
Bending and Shear Stresses in Beams: Theory of simple bending, neutral axis, bending stress equation, section modulus, shear stress distribution across rectangular, circular, and I-sections.
Torsion & Principal Stresses: Torsion of circular shafts, polar moment of inertia, torsional rigidity. Principal stresses and strains, Mohr's circle graphical method.

notes.title: Stress-Strain Relations & Elastic Constants
notes.explanation: Elastic constants relate longitudinal and lateral strains under multi-axial stress states.
definitions: The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial tensile stress.
notes.example: Determining volumetric strain in cylindrical pressure vessels using bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio.
exam_points: Relation between elastic constants: E = 2G(1 + nu) = 3K(1 - 2nu).

questions: Derive the relationship between Young's modulus (E), shear modulus (G), and bulk modulus (K).
Explain stress-strain curves for mild steel with salient yield points.

quiz.question: What elastic relation connects Young's modulus E, shear modulus G, and Poisson's ratio nu?
quiz.explanation: The standard elasticity relation is E = 2G(1 + nu).

subjects.name: Basic Thermodynamics
objectives: CO1: Understand fundamental laws of thermodynamics, work, and heat interactions.
CO2: Apply the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics to closed and open systems.
CO3: Analyze entropy, availability, thermodynamic cycles, and pure substance properties.

syllabus.topics: Fundamental Concepts: Thermodynamic system, state, property, process, cycle, thermodynamic equilibrium, zeroth law of thermodynamics, temperature scales, work and heat transfer.
First Law of Thermodynamics: First law applied to closed systems, internal energy, first law applied to steady-flow open systems (flow energy, enthalpy, steady flow energy equation).
Second Law of Thermodynamics: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, equivalence of statements, Carnot cycle, Carnot theorem, entropy, Clausius inequality, principle of entropy increase.
Properties of Pure Substances & Gas Power Cycles: P-v-T surfaces, dryness fraction, steam tables, Otto, Diesel, and Dual cycles performance analysis.

notes.title: First Law & Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE)
notes.explanation: The First Law of Thermodynamics establishes the conservation of energy principle across open engineering flow devices.
definitions: A thermodynamic property defined as internal energy plus the product of pressure and volume (H = U + pV).
notes.example: Applying SFEE to calculate turbine power output and compressor work requirements.
exam_points: For nozzles and diffusers, heat and work interactions are zero, simplifying SFEE to kinetic and enthalpy energy balances.

questions: State the First Law of Thermodynamics for closed systems and derive Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE).
Prove that energy is a property of a thermodynamic system.

quiz.question: What thermodynamic property equals internal energy plus flow work (pressure times volume)?
quiz.explanation: Enthalpy (H) is defined as U + pV, representing total energy associated with flowing fluids.
